en: The Cakrasaṃvara Tantra: The First Chapter, the Procedure for Entering the Maṇḍala. Om, homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara!
Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret [teaching] in brief and not in detail:
the union with Śrī Heruka, which accomplishes all desires and aims. (1)
A Commentary on the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara. Homage to the glorious Cakrasaṃvara!
O Hara, destroyer of passion, do not sink into the ocean of attachment; O Hari, do not consort with the serpent of hatred.
"Do not remain in the snare of delusion; O Brahmā, O Enemy of Bala, do not conceal the fire of envy!
Delight in Mind-Only, which is devoid of self and cause, and free from aspiration.
May Heruka, whose glorious body is thus revealed through these four faces, protect the world by bestowing this instruction.
For those yogis who possess faith and reasoning, afflictions such as leprosy and other physical and mental diseases come to an end through this treatise.
Who is capable of measuring the jewels of excellence contained within this treatise?
Who is able to perform the counting of the drops of water in the ocean?
This temple is like that of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), an inaccessible treasury of riches;
it is as if this very system (tantra) were the mental palace uttered by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi).
The meaning was entrusted to me, dull-witted as I am, by my teachers;
just as a treasure is found even when deposited within a heap of ashes.
If it were not stolen by lack of vigilance— as if by a thief who has forgotten to carry his weapon— I shall now explain it by dividing it.
The meaning of the words [of the Tantra] is indeed difficult to grasp firmly by one whose intellect is intent on total destruction;
without instruction, the private study of the Tantra is like placing fire inside a jar.

For nowhere is activity observed to occur without the perception of a purpose. And so it is said: "Of every scripture or any action whatsoever, as long as the purpose has not been stated, the reasoning [of others] is not accepted."
For even one of dull intellect does not engage in a means without perceiving a purpose,
according to the saying: "Indeed, not even a dull-witted person applies his mind without aiming at an effect."
Therefore, for those engaged in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, that [text] must be explained by the commentators as a constituent part of the practice (*pravṛttyaṅga*). Thus it has been said:

"The purpose, the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*), the meaning of the words (*padārtha*) along with their connections, the objection, and the resolution—these are to be stated by those who expound the meaning of the sūtras" (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 1.12–13).
And that is well-explained by first providing the statement of the names and so forth;
moreover, this has been stated by the Blessed One himself through such phrases as "atha ata" (now, therefore).
Therefore, we shall now explain the pairs of words here, and we will relate that.

The summarized meaning, however, should be expanded upon through reflection based on the very proof stated in the verse beginning with "from the position" (*pakṣāt sūtra*), and the explanation of the word-meanings and so forth should follow the method of commentary.
The teacher is Mahāvajradhara, who will assume the form of the four-faced one and others in the future.
And he himself resides directly within the state of emanation.

This tantra, existing as something to be revealed since beginningless time, sometimes becomes obscured due to the lack of merit in sentient beings, and at other times it manifests through their merit.
Furthermore, this inconceivable conduct of the Tathāgatas is like an illusion consisting of the taught, the teacher,
and so forth. Moreover, the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī is the requester, and Vajrapāṇi is the compiler.
It is generally handed down because it is his teaching.
Alternatively, the tantra—which expresses the entirety of the meaning, such as the four faces and so forth, and the teachings pertaining to each part of the body—is established.
The Sugatas teach [it], but they do not create [it].
Just as [the relationship between] cause and effect, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion, and merit and demerit [are established], so it is said here:
"The well-spoken words of ten million Buddhas and of ten million heroes. Elsewhere it is stated:
That which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, which the future ones will speak,
and which the perfectly awakened ones of the present speak again and again— [that is this].
"That which is fully proclaimed in this *Māyājāla-mahātantra*" (Nāmasaṃgīti 1.12–13).
Here, "speaking" (*bhāṣaṇa*) refers specifically to teaching (*deśanā*).
The *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Tantra* descends, being taught for an unlimited time through the cognition of identical words and so forth, both in terms of meaning and in terms of the text.
Desiring to teach that very [tantra], the Blessed One said: "Now, therefore," and so forth.

For the sake of those who have devotion to the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*, the Blessed One—having been requested by Vajravārāhī—extracts this from the root tantra consisting of one hundred thousand [verses] and teaches it, for [beings] have a preference for brevity. Thus, [the text begins with] the Blessed One...
This response begins with "atha ataḥ" and so forth.
The word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
The word *ataḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) used with the elision of a verbal suffix ending in *-lyap*.
The connection is as follows: immediately after the teaching of the Root Tantra, taking that very Root Tantra as the basis, I shall explain the secret.
For it is from that [Root Tantra] that the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Tantra* can be translated into another language, since its meaning is fully contained within this very [text].
The difference, however, lies merely in the brevity of the text.
Alternatively, it should be construed as follows: "Because I have been requested by Vajravārāhī, for that reason I shall speak the secret.
This is because the word "listen" (*śṛṇu*) in the tantra refers specifically to the act of requesting.
It is not better for one who has not been requested to teach the Dharma, because teaching the Dharma out of pride can give rise to a lack of respect.
If it is asked, "What is the rule that the requester must be a goddess? [the answer follows].
For it is heard from the lineage of gurus in the Root Tantra that she alone is the requester;
therefore, it is understood that she alone is so here as well.
Some, however, maintain that the Blessed Lord is the requester and the Blessed Lady is the teacher.
For the intention of the Tathāgatas is indeed inconceivable;
it is a secret,
for their time, place, and nature are not within the sphere of all people.
Time is that which is past and so forth;
it is a specific temporal state expressible by words such as "tu" (but/however) and the like.
Space is a location.
It is denoted by such terms as "the secret" (*rahasya*) and so forth.
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is its own form,
and that consists of the characteristics of the place for the meditation on Śrī Heruka, the observance of commitments (*samaya*), the formal request for instruction, worship, and so on.
Alternatively, Mahāvajradhara is denoted by the word "secret" (rahas), because his nature is not accessible to all people;
therefore, since he is beyond the comprehension of ordinary folk, he possesses solitude.
In that regard, there is the secret (rahasya).

And whatever is to be expressed therein— including the meditation on Śrī Heruka accompanied by twenty-four heroes and thirty-seven heroines, as well as the places of practice, the commitments, the conduct, and so forth—
this alone is therefore the subject matter (abhidheya).
And this very [work] is the body of the meaning of the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*.
"I shall speak" means I shall make it the body of the expression.
Making the expression the body is itself the illumination of the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
Therefore, there is a relationship between the designation and the designated, characterized as that of the signifier and the signified.
Herein, the purpose of the designation is the communication of the designated object without error;
and the purpose of the designated object is the direct realization of that very same object once it has been fully understood.
And its purpose is the accomplishment of the welfare of the world through teaching and so forth.
That which has been directly realized in solitude can be communicated to another.
Alternatively, the relationship is characterized by the means (upāya) and the goal (upeya).
The means (*upāya*) taught here is characterized by the maṇḍala-circle and so forth;
it is "conducive" because the objects of enjoyment are practiced according to one's inclination.
The goal (*upeya*) is non-abiding nirvāṇa.
And so it has been said:

"A statement that is consistent with a connection [to reality], possesses a means [to achieve an end], expresses a human goal, and is subject to critical examination is authoritative; anything other than this is not authoritative."

If it is argued that since I have already made a concise request for the sake of the essential meaning, that very [meaning] was stated in order to dispel doubts regarding Vajravārāhī, then he says: "In brief" (*samāsāt*).
"Brief" (*samāsa*) here signifies a collection of all [points] in a condensed sense.
To the question, "What is that [meant] in terms of meaning or in terms of the text?", he says: "But not in detail" (*na tu vistarāt*).
The particle *na* is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and not for the purpose of including both the meaning and the word.
The compound is formed with the word in order to exclude doubt regarding the meaning, not regarding the meaning itself.
The intention is that only the compounding of the text is intended.
"How is it known that there is no condensation of meaning? To this he says: "Because of the elaboration.
Elaboration has been accepted here; if the meaning were condensed in this [work], then the intended purpose would not be accomplished.
The *Khasamatantra* would not have been brought forth [separately].
For those who are devoted to it, the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaratantra* is its mantra, being condensed in its textual form as the very *Khasama*.
Indeed, the Teacher’s instruction is governed by the liberation from objects.
For it is thus: for those to be disciplined by passion and the like, there is indeed the teaching of passion and the like.
And so it has been said: "Just as those burned by fire are again purified by fire."
"Likewise, those burned by the fire of passion perspire from the flame of passion.
There is no other evil in the three realms equal to dispassion;
therefore, you should never practice dispassion.
Explaining that very same previously mentioned meaning with some further detail by means of the term "secret" (*rahasya*), he says "Śrī," and so forth.
Conventionally, the application of arms, faces, and so on, is "union" (*saṃyoga*);
the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an action.
The syllable Śrī denotes the state of non-duality;
the syllable He denotes the emptiness of causes and so forth; and the syllable Ru denotes the absence of aspiration.

The letter *ka* signifies that it does not abide anywhere; thus "Śrī Heruka" is established. Regarding this, it is said: the syllable *śrī* is non-dual gnosis, and *ha* is the emptiness of causes and so forth.
The syllable *ka* is free from conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*); as *ka*, it does not abide anywhere. Furthermore: the syllable *śrī* is non-dual gnosis; the syllable *he* is devoid of cause;
the syllable *ru* is liberated from form; and the syllable *ka* is conquered by means of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
It is called *rūpa* because it is affected (*rūpyate*).
The instrument is the sense faculty and so forth. Alternatively:
"He who has conquered the enemies that are the Māras with his roar, filling the quarters of space with it..."
Being liberated from the web of conceptual construction, he is celebrated as Heruka.
Thus is Heruka.
Śrī is Vajravārāhī; Heruka joined with her is Śrīheruka.
This is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*).
For example, a mantra that removes fever is called a "fever-mantra" (*jvaramantra*).
Indeed, the relationship between qualifier and qualified arises precisely from the intention to specify the conjunction itself as the object to be qualified.
"Śrīheruka" and "union" (saṃyoga) constitute that [term]; thus, it is so called.
"Śrīheruka" is one part of the referent of the word "secret" (rahasya).
The connection with the preceding action is simply "I shall speak of that."

Having indicated Śrī Heruka as one who has accomplished his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpanna*), the author speaks—beginning with "all," etc.—to further qualify him by way of his accomplishment of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*).
"All" refers to beings, whether enemies, friends, or neutrals, or gods, asuras, and so forth; their "desires" (*kāma*) are longings, that is to say, wishes.
Their object (artha) is the domain (viṣaya).
And that consists in the attainment of non-existent happiness, the non-separation from what is non-existent, and the non-occurrence of what is non-existent.
Its accomplisher is the one who realizes it directly. || 1 ||
Even higher than the highest is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, which abides eternally within the self of all, in the supreme and most delightful secret. (2)
He asks whether this means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) or common (*sādhāraṇa*), and says:
"Superior even to the superior," and so forth. For the excellence of the union with Śrī Heruka is the factor that impels one toward practice.
Because even for those who are devoted to what is not supreme, there is a lack of engagement due to the demonstration that it is not supreme;
nor do they have the notion of supremacy regarding it.
And because even for those who are devoted to what is supreme, there is engagement due to the demonstration that it is indeed supreme.
For this is their inherent nature (dharmatā) that what is described as uncommon [is so];
for there certainly exist other deities who are superior, and the meaning is that this deity Śrī Heruka is superior even to those who are superior.

Alternatively, by the phrase "the Blessed One is superior to the Śrāvakas and others due to his possession of the accumulations of extraordinary merit and gnosis," the perfection of his own welfare and the perfection of his means are demonstrated.
To the question, "Why is he progressively superior? he says: "The Ḍākinī," and so forth.
She is called a Ḍākinī because her nature (*śīla*) is to seize (*ḍātuṃ*) and internalize non-referential gnosis (*jñāna*).
By means of the etymological derivation involving the letter *ka*, the term *ḍākinī* is established.

Since the verbal root *ḍai*, meaning "to move through the air," is employed here, those who possess the means [of attainment] similar to birds—which move through the sky (*vihāyasaḥ*)—are themselves called "those of the sky" (*vihāyasaḥ*). They traverse the supportless path by means of their wings, and likewise, the yogins directly realize the supportless gnosis through skillful means.
Their knowledge is that of the sky;
therein lies movement and staying. Here, the root *gam* has the sense of "staying."
And that is rest:
having directly realized non-referential gnosis, there is the cessation of movement elsewhere,
because at that time nothing else exists.
Because that gnosis has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*);
*ḍākinī* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the "net" (*jāla*) is skillful means (*upāya*).

For by means of a net, the capture of fish and other creatures is accomplished; and by means of a skillful method (*upāya*), the fish of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth are restrained and rendered powerless. Because it protects (*saṃvṛṇoti*) bliss (*sukha*) from those defects that lie outside, it is called the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.

Because the term *saṃ* denotes happiness (*sukha*), it is "happiness" (*saṃ*); for it is stated [in scripture]: "It is called *saṃ* because it is happiness. This worldly word *śam*, moreover, is purely palatal (*tālavya*).
Alternatively, it is a verbal root (*dhātu*) because it maintains (*dadhāti*) within itself the manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) of the *Ḍākinīs*, such as *Lāmā* and others.
By means of this perfection of the method for accomplishing the welfare of others, there is a detailed explanation of every term.
Herein, "connection" (*sandhi*) refers to the underlying intention; "objection" (*codya*) refers to the turning back of what has been heard or reflected upon;
and "question" (*praśna*) is posed by way of its opposite.
The "refutation" (*parihāra*) is the removal of objections; it should be inferred for oneself according to the context of what has been said or will be said.
To the question, "Where situated shall I speak all this?", he says: "The secret," and so forth.

By the word "secret" (*rahas*), there are the thirty-seven yoginīs—the thirty-six *cakravartinīs* together with the one *vīra*, both those with heroes (*savīrā*) and those without heroes (*nirvīrā*)—known as the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, body, and the cremation ground.
In this context, "rahasa" means "secret"; the meaning is that it is suitable for the abiding of the yoginīs.
And that is the gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*).
To the question "What is the use of this?", he says: "Supreme" (*parama*).
The supreme is *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, it is "supreme" (*paramam*) because it is not surpassed (*na atyasya*) by anything whatsoever due to its being the ultimate task (*kāryatvena*). Or else, "others" (*pare*) refers to enemies,
and those are the afflictions (*kleśāḥ*).
And because by means of it others are measured, fully measured, and rendered insignificant, it is "supreme" (parama).
It is "delightful" (ramya) because one delights (ramyate) by means of it.
Because it appears like an illusion;

because it is but a single part of this [Reality], even though it is beautiful, there is no happiness in every respect even when it is directly perceived—thus he says, "in its entirety" (*sarvātmani*).
That which has the Self (*ātman*) in all things, whether stable or moving, is the "palace of Being" (*sattvātma-kūṭāgāra*).
Established therein, he is turned away from going elsewhere, because there is no other destination apart from that; "always" means as long as saṃsāra lasts. || 2 ||
The being composed of all ḍākinīs is Vajrasattva, the supreme bliss;
for he is the self-arisen Blessed One, the Hero, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. (3)
"Abiding" (sthiti) means "place" (sthāna).
He says "all ḍākinīs," etc., to show that even when [the state] is accomplished, it is not merely a matter of attaining a place;
for all ḍākinīs—such as Ḍākinī, Lāmā, and so forth—are constituent parts of that [state].
Because they have the nature of the applications of mindfulness, such as the mindfulness of the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*),
its greatness consists in being a constituent part of them. Alternatively, [it is] "in brief" (*samāsataḥ*).
By saying, "The speaker who speaks the truth attains authority," he addresses the assembly with the words beginning with "all ḍākinīs.
He states that there is no greatness in the teacher due to his failure to act for the benefit of others by saying "sattva" (being).
He is called a *sattva* because he is engaged in performing the welfare of sentient beings.
Nevertheless, he says "Vajrasattva" to show that for one whose meaning is not yet ascertained, it is not so;
the sense is that his intention is indivisible and his conviction is indivisible.
He says "supreme" (*parama*) because even liberation does not shine forth for one whose resolve is unbreakable.
It is "supreme" (*paramam*) because it delights in the supreme goal (*parārtha*);
this is an adverbial modifier.

The meaning is that he is Vajrasattva in the ultimate sense. He says "bliss" (*sukham*) because even conceptualization regarding the ultimate truth is not sufficient for the establishment of the object; [here] *su* means "well" and *kha* means "void" (*śūnya*).
Because it is free from attachment to both the ultimate and the non-ultimate;
this too is an adverbial modifier. The connection is: "I, endowed with the excellence of place and so forth, shall explain the union of Śrī Heruka."
Anticipating the objection, "If you have not directly realized the union with Śrī Heruka, how can you speak of it?", he says "asau" and so forth; here,
*hi* functions as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
This very [work] is the *Śrīherukasaṃyoga*.
"I myself, by my own self, shall speak the *Śrīherukasaṃyoga*"—
the meaning is that it is through the instruction of that very [deity] when the form of the *Śrīherukasaṃyoga* has been directly realized.
And this being so, he says "the Self-Become" (*svayambhū*) to show that you are not merely one who abides in the stages of virtue (*guṇasthāna*).

To the question, "How could I be such a ground (*bhū*) for the qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)?", he says "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*). [The Blessed One is defined by:
"Sovereignty in its entirety, beauty, fame, glory..."
"Furthermore, the traditional teaching (smṛti) holds that 'bhaga' refers to the six qualities consisting of knowledge and effort. Because he possesses these *bhagas*, he is "Bhagavān," O Haṃ.
To the question "From what does his state of being Bhagavān arise? he says: "The Hero."
He is a hero because he causes the afflictions to tremble;
thus it is said: "The Blessed One is so called because he shatters the four Māras, beginning with the afflictions.
This refers to the destruction of the Māras of the afflictions, the aggregates, death, and the son of a god.
Furthermore: "He says that *bhaga* is 'breaking' because of the breaking of the Māras of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
To the question "Why is there this very breaking of the afflictions? he says: "*Ḍākinī*, etc.
*Ḍākinī* is wisdom (*prajñā*).
And that [wisdom] consists of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and the nature of suchness (*tathatā*). "Net" (*jāla*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*);
from that, the restraint (*saṃvara*) or protection of the mind by means of the *ḍākinī* acting as the instrument is the "restraint of the net," which is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
The Hero speaks of the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* exactly as it is;
that is to say, he will explain the union with Śrī Heruka.
Accordingly, he says: "Those afflictions which are to be abandoned by wisdom—therefore, wisdom is called the Blessed One (*bhagā*)."
And from them comes victory over the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the protection of the mind;
for even though "net" (*jāla*) has the meaning of delusion (*moha*), all afflictions are included therein, since the root of the afflictions is the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Thus it is said:
The origin of all classes of defects is from the view of a self-identity;
that [view] is ignorance, from which arises attachment, and from that, the occurrence of defects and so forth.
"It is said that delusion alone is the cause of the defects,
for they are abandoned through its abandonment, except in the case of the view of a self-identity.
The meaning is that when the efficient cause exists, the effect must exist.
The collective meaning is: "I shall speak of that very same union with Śrī Heruka, which has become the assembly of all ḍākinīs.

Regarding the term *svayambhū* (self-arisen), some maintain that it exists by itself through the relationship of cause and effect and so forth; however, the intended sense is that it does not arise from cause and effect.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is not an effect produced [by causes], because there is no arising of what is either existent or non-existent.
Because that which already exists does not arise, since it is already present, like the entity designated as the cause.
If there were re-arising,
it would follow that existence does not cease;
or else, if there were cessation, [it would follow that there is no re-arising].
If there is the production of something unprecedented due to the destruction of what existed previously, it is not the arising of that which already exists.
In that case, let there indeed be the destruction of the former and the production of the unprecedented; nevertheless, it is the production of something that was [already] existent.
If it is argued that there is the production of something previously non-existent, we say no; for by [the existence of] what is already existent, its "previousness" is lost.

Indeed, if the previous existent is abandoned, then because it would already exist, its production—like that of something non-existent—is impossible; thus, there is no production of the existent either.
And if there is no arising of that which already exists, how can it be said to exist?
For rabbit's horns and the like, being unarisen, do not exist;
for existence is characterized by causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*).

If they are of no use in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), eternal entities are not to be accepted by anyone seeking such action, just like a human horn and the like. Alternatively, if [purposeful action] exists [already], it cannot arise from them, because that has been refuted.
Nor does it belong to that which is non-existent,
because it is being negated;
nor does it belong to that which is both existent and non-existent.
Because existence and non-existence cannot coexist through mutual exclusion,
and because the position of being neither consists in the simultaneous negation of both existence and non-existence;
nor [can it be established] by way of being the opposite of both existence and non-existence.
It must be of the nature of both existent and non-existent, because it cannot exist separately from the destruction;
for if it were to exist [separately], then, being an effect produced by a cause considered to be impermanent, it would necessarily follow that it is itself permanent.
This is because the refutation of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has already been undertaken.

Since it will be demonstrated that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*)— because, for an existent, there is no connection with arising and no utility in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and because, in general, all entities are shown to be without arising through their lack of both single and multiple natures— they are non-arisen; being non-existent, they are indeed eternal.
To this, it is replied: Would production be of that which exists prior to its arising, or of that which does not exist?
If it were of that which exists, then it is not so;
for that which exists has already established its being in its entirety.
Nor can it be that which is non-existent, because even that is subject to negation.
Now, if you argue that there is the production of that which exists in the form of a cause as power (*śakti*), but in the form of a manifestation (*vyakti*);
is that manifestation, which consists of production, existent or non-existent?
If it were existent prior to the operation of the cause,
it would not be produced by the cause— just like a potency— according to the reasoning previously stated.
On the other hand, if it were non-existent, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be abandoned.
Furthermore, the doctrine of non-selfhood (asatkāyavāda) would follow as a consequence.

If the power and its manifestation were of one and the same nature, the defect inherent in the positions of existence and non-existence would arise; if they were of different natures, however, the previously mentioned fault would apply.
Now, what is this *śakti* (potency)? Is it the essence of the cause or the essence of the effect?
If it were the essence of the cause, then since that [essence] already exists prior to production, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be abandoned.
If the effect were identical with its cause, it would have no power at the time of its production;

nor could it exist prior [to production], because it would already be that very essence. From what cause, then, could the effect exist within the nature of the cause as something possessing the nature of power?
Therefore, there is no such thing as power.
Nor is an individual manifestation possible.
If power were a distinct entity from both effect and cause, being inexpressible as either identical to or different from them, it would be neither power, nor an effect, nor a cause.
And that which is neither an effect nor a cause cannot be the apprehender or the obstructer of anything.

For those seeking liberation, since all other categories of entities are established as objects of cognition through the negation of their causal relationship— and because liberation is accepted as being achieved through the non-perversion of the mind—

it is not the case that power (*śakti*) is a separate entity from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). For, unlike a jar or similar objects, it is not perceived as distinct in its own nature, despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility.

Nor can it be [inferred] as something not meeting the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), because its existence would have to be inferred from its effect— consciousness— just as the eye and other [faculties] are inferred from their effects, provided that [the cause] exists when all causal factors are present and is absent when they lack capacity;
for it is impossible for an effect to be produced by that which is non-existent, and thus, due to the absence of such an effect, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) fails to be established.

It should be understood that even the claim that [an entity] is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [its parts] is refuted by this very same sequence, because it follows the same logical principle as the universal (*sāmānya*).
Likewise, all such cases should be understood as falling under the definition of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
Now, if existence arises, then existence is the very nature of the entity; how then can there be the absence of its existence?
Now, if existence is conceptualized in the absence of arising, then it would follow that non-existence— which is unarisen prior to arising— is what is called "existent.
For the arising of an entity is intended to have the sense of coming into being.
And if existence were established independently of arising, then what would be the use of arising?
If it is argued that "let the entity be unarisen," [we reply:]...
No; because of the fault already stated previously and because it will be stated again later.
Furthermore, this position—that there is some non-existent portion of that which already exists prior to its arising, and for the sake of which arising is not fruitless—also does not hold.
Because it would entail the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda);
because, given the impossibility of identity between the existent and the non-existent, existence would follow from non-existence and vice versa,
as the fault in that regard has already been demonstrated.
Since the position of the individual (vyaktipakṣa) has already been refuted,
if it is argued that what is to be produced is existence— that is, the production of the existent from the non-existent— this position also is untenable.

For indeed, since its entire nature is already established by the very first arising, a second arising would be purposeless; moreover, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, it is impossible for that which already exists prior [to an arising] to undergo a further prior arising.
Since the position of the unarisen has already been refuted, production from that which exists in every way is not tenable.
If there is no production from the existent, what then will happen for that which is non-existent?

For instance, even when causes such as the *kalala* and so forth are dissected in hundreds of ways, a body consisting of a collection of parts such as hands and feet—which has reached the conditions for perception—is not perceived; therefore, it is simply non-existent.
For instance, among the form, light, eye, and attention, the visual consciousness appears as the aspect of a form such as blue present before one,

and it is not the case that the auditory consciousness exists [therein] as the manifestation of sounds— whether they denote flutes, lutes, and so forth, or whether they are blue, red, and so forth, or whether they are pleasant or unpleasant. Likewise, the olfactory cognition appears as the scent of campaka, vakula, and other flowers— whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral— and it does not exist within the nose, the odor, or the attention.

Among the operations of the tongue and taste, the gustatory cognition appearing as tastes such as pungent, bitter, or astringent is non-existent [in the ultimate sense]. Likewise, among the mind and tactile objects, there is no tactile consciousness appearing as sensations such as soft or rough.
Furthermore, according to the scriptural statement: "That consciousness which has just passed away from among the six is indeed the mind (*manas*)."

The subsequent conceptual cognition— such as "this is blue"— which arises after the sensory cognition manifesting the form of blue and so forth (under another name, namely "immediately preceding mental attention"),
does not have the form of blue and so forth as its object within that non-conceptual cognition which possesses the aspect of the form of blue and so forth.

Likewise, the conceptual cognitions such as "this sound is non-existent," which arise after the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile cognitions that manifest sounds, smells, tastes, and touches individually, [do not have those forms as their objects] within the non-conceptual auditory and other cognitions that manifest sounds and so forth.
They do not exist.
Conceptual cognition arises in the form of "this is blue," "this is yellow," and so forth;

yet there is no cause for it therein other than the preceding preceding cognitions which manifest the forms of blue and so on present before one—even from a non-conceptual [cognition]. Thus, there is a succession of objects consisting of the forms of blue and so on present before one, occurring in the second and subsequent moments subsumed within a single continuum.
And conceptual cognition arises;
yet that [conceptualization] does not exist in its cause.
This should be understood in the same way regarding other objects as well, wherever it occurs.
There is the possibility of a succession characterized by a single continuum of a similar kind.

However, where there is no functioning of a single continuum, even there, because a single [entity] that is completely severed does not exist, and because another is present without interruption, there is non-conceptual sensory cognition (*nirvikalpaka-indriyajñāna*).

Due to the collection of objects such as sound, there arises—subsequent to the initial non-conceptual sensory cognition that apprehends the preceding sound—an immediate non-conceptual cognition and a conceptual cognition having that same object, which possess the same form as the sound and other objects. However, this is not possible; for according to their own doctrine, sounds proceed in a continuum like the ringing of a bell or like waves upon water, and thus there is no subsequent moment of sound apprehended by a non-conceptual auditory cognition following the non-conceptual cognition that apprehends the preceding moment of sound.
Non-conceptual auditory sensory cognition arises, as does other conceptual cognition whose object is sound or some other [object].
Furthermore, at the time of explanation,
subsequent conceptual cognitions proceed from each preceding conceptualization.
But why does the conceptual cognition not arise at the very first moment, such that another subsequent conceptual cognition would arise?
There is no fixed rule in this matter.
Sometimes it arises from a single sensory cognition, or from all [sensory cognitions] together;

for example, in the case of a person who is deeply asleep, it arises from the tactile sensory cognition of the body when a staff suddenly falls upon him and makes contact, producing a cognition whose object is touch;
and sometimes, during the fall of a great thunderbolt, it arises from the auditory sensory cognition of the Buddha.

Sometimes it arises from the non-conceptual sensory cognition of the sense of smell, produced by the contact of the nasal cavity with the fragrance of substances such as agarwood, camphor, and sandalwood; sometimes it arises from the non-conceptual sensory cognition of the sense of taste, produced by the tongue’s contact with substances that are pungent, bitter, or astringent;
and sometimes it arises from the sensory cognition of the eye, when one has opened one's eyes after a cognition of touch and beholds the form of a teacher or another venerable person.

Sometimes, for one whose sensory cognitions have all ceased, there arises again a conceptual cognition that imitates previous conceptual mental constructions, such as daydreams; this occurs when one is further conceptualizing.

That very same [cognition] may arise simultaneously from five or six sensory cognitions. For example, how could there be the arising of something non-existent—such as a hare's horn—for one who, immediately after six cognitions, while asleep, speaks in a dream about what was previously thought? [Objection: How can there be the production of the non-existent, like a hare's horn?
Because it would follow that everything could arise from everything.
For the arising and so forth of the world are like an illusion.
Now, how is it determined that sensory cognition is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and not conceptual (*savikalpa*)?

In this regard, concerning the position of the Sautrāntikas who maintain the existence of external objects, a mere indication is here related according to tradition for the sake of the instruction of beginners.
Therein, two entities are established: cognition and the object of cognition;
no third or further entity exists.
This is because the agent, the instrument, and so forth are included within that very [category].
For indeed, when these are postulated, they must be postulated preceded by the determination of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
since the establishment of categories of entities is dependent upon the means of valid cognition.

Otherwise, by excluding differences of place, time, and intrinsic nature— such as [thinking] "this is thus," "this is not," "this is now," or "this is not now"— there would be no cognition of other places and so forth, and the world would remain in a state of deep sleep, devoid from the very beginning of the worldly transactions consisting of the avoidance of the beneficial and the harmful;
for those things which do not perform causal efficiency are like the horns of a hare and the like.
These, too, do not exist externally;

rather, they are merely conceptual constructions arising from the beginningless latencies of conceptualization (*anādivikalpavāsanā*), which do not establish anything real and are not objects for others.
Thus, there are only two entities: [the subject and] the knowable (*jñeya*).
In that state, there is no identity between knowledge and the object of knowledge; rather, if they were identical, then knowledge alone,
or the object of knowledge alone, would be non-dual.
Moreover, that too would not be possible because both [subject and object] would depend upon one another.
If the knowable were on the side of the subject, the world would be blind and mute;
but if the knowable were non-different from knowledge and thus on the side of knowledge, the perception of external objects would vanish.
And this is not accepted by the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādins*).

In that case, since those two exist in mutual exclusion, because the object of cognition does not enter into the nature of the cognition, it is the cognition alone that shines forth as being unilluminated by anything else, and not the object,
because the latter has a non-luminous nature.
Because if it were of that nature (i.e., identical to itself), the aforementioned defect would follow;
furthermore, if cognition were not self-luminous, the defect pertaining to the object of knowledge would apply.
By being luminous through another, its luminosity would be dependent on something else.
Even another [cognition] would either be manifestable by something else or not;
otherwise, there could be no such thing as "this has been manifested by another," nor even the notion that "it has been manifested."
It would simply be of a self-luminous nature, because it is already manifested even when its illuminator is not apprehended; otherwise,
the cognition of its luminosity would also be impossible.
For if the illuminator is not apprehended, the state of being illuminated cannot be cognized.

Indeed, the cognition of the illuminator occurs through the necessity that the state of being illuminated would otherwise be inexplicable; yet, the cognition of the state of being illuminated depends upon that cognition of the illuminator—thus there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore, whatever entity possesses a certain intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it does not color other things by means of that intrinsic nature.
For example, through contact with a substance possessing the quality of redness, a white substance becomes red;
likewise, through a black substance it becomes black, through a green one it becomes green, and so forth.

Form becomes manifest through the light of a lamp; that is, it is accompanied by illumination. But how could that which has arisen as inherently non-illuminating in nature illuminate another thing that is also non-illuminating in nature?
For indeed, jars and other objects are not illuminated in the darkness by a staff, which is itself non-illuminating in nature.
Otherwise, it would follow that lamps and such things lack a material cause.

If it is argued that [the lamp] illuminates another object after having attained the state of illumination from something else, we say no; for that [lamp] possesses the state of illumination inherently.
For instance, that which is other cannot itself be self-luminous; how then could it illuminate another?

If its luminosity were dependent on something else, and that too on another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), whereby nothing would be either illuminated or an illuminator, and the world would become blind and mute.

Consequently, because of the absence of worldly transactions consisting of affirmations and negations regarding space, time, and nature—such as "this is thus" or "this is not this"—everything would simply vanish into obscurity.
But it is not so;
by this, the other position is refuted.
Let it be, then, that cognition is self-luminous in nature.
Even so, how could the object of knowledge be manifested by that [knowledge]?

For it has been established previously that the nature of knowledge does not bring about the object of knowledge, nor does the nature of the object of knowledge bring about knowledge, because of their absolute difference.

Now, if it is argued that even though there is absolute difference, just as a white substance becomes red through contact with a red substance, or just as cloth and other objects situated in darkness become luminous through proximity to a luminous substance such as a lamp, so too the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) becomes manifest through the proximity of the knower (*jñānavat*); [we reply:]...
No; for if there were an absolute difference between knowledge and the object of knowledge, the illustrative example would be unestablished.
To explain: an illustrative example consists of an object of knowledge, not of knowledge itself.
If there were an absolute difference between the two, how could an example—which is of a nature other than that [knowledge]—appear when knowledge, which is luminous by nature, is manifesting?
By what means could there be an example?
For an example is an object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and it exists as distinct from that means of valid cognition.
While that [self] is manifesting, how could that which is not-self manifest?
Therefore, since the illustrative example is unestablished, nothing desired is established; consequently, the entire world would be like the deaf and mute.
For instance, is cognition arisen or unarisen?
In the case of its production, there would have to be the existence of causes such as form (*rūpa*), and in their absence, it would be either with form, without form, or of another form.

Regarding the first position, since the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is distinct from the cognition (*jñāna*)—whether by identity or by origination—and because the object consists of luminosity (*prakāśa*), there is no connection between the cognition and the object; how, then, could there be the perception of anything?

Likewise, since knowledge that has not arisen from the object of cognition (jñeya) lacks its form, the perception of that object—by way of a knowledge possessing that form—is not established even figuratively. Thus, there would be no apprehension of the object whatsoever.

Furthermore, the positions regarding permanence or impermanence, existence or non-existence, need not be considered; for in the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causal origination (*tadutpatti*), these distinctions, lacking the possession of the object's form, cannot serve as a means for the apprehension of the object, as previously explained.

In the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), the postulation of another relation is not tenable, because such a relation is brought about by way of assistance (*upakāra*); for if there were no assistance, the aforementioned faults would necessarily follow.
Alternatively, if it were to assist, it would follow that it falls under the category of being produced [from that];
for this will be examined later.
In every respect, the position that [the cognition] is unproduced is not a factor for the apprehension of another object.
The position that [the object] does not exist is precisely the position that it has arisen from that [consciousness];
the only difference is that in that case there is no external object as a cause.
Consciousness itself arises even without an object, appearing in the form of that object.

The Vijñānavādins maintain that [cognition arises] from an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) produced by a beginningless stream of cognition, just like a dream-cognition. For instance,

when one has closed the door and is lying inside a house with eyes shut, a cognition in the form of elephants, horses, and so forth— whose dimensions exceed those of the house— arises even in the absence of external objects such as elephants.
Furthermore, those objects appearing in a dream, such as elephants, horses, and so forth, are not logically tenable,
because they appear even in the absence of the operation of the eyes;
for there is no perception of form for one whose eyes are closed, just as there is none for a blind person.
If it is argued that the activity of the eye is also perceived there,
that is true; its perception does exist, for what is being proven there is not the absence of perception, but rather the absence of the visual faculty.
How could the form of blue and so forth appear in a dream to one who is blind and asleep in the absence of such objects?
For they do not exist in that dreamless state or elsewhere,
since their bodies have been consumed by fire.

Or how is it that within the interior of a very small house, objects such as trees, mountains, oceans, and the orb of the sun— occupying the vast expanse of the earth and sky— are perceived? For they have neither entered nor remain there,
since these appearances occur during the state of sleep.
For all men indeed perceive a common range of objects by means of unimpaired faculties of perception.
And if objects exist in a dream, how is it that teachers and others, who were perceived there while engaged in explaining [the text], provide answers when questioned in the waking state?
If it is argued that all of that [is remembered] by them because of their lack of forgetfulness, we say no; for there is an absence of forgetting at all times.
Even if it were indeed useless during the state of deep sleep, [it would still not follow].
How can consciousness devoid of an object be established by this mere example?
For the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia being false does not imply that the cognition of one free from ophthalmia is false.
Indeed, that cognition is non-erroneous and not devoid of an object, because it is non-contradictory.

Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) consists in the attainment of an object through a cognition that arises without depending on another object; it is characterized by non-contradiction because false cognition and the like would not otherwise exist.
Furthermore, this [attainment] is observed to follow from the presence or absence of the production of the object in the case of sensory cognitions such as those of a healthy person.
For instance, when the eye is free from defects such as cataracts, cognition occurs; in the absence of such [a healthy eye], it does not occur.
For one with eyes closed, even though the mental attention directed toward the perception of form is present, [the cognition] does not arise; it arises again once the eyes are opened.
Likewise, it occurs when there is light and does not occur in its absence.

Even when other instruments such as the eyes are present, it occurs when there is illumination from a lamp or similar source, and likewise when there is the presence of an object situated in front, such as a jar.
It does not occur when that [cause] is absent.

Furthermore, while other conditions such as light are present, it occurs when that [specific cause] is present; likewise, while the cognition designated as "attention" (manaskāra) exists, it arises, and in its absence, it does not occur.
Even though objects such as jars are present, it occurs again upon awakening from a state of deep sleep.
In that regard, when each [defect] is individually absent, the capacity of all [the elements] for the arising of that elemental cognition is manifested.
Likewise, the visual organ functions with respect to form, not with respect to sound and so forth;
nor are sound and the others perceived by the eye.
For if one were to postulate the existence of the auditory faculty and so forth, it would follow that they are redundant, and it would also follow that deaf persons and others do not exist.
Furthermore, sounds and other objects are not the producers of that [consciousness], such that those objects would appear within it.
If even non-producers were to appear [in cognition], then all objects would be directly perceived, and everyone would be an omniscient seer.

In every case, this very determination of sensory cognition must hold: visual and other consciousnesses arise bearing the image of forms and so forth, neither being formless nor possessing the image of something else.
Because the cognition of an object is impossible through those two [the eyes].
For instance, just as a person’s own face is never directly perceived [by itself],
its experience occurs through seeing its reflection in a mirror by means of light.
For that person, the experience of his own face is nothing other than the experience of its reflection; there is no direct perception of it apart from the experience of the reflection.
Likewise, for all those who maintain that objects [exist externally], the object itself is never directly perceived.

The experience of that [object] is nothing other than the experience of its reflection in the mirror of cognition; the perception of that [reflection] is itself the perception of the object. For the object is not directly perceived in itself.
If that [object] were perceptible, then because cognition consists of perception, it would be cognition alone and not the object,
since the object would consequently attain the status of being cognition by virtue of being perceived.
Alternatively, if the perception belongs to the object itself and not to the cognition, [then...]
If that [reflection] were not perceptible, it would follow that everything is imperceptible;
for just as one's own face is imperceptible when its reflection is imperceptible, it is impossible for that [object] to be perceptible [if the reflection is not].
Therefore, the object is not directly perceived.
In that case, if consciousness were to have a form other than the blue form—that is, if it were not of the nature of the blue form—then that consciousness would be of the nature of existence alone.
Its apprehension would belong to that [existence] itself and not to the blue, because [the blue] is distinct from the blue form;
for the apprehension is devoid of both existent and non-existent forms, and thus it is neither the cognition of blue nor the cognition of yellow.
Wherever a certain form does not exist, there can be no cognition of it, as for example, the cognition of yellow cannot be a cognition of black.
Just as in a mirror, the reflection of one's own face— which is distinct from the form of another's face— is the cognizer of one's own face alone, and not of another's face.
Because that [consciousness] is devoid of that [object's] form;
likewise, a cognition with a different form cannot be the experience of an object possessing the form of blue, because that would lead to the over-extension [of the definition] to all experiences,
and because there is no actual experience [of that specific object].
Nor can a cognition devoid of form be the cognizer of an object such as blue;
for how could that [cognition], being devoid of the forms of all objects like a mirror-disk devoid of all reflections, be the cognizer of an object?
Indeed, a surface of a mirror, when devoid of all reflections, is not the cognizer of one's own face and so forth, which are themselves devoid of reflections.
If that cognition were to reflect the form of some object within itself, how could it possibly fail to make that object known?
Nor is an object directly perceived by itself, as if it were its own face.
Because of the previously mentioned fault.

Therefore, the cognition of an object is not possible through either a cognition with a different form or a cognition without a form; enough of this digression, for only a mere indication has been shown.
Beyond this, nothing more has been written for fear of excessive prolixity in the text. || 3 ||
Emerging from the form of the sound *nāda* within their own nature, they are the domain of the conduct of the samaya;
it is difficult to find in the three worlds that which is established as beginning, middle, and end.
He asks, "From where have you arisen in such a state? and replies with the words beginning "from the *saṃbhava*.
By means of this, the deities become fully distributed; thus, *saṃbhava* is the union of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*).
To the question "Even there, from what [do they arise]?", he replies: "From the form of *nāda*."
Nāda is mere sound;
its representative is the mere staff (daṇḍa);
its form is its own nature, which is the collection of vowels and consonants on one's own seat, with the syllable *hūṃ* above it.

One should meditate on the double-vajra (viśvavajra) produced from that, with a *hūṃ* syllable placed upon its hub (*varaṭaka*); above that, without any interval, a black *hūṃ* syllable; above that, a red *āḥ* syllable; and above that, a white *oṃ* syllable.

Of the *praṇava* and so forth, which are being rendered devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkriyamāṇa*), that which remains as mere sound (*nādamātra*)—in that mere sound, within the *bindu*, is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). That [half-moon] is in the *oṃkāra*; that is in the two side-*bindus* of the syllable *āḥ*; and that is on the staff (*daṇḍa*) outside of those sides.
He [is] with the side-staff attached behind the letter *ta*,
he [is] in the letter *ta*,
he [is] at the head.
That is the mere resonance (nāda) of the syllable *hūṃ*;
that resonance [dissolves] into the bindu, it into the half-moon, it into the crest (mastaka),
then into the bindu, it into the letter *ha*, it into the first half of the letter *ha*, and finally into the letter *ha*.
In the right half of the side-stroke of the letter *u*, there is the mere resonance (*nādamātra*) of the *hūṃ* syllable situated within the universal vajra;
that resonance is in the *bindu*; that is in the head-matrkā; that is in the first half of the letter *ha*; and that letter *ha* is in the second half of the side-strokes.
At the letter *U*, he is on the middle prong of the eastern side of the Viśvavajra, on its left prong;
on the southern side, on the right prong, on its middle prong, and on its left prong;
and on the western side, on the right prong, on its middle prong, and on its left prong.
Having reflected that he has entered the right awn of the northern side, the middle awn, the left awn; and the right awn of the eastern side, the middle pericarp, and the nature of emptiness,
he then [enters] again the right awn of the eastern side.
Then the left side of the northern flank, then the middle, then the right,
then the left side of the western flank.
Then the middle [finger], then the right;
then from the left hand of the right side, the middle, then the right;

then the left of the front side, then the middle, then the *ukāra* of the *hūṃkāra* situated on the central knob (*varaṭaka*), then the two staff-like strokes (*daṇḍa*) on the rear side of the *hakāra*, and by those two, the front half of the *hakāra*.
Then on the head is the letter *t*, then the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), then the point (*bindu*),
then the sound (*nāda*), and then the mere sound (*nādamātra*).
Then the letter *u*, then the letter *ha* (rā)— these are the side-staffs in the latter half; by means of those two, the former half [is formed].
Then the head,
then the half-moon,
then the bindu.
From that, the sound (nāda);
from that, the mere sound (nādamātra). From that, the head of the letter *ta*.
Then the letter *ta*,
then the side-staff,
then the other side-staff.
Then two dots (bindu),
then the letter *o*,
then the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
From that, the point (bindu);
from that, the sound (nāda); from that, the mere sound (nādamātra).

Arising from that, seated upon the throne, as subtle as a lotus fiber, the deity to be meditated upon—measuring eight cubits, white, the support for the latencies of purified karma and afflictions, having the nature of Prajñāpāramitā which is the object of consciousness, and having the nature of Vajrasattva who is wisdom and means—is to be meditated upon as the "line of Buddhas.
As for the phrase "in the form of sound," it refers to the realization: "I am born from the two [wisdom and means] as being like an illusion."
The word *hi* is used for emphasis.
Thus, having emerged from precisely these two [factors], he is primarily twelve-armed due to the purity of the twelve-linked dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The hand-symbols [are determined] by the oral instruction.
Or he will say, "And [the body] covered with an elephant hide," and so forth.
He says "emerged" and so on not merely to indicate that he himself emerged from it;
"occasion" (*samaya*) refers to the time of the *gokudahanā* and other rites.
Its practice is service.

Those ḍākinīs, lāmās, and so forth, for whom that very [practice] is their sphere of activity are "those whose sphere of activity is the practice of the samaya. Sphere of activity means the domain; samaya means emanation.
And some say that this is connected to the welfare of sentient beings. Furthermore, although the word *niṣkrānta* (emerged) is plural in form, it should be construed with Vajradhara in the singular,
by changing the case ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāmāt*).
Anticipating the question, "Are you the nature of the knowledge of ultimate reality (*paramārthajñāna*)?", he says: "Difficult to obtain," and so forth.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are two, and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the third;
these three [arise] due to the proximity of those two being conceptualized as a duality, whereby conceptualization becomes the third.
If, subsequently, no conceptualization occurs, there arises the thought, "I am easily accessible," just as in the case of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
This is because, through those two being practiced with non-attachment, one directly realizes the innate gnosis (*sahaja-jñāna*) which is distinct from all afflictions.
Therefore, I am of the nature of consciousness precisely because of being free from conceptualization.
Therefore, he says: "In the worlds.
"World" (*loka*) means seeing or perceiving; that is to say, it is the apprehension [of objects] through wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).
And those [worlds] arise from the apprehension of what is grasped by wisdom and skillful means.
Conceptualization is obtained from the word *loka* itself,
because perception is directed toward that;
or else, it is difficult to find [such conceptualization] in the supreme bliss (*ānanda*) and the ultimate cessation (*paramavirama*).
“Because of the statement that ‘the innate does not exist in these three,’ the remainder is as before.
Therefore, he says: ‘Ādi’ and so forth.”

Because it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), it remains divided into beginning, middle, and end, by which I am difficult to attain. Having established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that [I] am easily attained, [the text] speaks of [my] difficulty of attainment.
And this is the intended meaning (*bhāva*): "This form of mine, namely that which is called 'conceptual,' does not exist."
Since my very form is indeed non-conceptual, because it consists of such knowledge;
and that is difficult to attain through conceptualization.

Alternatively, when the moments of the crushing of various ripenings have occurred, [the self] has perished, meaning it has become invisible due to the absence of experience; therefore, I am difficult to attain.
For at the moment of the extraordinary [realization], there is the experience of the gnosis called "innate" (sahaja), which is devoid of all objective perception. || 4 ||
Just as there is the union of the churning stick and the base, so too is there the union joined with mantra-recitation, meditation, and so forth;
listen to the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual procedure as proclaimed in the Tantra. || 5 ||

It is well-obtained and accomplished through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), which is implied by the sense; nevertheless, he asks "how indeed is that so? and replies: "the union of the churning-stick (*mantha*) and the churning-rod (*manthāna*).
Here, the churning-stick is the aspect of wisdom, and the churning-rod is the aspect of means.
Due to the convention of the Dharma, those two are joined in a state of equal flavor (samarasatva); that in which this occurs is thus.
Just as the union of the churning-stick and the churning-vessel occurs, in that same way I am easily attained.
The connection is that "he will speak" regarding the union with Śrī Heruka.
The Blessed One is the very nature of innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*). To explain what that is like, he says: "as it is."
This four-syllabled statement is in every respect: "Ā, i, ṇa, anta; neither end nor middle; neither existence nor nirvāṇa;
this is that supreme great bliss, neither other nor self."
The yogi should press the two waves together with the thumb and the ring finger of his left hand during the act of union.
Subsequently, knowledge arises, like the pleasure of a maiden in sexual union.
Thus is the meaning of the word *yathā*.
"The fourth is likewise" (*tat punas tathā*): this is the meaning of the word *tathā*.
The meaning of these two sections of the text is to be understood from the oral instruction of the Guru.
Here, the meter (*chandas*) and so forth need not be analyzed, as this is a work of the *ṛṣis*.
It is designated by the term "secret" (*rahasya*) along with its qualifications.
Having stated the union with Śrī Heruka, he says "mantra," etc., in order to establish the yoga and other practices that constitute its very subject matter.
Mantras are those consisting of eight syllables and so forth; their recitation is *jāpa*, which is repetition.
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the contemplation of the form of the deity.
From the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it includes] the worship of the Kulikā, the female messengers (dūtīs), and the accomplishment of desire (kāmasiddhi).
The worship of the Bodhisattva-lamp through the drops of bodhicitta,
liberation from all misdeeds, and the accomplishment of the state of a yogin.
The observance of the samaya, the protection of the samaya,
and the consumption of the five nectars.
In the *gaṇacakra*, there is the tasting of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) like the drinking of soma,
the union of the two organs (*dvīndriyasamāpatti*), and divine bliss (*divyasaukhya*).
Praise,
locations such as mountain caves,
and the ten principles beginning with the maṇḍala.
The worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru, Vīra, and Vīreśvarī; the entry of the disciple into the maṇḍala;
and then the bestowal of the consecration (abhiṣeka).
The mudrās, the worship of the Ācārya, the manifestation of the realm of the Ḍākinīs, and the extraction of the mantras.
The expansion of the ritual activities of the Vidyārāja,
the means for accomplishing the eight mundane siddhis, and the procedure for the secret signs (chommaka).
The characteristics of the action-seal (karmamudrā),
the activities of speaking, going, and coming performed by those two, and the characteristics of the ḍākinī.
The display of mudrās and counter-mudrās, the proclamation of the names of the commitments (samayas),
and the eight great commitments (mahāsamayas) pertaining to both the mundane and the supramundane.
In one place: the consumption of sacrificial porridge (caru),
the offering of oblations (balidāna),
and the extraction of the mantra of Sumbharāja.
The accomplishment of the flow of his activity,
meditation on the form of the mantra,
and the cultivation of the reality free from conceptual construction.
The supreme supramundane [state];
then, the recitation of mantras beginning with Cittavajrā, which are included within the names of the Vīras and Vīreśvarīs together with the mantra-words of the Four-Faced One;
and the exposition of the twenty-four sites belonging to the ten stages, such as the Pīṭhas and so forth.
Dwelling at night and so forth,
the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,
and from that, the purification of the twenty-four elements beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla;
The transformation of the forms of the goddesses Bhūcarī and Khecarī; the authorities concerning the movement, experience, and dissolution within the wheel of the thirty-seven family channels (nāḍī);
and the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Then, there is the inclusion of these: the nature of the bodies of emanation, enjoyment, and the pure dharma-body, as well as the nature of the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion;
and "yoga" refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for performing activities such as pacifying, enriching, magnetizing, and subjugating.
Regarding the term "knowledge of the injunction" (*vidhijñāna*): that which is enjoined is an "injunction" (*vidhi*), namely,
action such as virtuous deeds and the like.
Its "knowability" consists in its being an object of knowledge; that this exists will be indicated [by the following]:
"Just as a vessel filled with ghee placed in the midst of fire..."
As clarified butter melts when heated, so does the time [of suffering] perish within the two vessels;
likewise, evil is destroyed by the name "Śrī Heruka."
By this statement;
or else, "vidhi" here refers to time, consisting of the past, future, and present;
and "jñāna" refers to the eight bodies of knowledge (jñānakāya).

The connection [of the treatise] is as follows: I shall explain that which is denoted by such terms as "yoga," "knowledge of the method" (*vidhijñāna*), and "secret. Here, "method" (*vidhi*) means knowledge; thus, it is "knowledge of the method. This constitutes the relationship.
In the tantra known as the *Khasama*, which contains the compendium of everything, that which is spoken is called the "Secret of Secrets.
Therefore, listen to that, O Vajravārāhī! The sense is that it is because that [tantra] is to be accomplished.
Furthermore, if the text of that tantra is concise, what loss is there in its being otherwise?

The passage beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth is not stated here because it has already been stated in that very [text]. If it is asked, "How can this be [considered] a summary of a new work, given its novelty?"—the answer is no; for there is no novelty insofar as it is connected to the subject matter of the *Mūlatantra*.

If it is argued that, because of the statement, "O monks, my teachings should be compiled as 'Thus have I heard,'" the connection now belongs only to the compiler, we say no; for the compiler compiles the tantra in the form of both the subject matter (abhidheya) and the expression (abhidhāna) spoken by the Blessed One.
If it is asked, "If the Blessed One is the teacher, then how is there the application of words such as 'how did he stand' and so forth? [the answer follows].
By means of the words beginning with "sthita," I shall explain the union with Śrī Heruka.
To the question "Of what nature is that?", he says: "In the supreme secret," and so forth, which should be applied accordingly.
That by which the meaning is extended is the "multitude of sounds" (śabdasandoha).
In this context, the subject matter (*artha*) is divided into three types by way of result, cause, and means.
The result is the state of Samantabhadra, which is of the nature of vastness (*vaipulya*).
The cause is that very [state] having reached a particular stage through repeated practice.
The cause (*hetu*) is the assembly of deities of the maṇḍala;
the means (*upāya*) consists of the four elements, Mount Meru, the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), and so forth.
Such is its nature as a tantra (*tantratā*). And thus it is said:
"Tantra is declared to be a systematic treatise (*prabandha*), and that treatise is threefold;
the compendium of the meaning of the tantra consists of these three: the basis (*ādhāra*), the form (*ākṛti*), and the means (*upāya*).
By the word "secret" (*rahasya*), the subject matter of the entire tantra has been stated in extreme brevity.
Then, from the passage beginning with "The union with Śrī Heruka," it was explained at length by way of a commentary;
now, to avoid excessive prolixity, he speaks [from] the conclusion of this tantra until verse 5.
One should constantly worship the Kulikā with the medium-superior breath together with scented water, and the female messengers (dūtīs) according to the specific times.
He says that very thing with the words beginning "madhyama" and so forth: *madhyama* means "middle"; *śvāsa* refers to that in which or by which one breathes, or it may mean the place or the time.
The middle fire is so called because it arises from the middle, according to the statement: "earth, water, fire, and air.
Although it arises from the middle, the means [of its attainment] is grasped because he will state that the supreme [fire] belongs to Mahendra, due to his being the king of the gods.
The meaning is that for the middle and superior [levels], there is breath, location, or time;
the connection is that one should worship the Kulikā by means of that. To the question "By what?", he says: "with perfume," and so forth.
"Gandha" is that which possesses fragrance; or, because it carries fragrance, it is the wind (*vāyu*). "Udaka" is that which possesses water; it is Varuṇa.
"Gandhodakasahita" means accompanied by the abode of those two; this is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyapadalopī samāsaḥ*).
Just as a jar full of clarified butter is called a "clarified-butter jar," the word *tu* serves to complete the meter; thus, the meaning is this: the *kulikā* is the Yoginī.
One should worship and propitiate her;
"constantly" means at all times, that is, every single day.
Regarding the specific time:
At specific times, during the half-prahara portions beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*), according to the instruction:

starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, in the morning during the half-prahara, one should meditate on *Pracaṇḍā*, born from the mantra "Oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," as being produced from the syllable *puṃ* at the head.

In the second [half-prahara], at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), one should meditate on *Caṇḍākṣī*, born from the mantra "Oṃ kuru kuru caṇḍākṣi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," as being produced from the syllable *jāṃ*.
In the third, on the right ear born from the syllable Oṃ, is Prabhāvatī, born from the mantra: *Oṃ bandha bandha prabhāvati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
In the fourth, on the back of the head born from the syllable Aṃ, is Mahānāsā, born from the mantra: *Oṃ trāsaya trāsaya mahānāse hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the fifth, on the left ear born from the syllable Goṃ, is Vīramatī, born from the mantra: *Oṃ kṣobhaya kṣobhaya vīramati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
In the sixth [petal], at the center of the eyebrows, one should visualize Kharvarī, born from the syllable *rāṃ*, with the mantra: *oṃ hrauṃ hrauṃ kharvarī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
In the seventh, at the two eyes, one should visualize Laṅkeśvarī, born from the syllable *deṃ*, with the mantra: *oṃ hraḥ hraḥ laṅkeśvari hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the eighth, at the two shoulders, one should visualize Drumacchāyā, born from the syllable *māṃ*, with the mantra: *oṃ pheṃ pheṃ drumacchāye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. This is the mind wheel (*cittacakra*).
The seat of the goddesses is the fire-maṇḍala; this is the daytime portion.
During the first *prahara* of the night, one should meditate on Airāvatī, born from the syllable *kāṃ*, located in the two armpits, with the mantra: *oṃ phaṭ phaṭ airāvati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the second [watch], she is born from the syllable *oṃ* in the two breasts: *oṃ daha daha mahābhairave*.
In the third [cakra], one should visualize Mahābhairavī, born from the mantra *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*;
and at the navel, one should visualize Vāyuvegā, born from the mantra *oṃ paca paca vāyuvege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, which arises from the three syllables.
In the fourth [face], born from the syllable *koṃ*, at the tip of the nose, is Surābhakṣī, produced from the mantra: *oṃ bhakṣa bhakṣa vasarudhirāntramālāvalambine surābhakṣi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the fifth, born from the syllable *kaṃ*, in the mouth, is Śyāmādevī, produced from the mantra: *oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa saptapātālagatabhujaṅgaṃ sarpaṃ vā tarjaya tarjaya śyāmādevi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the sixth, born from the syllable *laṃ*, at the throat, is Subhadrā, produced from the mantra: *oṃ ākaḍḍha ākaḍḍha subhadre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the seventh [petal], at the heart born from *kāṃ*, is Hayakarṇī, produced from the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ karakarṇe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the eighth, at the genitals born from *hiṃ*, is Khagānanā, produced from the mantra: *oṃ jṇauṃ jṇauṃ khagānane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. This is the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).
The seat of these goddesses is the Varuṇa-maṇḍala; this is the nocturnal portion.

On the second lunar day (tithi), during the morning third watch, one should meditate upon Cakravegā, born from the syllable *preṃ*, at the *liṅga*, with the mantra: *oṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
At the second [site], the anus, born from the syllable *gṛṃ*, one should meditate upon Khaṇḍarohā, with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hāṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
At the third [site], the two thighs, born from the syllable *sauṃ*, one should meditate upon Śauṇḍinī, with the mantra: *oṃ hīṃ hīṃ śauṇḍini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the fourth [circle], on the pair of shanks born from the syllable *suṃ*, is Cakravarmiṇī, born from the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ cakravarmiṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the fifth, on the collection of toes born from the syllable *naṃ*, is Suvīrā, born from the mantra: *oṃ kili kili suvīre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the sixth, on the two soles of the feet born from the syllable *siṃ*, is Mahābalā, born from the mantra: *oṃ sili sili mahābale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the seventh [petal], from the syllable *maṃ*, on the two big toes, is the mantra-born Cakravartinī: *cili cili* (*hili hili*) *cakravartini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
In the eighth, from the syllable *kaṃ* (*kuṃ*).
At the two knees of the causal [body], with the mantra "Oṃ dhili dhili mahāvīrye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," there is the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) known as Mahāvīryā.
The Maheśvara mandala is the seat of the goddesses; this is the daytime portion.
On that very night, during the first two watches, one should visualize Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Śūkarāsyā in the vicinity of Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā respectively;
during the second two watches, Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathanī should be visualized in the vicinity of Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā respectively.
In this manner, the day and night are completed through the mind and speech wheels on the third lunar day.
Then, on the fourth [day], one proceeds from the body and the cremation-ground wheels; thus is the movement of the thirty-two yoginīs.
It should be understood in this same way for the fifth and subsequent days.
Śrī Heruka and the four yoginīs, Ḍākinī and the others, constitute the consciousness wheel.
And there is no transference (*saṃcāra*) of these [powers], due to the absence of instruction.
Having performed meditation and recitation for six months and having attained the sign (*nimitta*), the yogi should then carry out the transference of the Yoginīs for seven months.
If there is thus no success, then he should meditate in that very same manner once again.

Thus, the instruction is that [the goal] is accomplished through thirty-six months by means of regular practice. Practice performed with devotion and without interruption for one year is followed by practice for six months and so forth; such is the sequence.

The application of fire and the other elements for rites such as *abhicāra* (sorcery) should be understood in the same way: for instance, in *abhicāra*, the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) is associated with the moment of fire (*vahnikṣaṇa*),
while in pacifying rites (*śāntika*), the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*) is associated with the moment of Varuṇa.

In the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), one should meditate upon any one of the Yoginīs during the *māhendra* moment of the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*); in the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), during the *vāyu* moment of the charnel-ground wheel (*śmaśānacakra*).
The *āgneya* wind is four finger-widths [in extent], and the *māhendra* wind is ten finger-widths.
The [mandala] of Vāyu is six finger-breadths, and that of Varuṇa is twelve finger-breadths.
