This is because of the statement: "The rule for the location of the exits for Agni, Indra, Vāyu, and Varuṇa is by means of fourteen, six, twelve, and [twelve] finger-breadths, respectively."
Furthermore, the fire-element is warm and rises upward;
the air of Mahendra fills the nostrils and is neither too cold nor too hot; and the air of Vāyu is horizontal and harsh.
Below, the water-circle flows very cold.
Within that [mandala], the circle of fire is triangular, red, and marked with seven flames;
the circle of Mahendra is square, yellow, and marked with a thunderbolt.
For Vāyu, there is a bow-like blue [disc] marked with a banner;
for Varuṇa, a circular white [disc] marked with a bell. To the right of the exit of Vāyu are those [deities] beginning with Agni.
By demonstrating the worship of the Kulikās, the accomplishment (siddhi) was first shown.
Because that [object] alone is primary by virtue of being the goal to be accomplished. || 6 ||
The innate siddhas of the two messengers are classified as inferior, superior, and middling;
one should contemplate the attainment of desire with a focused mind.
He states how many *kulikās* there are with the words "the messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*) and so forth.
The term "previous *kulikā*" (*pūrvakulikām*) is in the singular merely as a class designation.
Consequently, the term "messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*) is in the plural, meaning those who are distressed (*dūyante*) by the suffering of sentient beings and thus tormented.
"Kulikās" and "messenger goddesses" (dūtayas) are synonymous terms.
They are the four, beginning with Ḍākinī, who are innate (sahajā) and identical in nature to the Blessed One.
The word "they" (tāḥ) indicates that their essential nature is gnosis (jñāna).
The "Siddhas" are the eight yoginīs beginning with Yamadāḍhī.

The inferior ones are those belonging to the body-wheel (kāyacakra), dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla). The middling ones are those belonging to the speech-wheel (vākcakra), who roam upon the earth (bhūcarī).
The supreme ones are the sky-farers (*khecarī*) who reside in the wheel of the mind.
The sense is that these thirty-six yoginīs alone are to be worshipped.
Thus, it is established that Śrī Heruka is to be accomplished by means of both the body and the external maṇḍala.
He states what must be cultivated by one who possesses practice: "The intermediate," and so forth.
Desires are form, sound, and the rest; from them, or by means of them, comes the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of Śrī Heruka.
"One should cultivate the state" means that one brings about one's own being;
that is to say, the accomplishment of desire becomes real, according to the statement: "Form, sound, and so forth are desires."
To explain how this is so, he says: "by the mind.
This means by consciousness (*vijñāna*), according to the statement: "The mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and then consciousness (*vijñāna*) are representation (*vijñapti*)."
"By means of that which has entered within" means by means of the mind in the form of Śrī Heruka, who is non-different from oneself.
The intention is that the yogin of Śrī Heruka attains accomplishment through the enjoyment of all sensual pleasures.
And thus it is said: "One who enjoys all objects of desire indeed attains accomplishment.
Therefore, the word *tu* has the sense of the particle *eva*.
Because there is no accomplishment of the goal through a ransom-offering,
external worship— characterized by the enjoyment of objects such as form— is mental and consists of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*). || 7 ||
One should worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with drops of one's own semen, and by means of seeing, touching, hearing, and remembering them. (8)
He describes direct worship, beginning with "one should [emit] the sound" and so forth.
For the sake of worship within the external cognition characterized as described in other tantras, one should generate the *bodhicitta*.

Having purified its union of both [parents] by means of its drops in the form of the tasting of nectar, one should worship the Buddhas—the five aggregates such as form and sensation—and the Bodhisattvas—the forms of the eyes and so forth—by means of that enjoyment.
Thus, it should be practiced at the three junctions of the day; this is the direct worship. As it is said:
"The wise one of firm intellect should consume the secret semen;
this is the worship of body, speech, and mind for all mantras."
The meaning is that secret worship (*guhyapūjā*) is the realization of the co-emergent (*sahaja*), and it is accomplished through the perfection of the fourfold worship.

By means of this yoga, there arises merit that is unprecedented and free from attachment, due to the destruction of previously accumulated merit and demerit that were based on the adherence to objects of perception and so forth.
Then Siddhi said: "Seeing," and so forth.
Seeing is perception by means of the eye;
touching is [perception] by means of the body-faculty.
Hearing is by means of the faculty of hearing; recollection is by means of the mental faculty. || 8 ||
In this very way, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
The state of a yogi is supremely meritorious, pure, and the destroyer of sin.
By means of these factors associated with Śrī Heruka acting as instruments, even another person is liberated— that is, released—
from all sins, which consist of the misdeeds of body and so forth acting as agents. Freedom from sin is "niṣpāpatā."
"It is just so.
This means that this very thing is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
To the question "Is this true?", he replies: "There is no doubt."
The meaning is that there is no duality here.

One who is liberated from attachment to the apprehended object and so forth through [the process of] seeing and so on is liberated by virtue of the yoga of the moment of experiencing the innate secret.
This is the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*).
Regarding that, "in this very way" means that the triple world itself is nothing at all.
Some say, "there is no doubt" because of the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
He explains how this occurs through the vision of the yogin alone: "Yogitva" refers to the state of being a yogin of Śrī Heruka.
It is "supreme" because it removes all sins by mere sight.
For this very reason, it is "meritorious" (puṇya), as it purifies.
It is called "pure" because it is free from the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*);
it is called "the destroyer of evil" because it annihilates the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and others. || 9 ||
Success is achieved through the mantra of recitation, by means of chanting and meditation;
the practitioner, being well-composed, should constantly observe the rules of conduct.

He provides the detailed explanation of what was indicated by "one should meditate" with the words beginning "siddhyate": the vowel *e* is a modification of the position of the vowel *i*; the meaning is that it becomes manifest.
The term *japeti* (causes to recite) implies the elision of the third case ending;
it refers to a mental activity (*mānasa-vyāpāra*).

By means of that, one contemplates that [the mantra] "protects the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)" and "saves the world-realm (*lokadhātu*). Thus, the mantra of Śrī Heruka, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*), is accomplished.
In the phrase "by means of the mantra," the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative;
by "recitation" (jāpa), the activity of speech is indicated;
and by "meditation" (dhyāna), the activity of the mind is indicated.
The activity of the body consists of the nature of wisdom and skillful means.
To the question of with what auxiliary factor recitation and so forth become fruitful, he says: "The pledges," and so on.
The pledges have been explained.
The point is that even though those [elements] are eternal, they are nonetheless useful through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
And so it has been said:
"This water of yours, belonging to the hell realm, shall burn you for transgressing the rule (*samaya*)."
This is the explanation of the phrase "the sphere of the conduct of the observance":
namely, "the practitioner.
For the practitioner, while constantly performing meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), should consume pills made of cow-flesh and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) at the commencement of the cultivation.
Therefore, there is freedom from obstacles.

Regarding the term "well-composed" (*susamāhita*): it means well-composed, nourished, and sustained on all sides by the yoga consisting of wisdom and skillful means, which is perfectly even and free from unevenness.
And the convention (*samaya*) has been stated elsewhere. Thus it says:
"Neither beginning with *na*, nor beginning with *ga*, nor likewise beginning with *ha*, nor even beginning with *a*. (10)
Indeed, through the violation of the commitments (samayas), success is not attained in the initiation mandala.
[The offering should consist of] honey, red [substance], camphor, and mixed with red sandalwood. || 11 ||
Regarding that, he asks how there can be such a secret convention (*gūḍhasaṃketa*), and answers with the words "by means of distinction" (*bhedena*) and so forth.
"Distinction" (*bheda*) refers to the understanding of the conventional designations of the non-conventional (*asamaya*).
The particle *tu* is used in the sense of "because."
For those who do not understand the true nature of reality, there is the fault of both [denial and affirmation] due to their rejection based on differentiation.
Consequently, there is neither accomplishment nor an achiever.
The intended meaning is that accomplishment arises through the convergence of the systems of Tantra and Mantra.

Regarding the reading, “Success is not attained in the mantra-maṇḍala,” it should be explained as follows: *mantra* refers to the utterance that impels reality (*tattva-codana-bhāṣaṇa*); *maṇḍala* is so called because it brings (*lāti*) enlightenment (*bodhi*, i.e., *maṇḍa*) by means of that [utterance]. Thus, it should be understood as the Mantra Mahāyāna.
In all cases, the *samaya* must be observed and its violation must not be committed; this is direct worship (*sākṣātpūjā*).
He describes another form of direct worship consisting of the consumption of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) with the words beginning "honey" (*madhu*), etc.

Madhu is honey because of its similarity [to the nectar of flowers]; śukra is semen, as it is conventionally designated as such due to its quality of destroying the three doṣas when combined [with other substances].
Rakta is well known [as blood].
*Karpūra* is so called because it fills (*pūrayati*) the body with bliss (*kaṃ*).
Its establishment [as such] occurs through the addition and elision of phonemes;
and that is *māṃsa*.
Blood is so called because food and other substances are relished (*rasyate*) within it;
urine is *vairocana* because sandalwood (*candana*) brings about delight (*āhlādaka*). || 11 ||

Established in the midst of the assembly, bearing the marks and signs of all vajras, the knower of yoga should always cause [the disciple] to taste [the substance] with the ring finger and thumb joined in a hook-like curve. 12.

"In the midst of the assembly" means in the midst of the *gaṇacakra*. The word "midst" (*madhya*) indicates a general connection. "Established" (*pratiṣṭhita*) refers to that which is established (*pratiṣṭha*).
The meaning is exactly as stated.
To the question "What is its support?", he says: "All," and so forth.
"All vajras" refers to the Viśvavajra (the universal vajra).
That which has the mark of all vajras as its emblem is "sarvavajrāṅkacihna";
that is the skull-cup (kapāla),
and because it is held therein, it is so called.
To explain how it should be employed, he says "anāmā" and so forth.
That which is licked in the mouth is a *leha* (lickable substance);
one should prepare that, meaning one should cause it to be licked.
"Yogavid" means one who knows the yoga of tasting the nectar (amṛta),
or one who possesses the meditative absorption (samāpatti) in mind-only (cittamātra).
"Always" (sada) [means at all times].
The meaning is that one should consume the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) together with the assembly of deities of the maṇḍala. || 12 ||
Having tasted it like the drinking of soma, one attains eternal perfection;
herein, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) become the instigator of all accomplishments.
Regarding this, he says "Soma," etc., to show that no doubt should be entertained:
at the time of sacrifice, one should cause the juice of the *kaliṅga* creeper to be placed upon the hide of a tawny cow for the Brahmins.
That is *soma*; its drinking promotes longevity and increases merit.
Just as Soma is tasted by Brahmins free from doubt,
so too the yogi, having tasted the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), attains eternal perfection.
Because its nature is to bestow eternal fruit, the illustration [is given] by means of mere tasting without hesitation.
But not with the fruit. As it is said:
"One should never feel disgust for feces, urine, semen, and blood;
one should always consume them according to the rule—this is the duty born of the three secrets."
To the question, "What is this called 'honey' and so forth? he says: "The five," and so on.
The collection of the five nectars is *pañcāmṛta*.
The collective meaning is that by means of the yoga of the deity, being free from doubt, and through the procedure for tasting the nectar, all food, drink, and so forth, when tasted, becomes nectar.
How does this bring about the attainment of the eternal? He says: "All," and so forth.
It is thus because it brings forth all mundane and supramundane attainments. (13)
The fourfold worship, as well as the heroines who are the yoginīs desired by the mind;
and the upholder of reality, who has entered into the non-dual union with the heroes. (14)
He states the summary meaning of the brief indication and detailed explanation, beginning with "four" and so forth.
The meaning of "the fourfold worship" (*catuṣpūjā*) is as follows:
they are described according to the distinctions of external, secret, mental, and manifest [worship].
Therefore, he says "tathā" (thus).
The meaning is that they are indicated by the manner [described] starting with "the middle" and so forth.
"Yoginīs" refers to the four, such as Ḍākinī and the others, as well as the eight, such as Kākāsyā and the others.
The meaning of the term "vīrādvayasamāpatti" (heroic non-dual union) refers to those [consorts] with whom there is union in a heroic, non-dual form; this is due to the elision of the case ending.
"Samāpannam" means "having entered into union" in such a manner.

He who maintains the reality (tattva) that is the nature inseparable from Vajravārāhī is called Tattvadhṛk. By the substitution of *tu* for *ta*, and *caṇa* for *ka*, he is designated as Śrīherukasaṃyoga. || 14 ||
Even the bliss of divine and human states, gathered together as one, does not equal even a sixteenth part of that very [bliss] when compared to the tip of a vajra. 15.
That which exists in heaven is "divine," and that is happiness;
"mānuṣya" belongs to this [person], thus its nature is "humanity."
And that [bliss] is established when there is non-duality in the nature of happiness.
To the question "How is happiness obtained?", he says: "Bliss" (*saukhyam*).
Happiness is the well-being of the mind; that itself is bliss.
And that is common to those who have gone to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; it is the undivided mass. Vajra is stainless intellect.
That very [center] is the "kaṇikā" because of its subtlety.
It is called "vajrakaṇikā" because it is both the vajra and the kaṇikā; the meaning is innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*).

By means of the adamantine nucleus (*vajrakaṇikā*), which remains by unifying divine and human happiness and acts as the instrument, even the sixteenth digit (*kalā*)—namely, the afflictions (*kleśa*)—is not worth a fraction of it, nor do they honor it;
for this method has the conquest of the afflictions as its goal, thus there is a summary description of what was indicated by the phrase "in whatever way. (15)
One should draw that mandala in mountain caves, in bowers, on the shores of the great ocean, or in a cremation ground that has been perfected since the beginning.
Thus ends the first chapter, the procedure for entering the maṇḍala, in the Herukābhidhāna. || 1 ||
There is no accomplishment without consecration, and that [consecration] does not exist without entry into the mandala; thus he says "giri," and so forth.
"Giri" means a mountain.
By the word *gahvara* (thicket) is meant the space between two walls; by the word *kuñja* (grove), a place concealed by creepers and the like;
and by *mahodadhi-taṭāḥ* (seashores), the islands.
Regarding the term *ādisiddha*: it is so called because it is established (*siddha*) from the beginning (*ādau*) in that particular location. A *śmaśāna* is the abode of corpses.
In this context, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause;
that is, "one should draw the mandala for the purpose of consecration. || 16 ||
The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the chapter’s subject matter.
That by which the Śrī Heruka, together with his limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), is expressed is the *abhidhāna*, the Tantra, whose body is sound.
Within that, there is the chapter on the procedure for entering the mandala.
"Entrance" (*avatāra*) means that by which one enters;

"procedure" (*vidhi*) means that very entrance is prescribed. Thus, the "Entrance Procedure for the Maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka and Others" refers to the first chapter, which is a single division of the text that explains that procedure.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 1 ||
The second chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Wheel-Worship.
Therein, one should smear the ground of the mandala with cow dung that has not yet fallen [to the earth], combined with cremation-ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). (1)
He speaks of the mandala, beginning with "Therein," and so forth:
"In whatever ritual action one's own specific ritual injunctions do not exist,
there the wise resort to the injunctions prescribed in the general tantras."
This is the principle stated in the general tantras.
However, since a certain common rule has been mentioned here,
he says "therein" and so forth to address that point.

For the purpose of drawing the mandala, the preceptor should have the disciple smear the ground—the site for the mandala—in mountain caves and other such locations with non-falling cow dung mixed with *vairocana* (white mustard seed), in order to prepare the mandala ground.
Furthermore, he should smear over that with charnel ground ashes and so forth; thus it is said: "It should be joined with charnel ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). (1)
Having then smeared the ground, one should begin the mandala there;
having performed its meditative cultivation, one should practice the charnel ground ritual. (2)
The connection is as follows: after smearing the ground with cow dung that has not fallen [to the earth], one should begin the mandala.
After the smearing with cow dung that has not fallen, there is the smearing with cemetery ashes and so forth.
Nevertheless, to the question "Immediately after what does one begin the mandala?", he says: "Then" (*tataḥ*).
Immediately after the protection wheel and so forth, it says:
"One should perform the cremation ground ritual.
The meaning is that if the drawing of the mandala is performed elsewhere than at a cremation ground or similar location, then one should visualize a cremation ground there. (2)
With the charcoal powder of a city mixed with bricks from cremation grounds,
the preceptor should draw the divine maṇḍala, complete with all its characteristics.
The King said: "With funeral pyre embers," and so forth. Regarding "cremation-ground bricks":
the funeral pyre is the earth; its preparation is accomplished through the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of it as being cremation-ground bricks.
Some say that one should begin the cremation ground with the dust of city charcoal, cremation grounds,
and bricks; the brick should be short, and the two types of dust should be black and yellow.
It is "divine" because it is not within the sphere of experience of all people. Regarding the term "Ācārya":
he who teaches the True Dharma, who is an expounder and a giver of instruction, who performs the consecration and the ritual acts—he is the Ācārya.
This has been well-explained.
This refers to that which has been defined as such;
specifically, it is the Guru alone.
That is to say: "The Guru is designated by the term 'Ācārya' by the learned."
And this merit is for the sake of consecration;
if the drawing of the mandala is for the sake of accomplishment, the yogi should draw it, and he should do so perfectly with all its characteristics. (3)

One who possesses correct knowledge, is learned in the tantras, knows the secret mantras of Śrī Heruka, is free from anger, pure, skillful, a knower of yoga, and has reached the further shore of wisdom. || 4 ||
He states the definition by means of its qualifiers, beginning with "samyak" (correctly):
one who possesses knowledge that is *samyak*—that is, non-erroneous and free from [the triad of] the apprehended object and so forth—is a *samyagjñāna*.
Such a person, being also a knower of the *tantra* of restraint (*saṃvara*) and the rest, is a *samyagjñānatantrajña*.
"Śrīherukamantrajña" means one who knows Śrī Heruka and the mantras, such as the eight-syllable mantra and others, according to the oral instructions; thus he is so described.
Or, one who constantly recites the mantra of Śrī Heruka;
"anger" (krodha) is the mental state directed toward a present object of harm,
and its absence is "non-anger" (akrodha).
"Pure" means free from the stain of remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
"Dexterous" means possessing enthusiasm for what is skillful.

"One who has gone to the further shore of yoga"—yoga refers to rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*); one who has reached its limit or culmination is "one who has gone to the further shore of yoga. || 4 ||
With a skull for a crown, his limbs smeared with ashes, his body adorned with various ornaments, he stood amidst bones and heaps of bone-dust, his hair shorn into a single lock. || 5 ||
He whose crest is fashioned from five skulls is *kapālakṛtamūrdhajaḥ*.
He whose body is smeared with the ashes of the cremation ground, which adhere to it, is *bhasmānuliptāṅgaḥ*. By implication, his bodily form is adorned with various ornaments.

He is one whose body is specifically adorned with boneless [limbs] because they are present; "asthimala" refers to sentient beings who possess bones as their impurity, and he is "established" or seated among them.

Furthermore, because of the possibility [of this interpretation], some say that by the word *mātra* (only/merely), Amitābha mixed with Ratnasambhava is meant, and thus he is "one whose body is anointed" (*kṛtāṅgarāga*) by him.
In that regard, however, by the words "bones" (*asthi*) and so forth, it is precisely the ornament (*ābharaṇa*) that is being described.
Regarding the phrase "with hair made into a single lock" (*ekakhaṇḍīkṛtamūrdhaja*):
*khaṇḍa* means a portion or section. Those whose [hair] consists of a single *khaṇḍa* are so described.
He by whom the hair has been made into a single mass is "he who is thus";
the meaning is that his crown is formed from the hair of others. || 5 ||
Wearing a garland of bones and holding a khaṭvāṅga in his hand,
one should meditate on oneself as Śrī Heruka and then recollect Śrī Heruka.
"One who wears a garland of bones" (*asthimālāvalambī*) means one who possesses a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) that hangs down as a garland of bones.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction.
"Standing firmly with his left hand holding a skull-topped staff" (*khaṭvāṅgakarasaṃsthitaḥ*) means he stands properly with his left hand bearing a *khaṭvāṅga*.

Thus, he becomes distinguished by means of his ornaments and so forth. Having meditated upon himself as Śrī Heruka together with the deities of the maṇḍala according to the instruction, one should thus recollect Śrī Heruka. (6)
Having thus demonstrated the pledge (samaya), one should place the wheel upon his heart.
Thus, having armored oneself, one should visualize a rampart in all directions. (7)
"Thus": one should manifest such a pledge (*samaya*), consisting of the wisdom-nature of Śrī Heruka—the deity of the maṇḍala—to Śrī Heruka.
"One should place the wheel in his heart" means: in the heart of this self who has become Heruka.
"In the heart" means in the body.

Therefore, this is the meaning: one should place the goddesses such as Pracaṇḍā and the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla within one's own body, [and] in Pullīramalaya and so forth, as well as in the nails, teeth, and so on.
The root *as* (in *asati*) belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa and has the sense of "going."
"Thus, one should draw [the boundary].
Having visualized oneself as Śrī Heruka, one should first of all visualize a wall in the cardinal directions outside of the dust mandala that is to be prepared.
According to the etymological rule (*nirukti*), since it is thought (*manute*) that one becomes mere gnosis (*jñānamātra*), the letter *ma* is a consonant (*hal*).
This is a qualification of the self;
the meaning is that one should transform the self, which is mere consciousness, into Śrī Heruka.
The intended sense is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, this is nothing but mere consciousness. || 7 ||
Having thus armored oneself, one should indeed place the weapon below;
the self is level with the wheel, while the mass of arrows is above.
He explains how one should meditate on Śrī Heruka himself: "Thus, having equipped oneself.
The letter *ma* is as before.
Having made oneself the one who has begun [the practice] through the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, [one meditates on] Śrī Heruka.
"Should place" is the verb. "For the weapon below" means that one should indeed place the weapon below as well.
Above the lattice-work of arrows is the wheel;
then one should install Śrī Heruka, the deity of the maṇḍala. || 8 ||
Having made his own body a cage for the sky-dweller [the mind], he, being well-composed,
thus equipped himself with armor that is impenetrable even by the gods.
The connection is as follows: having created a sky-faring vajra above oneself and a cage consisting of that same substance, one should install Śrī Heruka.
Furthermore, regarding the state of being armored, it refers to the procedure for the armor-mantra of the Six Heroes and others during the accomplishment of Śrī Heruka. || 9 ||
Having thus well-protected oneself and adorned with mudrās and mantras,
one should draw the formidable maṇḍala that bestows great siddhis.
"Thus, having well protected oneself"—
the letter *ma* is etymological,
as before.
The mudrā is Vajravārāhī;
the mantras are the root mantra and so forth.
Alternatively, mudrā refers to the symbolic seal (cihnamudrā).
The mantras are those such as *om kara kara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* and others, whose constituent parts are distinct.
The connection is that one should thus draw oneself as the well-protected maṇḍala.
It is "terrible" (*ghora*) because of its aversion to the worldly conventions of the Vedas, Smṛtis, and so forth.
By the words beginning with "mahā," he shows that one should also construct the mandala for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

The intended meaning is that one should achieve accomplishment through recitation and so forth for a day and night, preceded by the mandala, culminating in diligent and uninterrupted meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) according to the previously stated procedure. || 10 ||
Then, with a thread made from a corpse or one honored with great blood,
one should delineate the formidable mandala, the supreme city of Heruka.
One cubit [in height], four or eight [cubits] in extent, square on all sides,
provided with four doors, and adorned with four archways.
He states the cause for its being "terrible" with the words beginning with "tataḥ":
immediately after [the rites of] smearing with cow dung and the vajra-fence, and so forth;
or, by means of that which is honored with great blood.
Because its intrinsic nature is that of being entwined by a corpse and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff;
it is "terrible" because it is surrounded by a cremation ground.
Because it reveals the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of the mandala through an exposition of the meaning of the term *Śrīheruka*, or because it generates fear in the ignorant;
[it is called] "the city of the *pāṃ*s" because it is the very nature of Śrīheruka.
"Caturaṣṭam" means that its measurement is four or eight cubits; the rest is easy to understand. (11–12)
The practitioner of mantra should wander for twice [the duration] and worship the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
Having established a lotus in its center, complete with petals and radiant with a pericarp.
And with lotuses possessing filaments. || 13 ||
"One should traverse it twice" means two cubits, eight cubits, or sixteen cubits;
this is an attribute of the measuring cord (*sūtra*).
It has been established that the length of the thread is double that of the wheel.
"Mantrin" means one who has recited the vidyā-mantra.
The meaning is that one should worship the Ḍākinījālasaṃvara in the center of that maṇḍala.
Having done what? He says: "having established," and so forth.
It is "with petals" (sapatram) because it exists together with petals of all colors.
What is that? He says: "radiant with a pericarp" (karṇikojjvalam).
This is the name of Viśvapadma; it is characterized by lotuses, that is, seed-pod receptacles. The plural number is used because of their multiplicity through emanation.
From the word "and" (*cakārāt*), [qualities such as] being fully blossomed are understood. *Kesara* means the filaments;
by them, there is a corresponding encircling, and by that, this [state] is attained.
The sense is that the filaments are fully developed.
The remainder is easily understood. || 13 ||
Upon the pericarp, one should place the Hero, who is terrifying as Mahābhairava,
possessing splendor with brilliantly blazing limbs, and emitting a great roar of boisterous laughter.
It is "terrifying" (bhīṣaṇa) because it generates fear even from such hells as Mahāraurava and others, and from such beings as the Piśācas.
It is "radiant" (tejaska) because it produces brilliance;
the particle *tu* is used here in the sense of "because."
Because it possesses the nature of fire, it is intensely blazing;
in the reading "sudīptaṃ ca," the particle *ca* serves to complete the meter.
[It is] characterized by the great sound of a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*).
He is one whose great roar, consisting of loud, mocking laughter, spreads through the sky, and whose clamorous sound arises from false manifestations out of curiosity. || 14 ||
Adorned with a garland of skulls, divine, three-eyed and four-faced, covered by an elephant hide, and possessing beautiful brows marked by a vajra; 15.
He who bears a garland of skulls is "adorned with a garland of skulls" (*kapālamālābharaṇaḥ*).
This is the purification of grasping the skulls of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
That which exists in heaven (*divi*), which is of the nature of bliss, is "celestial" (*divya*).
Through the purity of the three liberations, he has three faces, each with three eyes;
through the purity of the four liberations, he has four faces;
and he is covered by an elephant hide.
Because he uses his two arms as a covering for that [elephant hide].
The mass of afflictions (*kleśa*) is likened to an elephant because of their shared characteristics;
thus it is said: "Wearing a fresh garment of elephant-hide."
For even when that [body] is divided, its state remains like an illusion;
thus, the "skin" is its covering, and conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is like an illusion.
For this very reason, it is held behind one's back and not in the heart.
"Because it is not grasped due to its insignificance"—this refers to the covering with an elephant hide.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that this very [elephant hide] is what covers [the body].
One whose two eyebrows are well-parted and have attained a state of distinctness like a diamond is *vajrasambhinnasubhrūḥ*; the space between the eyebrows is the *varaṭaka*.

The two eyebrows and the eyes below them constitute the "three-pronged" [point]; thus the *vajra* is established. As it has been said: "The middle of the eyebrows is the central hub (*varaṭaka*) of the *vajra*. (15)
His hand holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, and he is adorned with half a garland of a hundred skulls;
embracing him stands the goddess Vajravārāhī, who is most formidable.

Regarding the phrase "with a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) held in his hand": that which performs the welfare of sentient beings is "done" (*kṛta*); thus, the third hand is "the one that has done [this].
Consequently, he is "one whose hand holds a skull-topped staff."
The intention is that he holds a *khaṭvāṅga* due to the purity of his performance of the welfare of sentient beings.
Regarding the verb "he should place," the accusative case is used throughout.
"Adorned with half a garland" means half of a garland; half of a hundred [beads] is fifty, and by that [garland] he is adorned.
The meaning is that the garland of mantras, composed of the vowels and consonants, has reached the throat.
Regarding the phrase "standing before her":
she stands having embraced him face-to-face.
She plays together with the Blessed One, thus she is Devī.
She strikes the wretched afflictions (kleśas) with the vajra, thus she is Vajravārāhī. She is most terrible through her threatening of the wicked and so forth. 16.
Having made her face the deity Śrī Heruka, she is three-eyed and of fierce form;
she holds a skull-cup filled with entrails, which drips blood from her mouth. (17)
He provides the detailed explanation for the previously mentioned "embracing in front" (*sammukhāliṅgana*), stating: "facing Śrī Heruka.
Because the action [of facing] pervades the entire phrase, the accusative case is used everywhere.
He further qualifies the Goddess before him as "filled with the mantra within the skull"—that is, the *kapāla-mantra*—meaning she is not inferior to her husband.
And the mantra of the skull-bowl for the Māras is "stravantīṃ rudhiraṃ mukhāt" (flowing blood from the mouth); this is through the purification of passion. 17.
Threatening all the directions, including the gods, asuras, and humans, there are twenty-four ḍākinīs born of the family of Vārāhī. || 18 ||
"Threatening all the directions" means threatening all the guardians of the directions (*dikpati*).
"Together with gods, asuras, and humans" implies the worlds (*loka*).

Regarding the reading "all the directions" (diśān sarvān), it should be understood that those who possess directions are the "lords of the directions" (dikpatayaḥ). And as for the "twenty-four ḍākinīs," they are the twenty-four beginning with Pracaṇḍā.
By virtue of the word "and" (ca), one should worship all twelve [goddesses] beginning with Kākāsyā;
these too are born from the family of Vārāhī.
Together with Vārāhī, those born of the families beginning with Citta [are included];
by this, the rule of the families has been stated. || 18 ||
One should worship within the center of the wheel, as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
likewise, one should worship the heroes situated here within the wheel.

Regarding the phrase "within the center of the wheel": having drawn the mandala and meditated upon Śrī Heruka there together with the goddesses who form his retinue, one should worship him; this is the intended meaning.
To explain how the deities are to be installed, he says: "in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions."
"And likewise the heroes here"— "here" means within the center of the wheel; it means those born of the Kula.
"One should worship the entire circle of deities"—this is the summary.
The word "cakrasaṃsthāḥ" ends in the accusative plural; the nasal *n* has been elided.
By this, it is confirmed that [the deity] is within the circle (*cakragarbha*).
The word "tu" (but/however) serves to negate [the deity's] abiding within the body, and is for the purpose of prescribing the rule of worship, namely, that one should worship again. || 19 ||
If the seeker of accomplishment desires success, he should worship the non-dual Hero; thereafter, he should prepare the ritual jars, free from the influence of the root-time and other such factors.
By this, he states whose worship it is: "the non-dual hero" (*vīramadvaya*).
He is called a *vīra* because he emits (*īrayati*) dissimilar forms such as the perceived object (*grāhya*) and so forth;
and he is nothing but consciousness (*cittamātra*).
Therefore he says: "non-dual.
The intended meaning is that one should worship the Hero as non-dual precisely for that reason. Why? He says: "if one desires to be an achiever of siddhi."
"Siddhi" [is used] with the elision of the accusative case ending.
Since the practitioner should desire accomplishment (*siddhi*), he should worship from that [point].
One should know that the mandala is mind-only (*cittamātra*).
The passage beginning with "kalaśāṃśca" (and the jars) is easy to understand.
[They are] "devoid of the root-time and so forth.
The "root" (*mūla*) is the portion fashioned by the potter from the wheel.
Time is the black portion;
from the word "and so forth" (ādi), qualities such as being dark are included. || 20 ||
[He should offer] vessels filled with pearls, gold, gems, coral, silver, copper,
and all kinds of edible foods, placed upon skull-bowls.
"Gold and those jewels" means gold-jewels (*hemaratnāni*).
The word "jewels" (*ratna*) applies everywhere. By this, the five jewels are indicated, ending with the phrase "those [along with] copper."
And "all edible things" (*sarvāṇi ca bhakṣyāṇi*) refers to all edibles (*sarvabhakṣyāṇi*). By the word "all," the five grains and the five medicinal herbs are intended;
by the word "edible," the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are meant.
"Resting upon the skull" is an epithet for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Therefore, the word "but" (tu) has the sense of specification.
The five jewels and the five medicinal herbs are within the interior of the vase, whereas the five nectars are located in the skull; one should place them in its mouth.

"Resting upon a skull" means either by means of the word ending in the third case (*kapālopari saṃsthitaiḥ*), qualifying the jar, or, according to some, "resting upon a skull fashioned from colored powder" (*rajonirmitakapāloparisaṃsthitaiḥ*). || 21 ||
Having placed eight [vessels] wrapped with thread around their necks and provided with tips of sprouts at the eight gates,
well-enveloped with a pair of cloths; || 22 ||
Having placed the ninth pitcher in the center, wrapped with a pair of cloths, and adorned with silver or gold, as well as jewels and pearls; 23.
The neck of those jars is *tatkaṇṭhaḥ*.
"Endowed with the tips of sprouts" refers to their mouths.
By the words beginning with "having made," he shows the insertion of the five jewels into the ninth jar, named Vijaya: "having made [an image of] silver or gold."
The nominative singular is used in the sense of the instrumental.
In the phrase "ratnamauktika," there is an elision of the dual instrumental ending.
The connection is that one should worship the excellent city after placing the ninth pitcher, adorned with silver and other materials, in the center. || 22-23 ||
One should scatter all those beautiful objects made of jewels and gold within the maṇḍala and worship the delightful, excellent city; success will surely follow, there is no doubt. || 24 ||
Having sprinkled oneself with scented water in every direction, one should offer a hundred lamps if one desires the highest accomplishment. || 25 ||
By what means? He says: "One should scatter all [of them] upon the mandala," and so forth.
"Jewels" refers to pearls and the like.
"Gold" (*sauvarṇa*) means that which is gold itself.
"Adorned by these" means beautiful ornaments;
that is, both ornaments made of jewels and gold. With all of these, as they have been obtained, from where should one scatter the offering?
In the mandala, those are worshipped here and there:
the jewel of the elephant and the jewel of the horse.
the jewel-treasure, the sword-treasure, and the wheel-treasure.
The counselor and the jewel of a woman— these are the seven jewels.
Some say that because they exist within gold which possesses qualities, they are "golden" (*sauvarṇa*).
"The self facing in all directions"—the connection is that one should worship the self as Śrī Heruka in the center of the city. (24–25)
One should mentally place all the ḍākinīs in the sky above;
and those ḍākinīs who are in the world of Bhūr, one should place them everywhere within the maṇḍala.
Whatever ḍākinīs there may be in the netherworld (pātāla), one should place them therein;
all the Mothers (mātṛs) should be assigned to the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions. || 27 ||
In the *bhūrloka*, that is, on the earth;
"whatever *ḍākinīs* there are in the netherworld (*pātāla*)" refers to twenty-four.
In some versions, where the reading is "mātaraḥ" (mothers), the meaning is the same;
by the word "mother," the twelve [goddesses] beginning with Kākāsyā are intended. || 26–27 ||
With flowers, perfumes, and likewise incense, one should offer a hundred lamps;
thus one who seeks to accomplish spiritual success should worship the Lord according to the prescribed rite. (28)
One should worship the Hero-Yoginīs situated within the mandala of Śrī Heruka with banners that are red, yellow, white, and dark brown. (29)
With various garlands, as well as diverse kinds of garments,
with canopies and beautiful cloth hangings,
and with foods to be chewed, eaten, tasted, and drunk, one should perform [the rite] with a well-concentrated mind. (30)
Thus ends the second chapter, the ritual procedure for the wheel-worship, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

By the phrase "prior to the lamps," a hundred oil lamps were mentioned in general; however, the phrase "a hundred lamps" refers specifically to those produced from great oil. Therefore, the word *tu* (but/however) serves to indicate this distinction.
The rest is self-evident.
"Bhakṣya" refers to flour-based foods and the like; "bhojya" refers to cooked rice and the like.
"Edible" refers to side dishes;
"drink" refers to that which is to be drunk, such as whey and the like.
"One should perform" implies "one should perform worship"—this is the ellipsis.
Thus, the external worship has been shown. (28–30)
The *cakra*, its worship, the ritual procedure for those two, the means of accomplishment, and the chapter that explains them—this is the second [chapter].
This concludes the second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 2 ||
The third chapter on the initiation of the fee (*dakṣiṇābhiṣeka*).
Then:
"The practitioner should first satisfy the preceptor with his entire being."
One who desires spiritual accomplishment should worship the Guru with full concentration, according to one's ability. || 1 ||
Without the instruction of a guru, there is no accomplishment of mantra whatsoever; therefore,
he says "then" (*tataḥ*) to indicate that worship of him [the guru] must be performed at the time of initiation,
because there is no success without the teacher’s instruction.
Then follows the propitiation of the Guru.
The word "then" (*tataḥ*) is a separate term.
He explains this very point with the words beginning with "the teacher" (*ācāryam*).
"Previously" is an epithet of the teacher,
characterized by such attributes as "one who knows the system of right knowledge.
Alternatively, it is an epithet of time.
"First, one should please the teacher"— this means one should request instruction from him.
"With one's whole being" means with all things,
such as one's own self and so forth.
"One who desires accomplishment should worship the Guru with all his concentration according to his ability.
The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of specification.
Therefore, in this context, the disciple should worship the Guru alone—that is, the Ācārya—with his whole being.
Thereafter, the construction of the maṇḍala [is performed].
One should worship there for the purpose of entry and so forth.

"Siddhikāmaḥ" refers to one who desires that accomplishment (siddhi) be achieved by means of the initiations and other rites received by me; such a person, having performed the recitation of mantras and so forth, remains well-composed. || 1 ||
Relying on the sound of a bell and having adorned it with flowers and incense,
the practitioner should ring a sweet-sounding bell or even a small drum,
and cause the cry of "Hā hā" to be uttered.
By the passage beginning with "the sound of the bell" (*ghaṇṭānāda*), the consecration of the bell (*ghaṇṭābhiṣeka*) is set forth. The connection is that the practitioner should ring the bell.
"Adorned with flowers and incense" means it has been worshipped.

By the term "possessing a beautiful sound" (*susvarām*), all the characteristics are indicated by way of illustration. Having done what, should one ring [the bell]? To this he says: "The bell," and so forth.
The bell is *saṃvṛti* (conventional truth).
Its sound is as follows:
"All phenomena are pure by nature; through their natures they are rendered non-existent. By sentient beings who are pure by nature, the supreme existence is brought about."
Such is the recitation of the verse and the understanding of its meaning.
This is that wisdom of all the Buddhas known as "following the sound";
it must indeed always be maintained by you as well, for awakening is considered supreme by the Victors.
The meaning is that, by reciting this verse, one should ring the bell given by the venerable Guru, taking hold of the resonance of the bell's sound.
"Paṭahikām" refers to the auspicious drum;
the word "vā" (or) is used for the purpose of including another characteristic.
Even the practitioner may play that [instrument] according to the manifest sequence;
the word "even" (*api*) indicates that she has been given everything by the Guru, since she is not established as one who performs the act of taking.
"And he should cause a cry of 'Hāhā' to be made.
The "cry of Hāhā" is the consecration (abhiṣeka); that he should cause to be performed for himself by the venerable Guru.
"By such devotion as this, he would perform a hundred [times]"; the expression "he would cause to be performed" indicates that his devotion to the Guru is even greater than that.
The term *hāhākāra* is also called such because it is similar to the other in being composed of sound; thus it is so designated.

From that, the reception of the water, crown, and vajra-sovereignty initiations follows, since those two [initiations] are preceded by them. Furthermore, it should be understood that the teacher should ring the bell for a different purpose.
Having done what? He says: "The sounding of the bell" is the instruction for producing the sound of a subtle bell in the ten directions.

Alternatively, as before, the practitioner should likewise cause the recitation of the verses, the beating of the drum, and the cry of "hā hā. The cry of "hā hā" is a resonant humming sound (*jhaṃkāra*).
By the word "and" (ca), it should be understood that there is another specific type of instrumental music, namely song (*gīta*).
The resonance of the bell (*ghaṇṭānāda*) resides in its own characteristic form (*svaliṅga*).
It is designated as the "Twenty-fivefold" (*pañcaviṃśatikā*).
The bell is twelve years old;
the drum is sixteen years old.
The sound of the bell is the Vajra family.
The bell belongs to the Ratna family,
the small drum to the Padma family,
and the sound "hā hā" to the Tathāgata family.
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that one should practice another [rite] as well, such as the sound of a bell or any other [sound].
The meaning is that the practitioner—the disciple—should cause the sound of the bell to be made, or should utter the mantra "O, what bliss! (*aho sukham*).
To the question "Immediately after what?", he says: "The ring finger," and so forth.
The knower of yoga should always lick [the substance] with the curved ring finger and thumb;
having tasted it like the drinking of soma, he attains eternal perfection.
Thus these verses are to be applied here.

Then, its further meaning is as follows: that which has arisen through the previously mentioned cultivation of wisdom, the teacher should cause the disciple to taste with his tongue using the ring finger and the thumb.
And that disciple, having savored it like the drinking of *soma*, attains accomplishment; this is the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*).
For this very reason, the master initiation is established, because it is preceded by that [the disciple initiation]. || 2 ||
Having thus worshipped the mandala that fulfills all desires according to the prescribed rite,
he should cover the faces of those "spiritual sons" with a cloth.
To the question "Immediately after what does all this occur?", he says: "In this way," and so forth.
By means of the flowers and other items previously mentioned;
the mandala is that which was previously described, whether constructed with colored powders or depicted on a cloth.
The connection is as follows: "Having worshipped" means having performed full worship, one should cause [them] to enter there after the obstacles have been destroyed.
To the question "Whom?", he says: "the *putrakas*.
They are called *putras* because they purify (*punanti*) and protect (*trāyante*).
Therefore, in this context of praise, "sons" refers to the disciples of the poet's work;
they are such because their knowledge has been mastered through recitation and because of their noble lineage and so forth.
Having done what? He says: "having concealed," and so on.
With a cotton cloth or a saffron-colored robe;
the plural number used for "those sons" is for the sake of generality, whereas in reality, one should cause each one individually to enter. || 3 ||
Having made a handful full of flowers, the practitioner, being well-composed, should then cast them forth correctly and perform a circumambulation. || 4 ||
Having composed his mind, the wise one should cause him to enter the beautiful city;
then, taking recourse to the southern form, he should cast a handful of flowers. || 5 ||
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "filled with flowers" (*puṣpapūrṇa*).
Immediately after entering, the practitioner should cast a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while turning clockwise;
that is, he should cast the handful of flowers while taking recourse to the southern image.

The instruction is that one should cast [the flowers] facing south, either by way of the clockwise circumambulation of the Blessed One or according to the sequence of the worship of the caitya. || 4-5 ||
Wherever [the flower] should fall upon the mandala, one should indicate that as his family (kula).
The preceptor should point out the sacred seats (pīṭha) of Śrī Heruka and so forth, and designate the name.
Then, on the second day, the preceptor, being well-composed, should worship the mudrā and duly perform the ritual for the disciples.
One should apply a tilaka-mark upon him with blood over which the mantra has been recited three times;
then, having unveiled the face of the disciple, one should show him the maṇḍala.
In the phrase "the seat of Śrī Heruka and so forth," the second case ending is elided.
It should be construed as: "having opened the mouth, one should then show the mandala.
The meaning is that immediately after showing the mandala, one should show the seats and so forth, characterized by Śrī Heruka and the rest.
With the words "Then," and so forth, he demonstrates the wisdom-consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*).
"Then" means immediately after the secret consecration; "the master" (*ācārya*) refers to one endowed with qualities such as fortitude and the like.
In that context, one should apply a *tilaka* mark using the blood of a menstruating woman, over which mantras such as *karakarādi* have been recited.
The meaning is that among those [initiates], whichever one has been introduced with his mouth opened, he must apply the *tilaka* mark. (6–8)
Whichever deity’s station belongs to whom, one should show those [deities] there;
then, having prostrated correctly, one should afterwards [show] the city together with the preceptor.
The meaning is that one should visualize that deity in whatever place belongs to that deity;
thus, one should visualize deities such as Śrī Heruka upon the seats (pīṭha) and so forth.
In the application of mindfulness of the body (kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna), there is Ḍākinī.
In the application of mindfulness to feeling is Lāmā; in the application of mindfulness to phenomena is Khaṇḍarohā;
and in the application of mindfulness to mind is Rupiṇī—one should thus explain the reality of the maṇḍala and the reality of the deities.

Then, having prostrated correctly together with the preceptor, [the teacher] should show the mandala in front [of the disciple]. That is to say: after the opening of the disciple’s mouth, having prostrated to the mandala and having applied the tilaka, he should display the mandala before him. || 9 ||

Having again performed a circumambulation, and having prostrated correctly before the mandala according to the ritual rules, one should offer it to the Guru from the left side at the commencement of the return.
Then one should give to the guru the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as spoken by the Tathāgata:
gold of pure origin amounting to one hundred thousand [units], and various kinds of jewels.
A hundred pairs of garments, as well as an elephant, a horse, and the kingdom itself; earrings, bracelets, necklaces, armlets, and the most excellent [ornaments]. (12)
Having again performed a circumambulation, one should turn to the left by reversing the starting point;
that is, having again performed a circumambulation, one should encircle the mandala by turning to the left and then moving counter-clockwise.
Then, having prostrated before the mandala and the guru, one should give the teacher the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as prescribed by the Tathāgata.
Following the explanation of the reality (*tattva*) of the deities of the mandala, the disciple offers a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru;
thereafter follow the water and other consecrations, preceded by the offering of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), up to the conclusion of the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).
Then follows the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*).
This is the collective meaning of the text analyzed individually.
He states the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the words beginning "nirjātya" and so forth.
That which exists in the genus (*jāti*) is "genus-born" (*jātya*).
"Nirjātya" means free from all impurities;
that which is both "nirjātya" and "suvarṇa" (gold) weighing a hundred thousand [palas] is so described.
It refers to gold numbering one hundred thousand palas.
The word *gaja* is a term with its case-ending elided.
*Aṅgulikaiḥ* means "with finger-rings"; the third case is used here in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).
The most excellent crown. || 10-12 ||
Having prostrated, he should offer a golden sacred thread, or his own wife, daughter, male or female servant, or even his sister. (13)
The golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) means a *yajñopavīta* made of gold. "O slave" (*dāsa*) is used without a case ending. All of this he should offer to the guru.
One should constantly serve a teacher of the excellent tradition even at the cost of one's own life;
how much more so with sons, wives, and other things that ought not to be given away, let alone with unstable wealth?
Because of this statement. || 13 ||
The wise person should offer themselves to the guru with their whole being:
"From this day forward, I am your servant; I have been surrendered by me unto you. (14)
"The wise one should offer himself to the guru with his whole being.
"Whole being" refers to the activity of the body and so forth.
"Buddhi" (the intellect) refers to the realization that "this is inexhaustible" and "it is thus limitless."
He speaks of the gift of oneself—beginning with "the self," etc.
The word "samarpitā" (offered) is used without a case ending. || 14 ||
Having thus performed this rite with firm resolve, the ḍākinīs and the Mothers of Yoga will then be pleased with him. (15)

With the words "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth, he provides the conclusion of the section: the procedure for the gift of gold and other items mentioned immediately above has been "well-ascertained" (*suṣṭhu niścitaḥ*) by the practitioner; that is to say, it has been accepted as excellent and approved.
"From that" (*tataḥ*) refers to the ritual procedure.
He states the fruit of the completed rite with the words "The *ḍākinīs*" and so forth.
"Ḍākinīs" refers to the classes of ḍākinīs.
He states the distinction with the words "yoga," and so forth:
there are twenty-four Yoga-mothers (yogamātṛ). 15.
The ḍākinīs, as well as the lāmās, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rupiṇī—the practitioner should wander throughout this entire world together with these ḍākinīs. (16)
All of them become servants to that practitioner, there is no doubt;
for these, the perfection of yoga arises, unimpeded throughout the three worlds. || 17 ||
Invisibility, emergence from a hole, and the power of moving through the air, as well as foot-ointment and elixirs—these always arise eternally for the practitioner according to his will. (18)
She assumes many forms and travels through space;
as a ḍākinī, she especially crushes all living beings. (19)
The *ḍākinīs* are those such as Kākāsyā and others; the *lāmas* are those belonging to the *lāmā* class.
The word *lāma* is a synonym for *lāmā*.
Alternatively, this is a word ending in the plural number, resulting from the elision of the vowel *ā* and the substitution of the letter *ya*.
"By these," and so forth.

By entering such a mandala, by performing worship, and by receiving initiation, one should traverse the entire world with the ḍākinīs acting as the instruments, for the sake of accomplishing the siddhis, preceded by its [the mandala's] construction.
The meaning is that one makes even the inaccessible accessible.
The [mantra] beginning with "by these ḍākinīs" and so forth is to be accomplished through the addition, elision, transposition, and modification of phonemes as prescribed by etymology (*nirukta*).
This is because the Vedic [mantra] is to be accomplished primarily through those [etymological methods].
Thus it is in all cases.
Alternatively, one should not suspect the presence of incorrect words (*apaśabda*) due to the unconventional nature [of the text]:
"arise" (*uttiṣṭha*) refers to the reviving of the dead,
and "destruction-knowledge" (*niṣūdana-jñāna*) means killing.
The remainder is easily understood. || 16–19 ||
Through the yoga seen but once, the state of a yogi arises in an instant;
yet he who seeks the state of a yogi without having seen the maṇḍala [is not so]. (20)
One strikes at the sky with one's fist and drinks a mirage;
this is the best and most excellent yoga, the highest among all yogas. 21.
"Without having seen the maṇḍala," and so forth, refers to the praise of the maṇḍala.
Just as one might strike at space with a fist, yet those functional effects characterized by striking are not accomplished;
or as one might drink from a mirage, yet there is no functional effect characterized by drinking, nor any characterized by the quenching of thirst.
Likewise, he who desires the state of a yogin without having seen the maṇḍala does not obtain the fruit of yoga. || 20-21 ||
Whoever desires it shall overcome the world including the gods, asuras, and humans; he who has been consecrated here in this mandala is a practitioner of all the tantras taught. || 22 ||
Having performed the secret gaze, the joining of hands, the embrace, the union, and so forth, one becomes consecrated therein as the sole supreme authority over all tantras. (23)
Whether in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Saṃvara*, the *Guhyasamāja*, or the *Vajrabhairava*, this King of Maṇḍalas has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. || 24 ||
Whatever has been said and whatever has not been said, all that resides within Śrī Heruka. || 25 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, the ritual procedure for the initiation of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇābhiṣeka*), in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"Whoever shall desire"— that is,
whoever shall desire the boon of Śrī Heruka in this manner, he shall go forth having overcome the gods and others.
Here, the root *gam* has the sense of "to abide."
The sense is that it will remain.
In order to show that it is neither past, nor future, nor even presently arisen, there is the future designation beginning with "it will desire" (*kāṅkṣiṣyati*).
And [the phrase] "whether stated or unstated."
Whatever has been stated and whatever has not been stated elsewhere—all that ritual procedure for the mandala is established within the Śrī Heruka Cakrasaṃvara. 22–25.
The "gift" (dakṣiṇā) is the giving [of offerings] out of an excess of reverence;
the "consecration" (abhiṣeka) is the removal of the stains of the afflictions;
[this is] the procedure for those two.
The chapter that expresses this is the third.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 3.
The fourth chapter on the ritual procedure, titled "The Non-duality of the Hero and the Yoginī.
Thereafter, the ḍākinīs cause the worlds to expand:
Mahāvīryā, Cakravartinī, Mahābalā, and Suvīrā. (1)
Cakravarmiṇī, Śauṇḍinī, Khaṇḍarohā, Cakravegā, Khagānanā, Hayakarṇā, Subhadrā, and likewise Śyāmādevī. || 2 ||
Surābhakṣī, Vāyuvegā, and likewise Mahābhairavā;
Airāvatī, Drumacchāyā, Laṅkeśvarī, and Kharvarī as well. || 3 ||
Vīramatī, Mahānāsā, and Prabhāvatī,
as well as Caṇḍākṣī and Pracaṇḍā— these are the accomplished ones for the practitioner.
Indeed, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, there are twenty-four ḍākinīs in the east.
Just as it is externally, so it is within oneself—in the midst of body, speech, and mind—the mantras consisting of the utterance of one's own name are joined with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end. (5)
Immediately after the description of the foundational maṇḍala, the fourth chapter is introduced with the words "Then," etc., in order to show the yoginīs who reside within it.

Since those ḍākinīs who are said to be within the sphere of conventional practice (*samayācāra*) consist of the nature of the Emanation, Enjoyment, and Dharma bodies (*nirmāṇa-sambhoga-dharmakāya*) of body, speech, and mind, for that reason the twenty-four ḍākinīs pervade— meaning they extend through— the twenty-four worlds and the three wheels (*cakras*) of body and so forth.
He states those very [names] as "Mahāvīryā" and so forth:
Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Śauṇḍinī.
Cakravarmiṇī, Suvīrā, Mahābalā,
Cakravartinī and Mahāvīryā—these are all white; this is the body wheel (kāyacakra). Airāvatī and Mahābhairavā...
Vāyuvegā,
Surābhakṣī,
Śyāmādevī,
Subhadrā, Hayakarṇā,
and Khagānanā— these are red; such is the wheel of speech (vākcakra).
Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, Mahānāsā,
Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī,
"Drumacchāyā" and these others are "Kṛṣṇā"; this is the wheel of the mind (*cittacakra*).
Since in the previous tantra the sequence was indeed reversed, he says: "But beginning with Pracaṇḍā.
Taking Pracaṇḍā as the first, Caṇḍākṣī and the others are to be understood [in their proper order].

The utterance of each respective name; by that [utterance], they are joined with the preceding [syllables] according to the sequence stated in the *Sādhana*, such as the mantras beginning with *kara-karā*. These are the "mantras consisting of the utterance of one's own name. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative (*prathamārthe*).
They are "joined with *hūṃ hūṃ* and ending in *phaṭ*";
that is, those for which *hūṃ hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are joined at the end of the name. || 1–5 ||
Having seen the most excellent and supreme yoga, all other [practices] are like chaff;
it is the lamp of the syllable Om, which bestows all perfections and fulfills all desires.

Regarding the term *omkāradīpikā*: those [mantras] for which the syllable *oṃ* is the illuminator (*dīpaka*) in the preceding [part] by means of mantras such as *karakarādi* are thus [called]. Therefore, this is the meaning.
*Oṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, etc., for the eight [deities] beginning with Cakravega;
*oṃ phaṭ phaṭ airāvatī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, etc., for the eight [deities] beginning with Airāvatī;
*oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, etc., for the eight [deities] beginning with Pracaṇḍā.
Thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the mandala and the body.
From that very [placement] arises the wheel of mind (cittacakra),
and from that, the wheel of speech (vākcakra).
Then there is the body wheel (*kāyacakra*).
However, in the tantra, that [order] is transposed for the sake of instruction.
Furthermore, there is another meaning for the phrase "joined with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end."
The phrase "joined at the end of the mantra *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*" uses the nominative case in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*);
because they are situated within [the mantra], the eight [deities] beginning with Kākāsyā are "joined at the end.
The four [deities] beginning with Ḍākinī are situated in the center.
These mantra-born goddesses are to be visualized according to their specific times.
For instance, [the mantras] such as *om hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, *kākāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, and so forth.
Pracaṇḍā and the others, ending with Drumacchāyā, reside in the mind wheel (*cittacakra*).
And that [wheel] is black. Airāvatī and the others, ending with Khagānanā, reside in the wheel of speech; and that [wheel] is red.
Cakravega and the others, ending with Mahāvīrya, reside in the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*);
that [wheel] is white.
The four, beginning with Ḍākinī, are respectively black, dark green, red, and pale yellow, arranged in a counter-clockwise direction; Yamadāḍhī and the others have attained two colors each.
"Granting success and fulfilling all desires"—these [deities] joined together are the lords of Śrī Heruka; these two are the qualifiers of the term "maṇḍala. || 6 ||
The perfected ones (siddhas) have attained heroism by beholding the maṇḍala in the home;
therefore, having understood this, one should constantly cultivate existence, for such is the word of the Tathāgata regarding accomplishment.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the chapter on the ritual procedure for the dyad of the Hero and the Yoginī, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 4.
"Attained the state of heroes" is an epithet for the twenty-four yoginīs.
This means they have attained the state of heroes— that is, the status of being the limbs of the heroes— meaning they are joined with the embrace of the heroes.

The heroes, however, are Khaṇḍakāpāla and the others. They have one face, four arms, and three eyes; they wear a crown of matted hair and a cloth garment, and are clad in tiger-skin robes. With their two left and right hands holding a vajra and a vajra-bell while embracing [the consort], and with their other left and right hands holding a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaru, they stand in the ālīḍha posture and are endowed with ornaments such as bracelets and earrings. Their colors correspond to those of the consorts who match them.
Pracaṇḍā and the others also have their two arms embraced [by their consorts], while their other left and right hands hold blood-filled skull-cups and display the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
Ḍākinī and the others hold a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup with their two left hands, and hold a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and a flaying knife (*kartī*) with their right hands.
Kākāsyā and the others bear the same emblems as Ḍākinī and the others.
Yamadāḍhī and the others hold a *ḍamaru* drum and a flaying knife in their two left hands, and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff and a skull-cup in their right hands.

The thirty-six yoginīs, beginning with Ḍākinī, have three eyes and one face; they have disheveled hair, are naked, stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, and possess fierce forms. They are adorned with necklaces and other ornaments, as well as garlands of vajras upon their foreheads; such are the heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīriṇī*).
The nature of the deities is stated as follows: Ḍākinī has the nature of the application of mindfulness to the body;
Lāmā has the nature of the application of mindfulness to feelings;
Khaṇḍarohā has the nature of the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
The wheel of gnosis is material in nature, having the mindfulness of mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*) as its intrinsic nature.

Pracaṇḍā has the basis of psychic power through desire (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*) as her intrinsic nature; Caṇḍākṣī has the basis of psychic power through effort (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*) as her intrinsic nature.
Prabhāvatī has the nature of the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation;
Mahānāsā has the nature of the basis of psychic power consisting of mind;
Vīramatī has the nature of the faculty of faith.
Kharvarī has the nature of the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*); Laṅkeśvarī has the nature of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*);
and Drumacchāyā has the nature of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)—this is the wheel of mind (*cittacakra*).
Airāvatī has the nature of the faculty of wisdom;
Mahābhairavā has the nature of the power of faith;
Vāyuvegā has the nature of the power of vigor.
Surābhakṣī has the nature of the power of mindfulness;
Śyāmādevī has the nature of the power of meditative concentration;
Subhadrā has the nature of the power of wisdom.
Hayakarṇā has the nature of the concentration factor of enlightenment (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga); Khagānanā has the nature of the vigor factor of enlightenment (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Thus is the wheel of speech (vākcakra).
Cakravegā has the nature of the awakening factor of joy; Khaṇḍarohā has the nature of the awakening factor of tranquility;
Śauṇḍinī has the nature of the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena.
Cakravarmiṇī has the nature of the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; Suvīrā has the nature of the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity;
Mahābalā has the nature of right view.
Cakravartinī has the nature of right intention;
Mahāvīryā has the nature of right speech—this is the body wheel (kāyacakra).
Kākāsyā has the nature of right action.
Ulūkāsyā has right livelihood as her intrinsic nature; Śvānāsyā has right effort as her intrinsic nature; Śūkārāsyā has right mindfulness as her intrinsic nature.
Yamadāḍhī has the nature of producing unarisen wholesome dharmas; Yamadūtī has the nature of protecting arisen wholesome dharmas;
Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī has the nature of not abandoning arisen unwholesome dharmas.
The nature of not producing unarisen unwholesome dharmas is Yamamathanī; this is the cremation ground wheel (*śmaśānacakra*).
Śrī Heruka has the nature of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Thus it is said, "the accomplished ones" (*siddhāḥ*).
"Having seen the twenty-four yoginīs in the house as the maṇḍala" means having seen the maṇḍala within one's own body.
The intended meaning is that, having understood that accomplishment arises from the meditation on the maṇḍala, one should then perform that meditation.
"According to the word of the Tathāgata":
the intended meaning is that one should meditate by means of the word of the Tathāgata. || 7 ||
The twenty-four Vīrayoginīs are those endowed with heroes (vīra).
The twelve non-dual ones are those devoid of heroes;
their short vowel length is due to Vedic usage.
The chapter that explains their ritual placement and procedure is the fourth.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 4.
The fifth chapter on the procedure for extracting the syllables of the root mantra follows: Then—
in the *Sarvadharmodaya*— the universe [is located] in the pericarp, and the unstruck (*anāhata*) Śiva [is located] there.
The mantra-practitioner should, according to the prescribed rule, draw that which is the sole compendium of all dharmas. || 1 ||
The accomplishment of *siddhi* is achieved not through mere meditation alone, but also by means of [the extraction of mantras]; thus he says "therefore," and so forth.
For that reason, the mantra is to be extracted.
He states the method of extraction with the words "all," and so forth.
It is the arising of all phenomena,
because they arise from it;
it is the universe, because it possesses all colors.
"By the pericarp" means by means of the *karṇikā*.
"Anāhata" means pervaded on all sides (*samantād āpta*) because it brings about auspiciousness (*śiva*).
The meaning is that such is the lotus.
Because it is specified by the pericarp according to the principle that "a cognition of the qualified does not arise without the qualifier having been apprehended.
Alternatively, *dharmodaya* and *bhaga* are synonymous;
the universe (*viśva*) is endowed with the universal lotus (*viśvapadma*) because it is struck by the pericarp.
The connection is that one should not spread [the mandala] solely within the *viśvapadma* (double lotus) or inside the *dharmodayā* (source of phenomena).
Having done what? He says: "having drawn," and so forth.
All phenomena (*sarvadharma*), consisting of the vowels beginning with *a* and the consonants beginning with *ka*, are gathered together as one by means of this.
Thus, "the world consisting of forty-nine squares" and "the diagram" (prastāra) are synonyms. || 1 ||
In this regard, there are these mantra-words:
"O best of sages, having made the *āli* and *kāli* equal and transformed them from their groups, one should know that [the syllables] are arranged four by four upon the grid. (2)
Regarding this, it is said that there are mantra-words here.
Here, in the world consisting of forty-nine squares, there are locations for mantras;
these are eight, and this is the root-mantra of the Blessed One because it contains all parts.
The designation "mantra" applies to the light of the syllables, just as the term "cloth" applies to a continuous series of threads.
To the question, "What, then, should one spread out? he says: "Ālī," and so forth.
Here, "ālī" is [the form] when the dual case-ending is elided, and "kālī" is likewise.

"Equal" means that there is no accompanying vowel even for a single consonant, as seen in other grammatical rules where it is stated that [the *anusvāra*] is excluded except in the case of *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*.
Having thus made Āli and Kāli, one should spread them out—that is, one should strew them.
They are transformed; that is, they are directly transformed.
Transformation is a specific state.
He asks, "What is this? and replies: "From the groups. This is the ablative case used with the elision of a gerund (*lyap*), meaning: having reached the eight groups, she has been transformed.
The meaning is that it is a specific state consisting of eight groups.
Therefore, he says "caturbhiḥ" and so forth: one should arrange it in such a way that what is to be known is known by means of four groups each.
He is called a *muni* because he possesses wisdom (*manana*).

Between the two systems—the system of the Perfections (*pāramitānaya*) and the system of Mantras (*mantranaya*)—this follower of the Mantra system is the most excellent. He who knows the expansion [of the alphabet] is a follower of the Mantra system and the best of sages (*munisattama*). In that regard, the sixteen vowels beginning with ‘A’ constitute one group.
There are five groups [of consonants] consisting of five letters each, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
There is one group consisting of the four letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*;
another consists of *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*.

Here, the letter *kṣa* is not shown because it is not employed [in this context] and because it is produced from the conjunction of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*. In this manner, the eight groups (*varga*) are to be understood. || 2 ||
One should extract the Hero situated therein, which accomplishes all desires and goals:
that which is the fifth of the fourth and also the fifth of the fifth.

"One should extract the Hero situated there" means that one should extract the eight-syllable mantra of the Hero residing within the *ālikāli* (vowels and consonants), like butter from curd. The rest is clear.
"Of the fourth, that which is the fifth":
the letter *na* is the fifth of the fourth group;
the fifth of the fifth [group] is the letter *ma*. (3)
The fourth of the fifth, the third of the first, likewise the twenty-ninth, and the first of the fourth. (4)
The fourth letter of the fifth [group], which is *bha*;
the third letter of the first [group], which is *ga*.
The word "tu" (but/however) distinguishes it by way of praise.
Because one destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of this, it is "bha";
and that is the meaning of *bhaga*.
The letter *ga* is to be explained afterwards.
And thus it is said: "The letter *bha* they call *bhaga*.
Likewise, the letter *va* is the twenty-ninth;
the phrase "and likewise that" indicates the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārtha*).
The letter *va* is so called because it connects (*vāti sambadhnāti*) wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
It is the first letter of the fourth [consonant] group; that is, starting from the *ka*-group, it is the first of the fourth group. (4)
Taking the fourth of those [consonants] situated within, its very second, as well as the thirtieth and likewise the twenty-sixth; || 5 ||
The fourth among those situated within [the semivowels] is the letter *va*;
the meaning is that it is dental-labial (*dantauṣṭhya*).
"Of that very [letter], the second" refers to the letter *t*.
The connection is as follows: having taken the second syllable of that very same internal group, one should extract the Hero (vīra).
Regarding the phrase "the thirtieth":
the letter Śa is palatal (tālavya).
And the word "tu" (but/and) has the sense of "for the purpose of pacification.
The meaning is that it is the thirtieth;
likewise, it is also the twenty-sixth.
The twenty-sixth is the letter *ya*.
Its meaning is likewise that of wind. (5)
Having extracted all of this, and likewise again half of half of fifty,
one should then take the thirty-third, which is the first of the first.
The letter *ma* is half of half of a hundred;
"likewise again" means that this [letter] is the indicator that all phenomena have reached death.

"Then, having taken the thirty-third"— the connection is that one should extract the *vīra* after taking [the letters] following the letter *ha* and the letter *ma*. "The first of the first," however...
In the section on consonants (*vyañjana*), the *ka*-group is first. Its first letter is the letter *ka*.
It does not abide anywhere.
The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of "the meaning of the letter 'ka'. || 6 ||
The third of the labials, the third of the first [class], and the thirty-second of the fourth, which is the fifth [of the consonants]. (7)
"The third of those situated within" refers to the letter *la*,
which establishes the quality of being earthy (*pārthivatva*).
"The third of the first," however, refers to the letter *ga*.
The meaning of the word "tu" is that its nature is the profound reality of the Dharma.
"And indeed the thirty-second" means that the letter *sa* is the thirty-second.
The word "ca" (and) itself indicates its dental nature;
it is the letter *na*, which is the fifth of the fourth [class]. || 7 ||
