The fifth [consonant] is that which is the fourth; the [fifth] is that which is the first of the semivowels (āntastha);
the second [consonant] is that which is the third; and the third [consonant] is that which is the first. (8)
The fourth [letter] of the fifth [group], which is the letter *bha*;
and the first [letter] of the semivowels (*āntastha*), which is [the letter *ya*]. This group of semivowels is called "semivowel" (*āntastha*).
Of that [word], the first is the letter *ya*.
Of the second, it is the third, namely the letter *ja*,
when it has the sense of "muttering" (*japa*).
Of the third [syllable], that which is the first is the letter *ṭa*. || 8 ||
The fifth of the fifth, the first of the first,
as well as the eleventh and the sixteenth— thus they know them.
"The fifth of the fifth" refers to the letter *ma*;
"the first of the first, however" refers to the letter *ka*.
The word "tu" (however) indicates that the conjunction of the letters *ra* and *ka*, and so forth, serves as an illuminator of desire (*kāmadīpaka*).
"Likewise, and indeed the eleventh.
The word "likewise" (tathā) indicates that, as a constituent part of the syllable *phaṭ*, it serves the purpose of causing the falling [of obstacles].
The "eleventh" refers to the letter *ṭ*.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), he states that the letter *pha*, which occurred previously for him, must necessarily be joined at the end of the mantra; this is why the particle "eva" is used.
Regarding the phrase "they know the sixteenth thus":
the sixteenth itself is the sixteenth.
The suffix *ma* is used in the sense of the base word itself; it is like the word *druma*.
And that [suffix] is the letter *t*.
The word *taṃ* (that) is in the accusative case because it is governed by the verb *viduḥ* (they know).

Furthermore, in expressions such as "the fifth of the fifth," and likewise "the fifth of the fourth," one should understand that having taken the fifth letter of the fourth group (*varga*), and then taking the fifth of that fifth [group], one should extract the *Vīra*.
Or rather, they know [the procedure] thus: having taken the letter which is the fifth of the fourth group, and then taking the fifth of the fifth [group], one should extract the *Vīra*.
In this way, that which is the fifth letter is the fourth, and so forth.
The word "tathā" (thus) demonstrates that its nature is to establish the sixteen emptinesses. || 9 ||
The first of the third [group], as well as the twenty-sixth;
the third of the fourth, and indeed two of the sibilants (ūṣman). || 10 ||
The first *ṭa*-kāra of the third [chapter] is the twenty-sixth, which they know to be the *ya*-kāra; this is the second [syllable] by virtue of the action [of knowing]. Thus it is everywhere.
There is the elision of the letter *ta* in the twenty-sixth and subsequent [syllables].
Likewise, "thus" (*tathā*) indicates its nature as the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu*).
"The third of the fourth," however, refers to the letter *da*.
The word "tu" (but) indicates that its purpose is to burn away evil. Regarding the statement "only two of the *ūṣman*s":
*ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h* are the *ūṣman*s.
"Of the *ūṣman*s" [is stated] because of the addition of that phoneme (*varṇāgama*).
"The pair" refers to the second *ṣakāra*. "And likewise" means: [and so forth].
And the word "another" (anya) is for the purpose of restriction (avadhāraṇa). || 10 ||
The first [syllable] of the first [group], as well as the twenty-seventh and the twenty-eighth;
then again, the third of the first [group]. || 11 ||
The first [syllable] of the first [word], namely the letter *ka*;
the twenty-seventh [letter], which is *ra*;
and its status as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Agni is indicated by the word "thus" (*tathā*).
The twenty-eighth is the letter *la*.
The word "again" (*punar*) indicates that it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Earth.
"The third of the first," however, refers to the letter *ga*.
The word *tu* proceeds with a specific sense: emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is that which "always abides" (*sadā-vatiṣṭhate*); because it denotes that [state], its meaning is "to go" (*gaty-artha*). || 11 ||
From the fifth [chapter], one should take the thirty-first;
likewise the fifteenth and the twenty-fifth. (12)
The fourth letter of the fifth [varga], the letter *bha*, is also included;
the word "also" (*api*) indicates the meaning previously stated.
Thus, the thirty-first is taken from there.
Having taken the letter *ṣa*, which is the thirty-first [letter] of *kāli*,
as well as the fifteenth;
"likewise" (*tathā*) means the fifteenth [letter] of *kāli*, which is the letter *ṇa*.
The word "evam" (thus) serves to determine the connection with "kāli" (the letter K).
"The twenty-fifth likewise" refers to the letter M. The meaning of the word "tathā" (likewise) is precisely that. || 12 ||
The second of the first [group], likewise the twenty-sixth, the thirty-second syllable, and indeed the last of the sibilants (ūṣman). || 13 ||
"But the second of the first" refers to the letter *kha*. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that its meaning is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Likewise, "the twenty-sixth again":
"likewise" (tathā) means the letter *ya* as before;
the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is a rhetorical ornament for the sentence.
"And the thirty-second syllable as well.
The thirty-second syllable is the letter *sa*.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that its nature is that of water.
The particle *eva* here functions as a restrictive [particle].
"And the very last of the sibilants" refers to the letter *ha*.
"And likewise" serves to restrict the connection with the end of the [first] half-verse. || 13 ||
Furthermore, the thirty-second [letter], then the fourth of the fifth [vowel], the third of the second [vowel], and the fourth of the fifth [vowel]. (14)
"Furthermore, the thirty-second" means the letter *sa*, which consists of thirty-two syllables. "Furthermore" indicates that this statement refers back to the meaning of the preceding sentence.
"But the fourth of the fifth" refers to the letter *bha*. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that this [letter] removes fear.
"And the third of the second [consonant class]" refers to the letter *ja*. The word *caiva* (and indeed) emphasizes that this [letter] serves the purpose of victory (*jayārthatva*).
"But the fourth of the fifth" refers to the letter *bha*.
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates its previously mentioned meaning. || 14 ||
The third of the sibilants (ūṣman), and the twenty-seventh which follows;
the first of the semivowels (antaḥstha), and likewise the twenty-first again. (15)
"And the third of the *ūṣman*s" refers to the letter *sa*,
as before. "The twenty-seventh, supreme" refers to the letter *ha*.
The letter *ra* [is the first],
because it generates fire;
and it is the first among the semivowels (*antaḥstha*).
The letter *ya*;
and the word *caiva* (and indeed) expresses both conjunction and restriction;
likewise, the word *punar* (again) refers to the twenty-first [syllable].
“Tathā” indicates that it was spoken by the Tathāgata.
The letter *pa* is the twenty-first.
Furthermore, [the syllable] *gu* is without elaboration. 15.
That which is the second of the semi-vowels (antaḥsthā), and likewise the thirtieth;
that which is the first of the fifth [class], and also the first of the sibilants (ūṣman). || 16 ||
"Of those situated within, that which is the second" refers to the second syllable, the letter *ra*. "The thirtieth, likewise" refers to the same.
The letter Śa is the thirtieth.
The word "punaḥ" (again) indicates its repetition.
Likewise, the term "tathā" (thus) is indicative of the meaning: "it teaches peace," hence it is "śa."
The first letter of the fifth [varga], which is the letter *pa*;
and the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*),
which is the letter *śa*.
The particle *ca* signifies "and," while *eva* signifies "peace" (*śānti*), "primacy" (*prathama*), and "restriction" (*avadhāraṇa*). || 16 ||
Likewise, the first of the fourth [varga] is the letter *ya*;
and the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is likewise the twenty-eighth. (17)
And likewise,
"having taken up the form *dyā*": the connection is that one should extract the *vīra* [syllable] after having taken up the form *dyā*.
The first *takāra* of the fourth [varga],
the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) which is *śakāra*,
and the twenty-eighth, which is *tatha*.
The letter *la*.
By saying "so be it," he indicates that this [letter] possesses the same meaning as what was previously stated. || 17 ||
The second [syllable] of the first [word], however, is said to be the first of the third;
likewise, the third of the first and the fourth of the fourth. (18)
"But the second of the first" refers to the letter *kha*, as before. "The first of the third" is now stated.
The letter *ṭa*;
the third [letter] of the first [group], which is *ga*;
and the fourth [letter] of the fourth [group].
The syllable *dha*: it indicates that *dha* signifies "he blows away evil" (*dhamati pāpam*); the word *tu* is used as a particle of emphasis. || 18 ||
The second of the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), the fifth of the third [class],
the letter *vī* (the fourth of the first class), and likewise the eighth— these they call the "Hero" (*vīra*). 19.
Of those [consonants] situated within, the second is *repha* (the letter *r*).
Regarding the phrase "also the fifth of the third," the word "also" (*api*) is used for emphasis.
Thus it is everywhere.
The fifth is the letter *ṇa*. They call the letter *vyā* "the Hero."
Because he attains distinction (*viśeṣa*), he is *vyā*. They call that hero Śrī Heruka.
The fourth letter of the first [vowel] is the syllable *gha*.
"And likewise, it is indeed the eighth.
The word "likewise" (tathā) indicates the pursuit of victory;
the particle "indeed" (eva) serves to emphasize that [point].
The letter *ja* occurs every eighth [time]. The word *eva ca* indicates the number eight for the time (*kāla*). || 19 ||
The fifth of the fourth, and also the fifth of the fifth;
likewise, the twenty-seventh, and the fourth of the fourth.
The fifth of the fourth is the letter *na*;
the fifth of the fifth is the letter *ma*;
and likewise, the twenty-seventh is the letter *ta*.
The letter *ra*.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates the meaning previously stated.
[This refers to] "the fourth of the fourth."
The syllable *dhakāra*.
The word *tu* has the sense of "again" (*punar*). || 20 ||
Furthermore, taking the twenty-seventh, as well as the twenty-sixth, the twenty-fifth, and the thirty-third. (21)
"Furthermore, the twenty-seventh" means the twenty-seventh letter, *ra*. The word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) is used in the same sense as before.
"Likewise, indeed, even the twenty-sixth.
The word "likewise" (tathā) means "in that very manner" (tathaiva), with the elision of the middle member (madhyamapadalopa).
The twenty-sixth is the letter *ya*.
The phrase "and thus" indicates that this [mantra] possesses the same meaning as what was previously stated.
Regarding the expression "having taken the twenty-fifth," the connection is: "having taken the letter *ma*, one should extract the Hero (*vīra*)."
"Having taken up" (samādāya) [the vow] elsewhere as well, and specifically in the case of the Thirty-three [Heavens], he emphasizes the syllable *ha*.
He determines that the meaning of *ha* is "it destroys (*hanti*) the evil of sentient beings"; indeed, this is precisely what the word *ca* ("and") signifies. || 21 ||
The fourth of the fourth, the fifth of the fifth,
the fifth of the fourth as well,
the first of the first, and likewise the twenty-seventh. (22)
The fourth of the semivowels (antaḥstha), likewise the twenty-first;
the second of the sibilants (ūṣman), and likewise the twenty-sixth. (23)
"Regarding 'the fourth of that, however, is the fourth': [this refers to] the letter *dh*. The word 'however' (*tu*) has the sense of 'again' (*punar*)."
The fifth [letter] of the fifth [group] is the letter *ma*.
The fifth [letter] of the fourth [group] is the letter *na*.
The word "also" (*api*) implies that it is likewise the first [letter] of the first [group] in the collection of the fifth.
The letter *ka*;
the word "and" (*caiva*) indicates the meaning previously stated;
and likewise, the twenty-seventh is the letter *ra*.
The word "tathā" indicates the state of being a producer of fire.
Regarding the phrase "the fourth of those situated within," it refers to the letter *va*.
The word "tu" indicates that it is the seed-syllable of Varuṇa.
"Likewise, the twenty-first" refers to the letter *pa*.
The word "tathā" (likewise) indicates its connection with the *āl* vowels.
And [the rule applies] to the sibilants (*ūṣman*) as well;
that is, to the letter *ṣ*.
The word "caiva" (and indeed) indicates a restriction regarding its position here;
likewise, it refers specifically to the twenty-sixth [letter],
which is the letter *ya*.
This is the extraction of the syllables of the root mantra. || 22-23 ||

KARA 2 KURU 2 BANDHA 2 TRĀSAYA 2 KṢOBHAYA 2 HRĀṂ 2 HRAḤ 2 PHEṂ 2 PHAṬ 2 DAHA 3 PACA 2 BHAKṢA 3 O YOU WHO ARE ADORNED WITH A GARLAND OF FLESH, BLOOD, AND ENTRAILS! GRAB 2 THE SERPENT RESIDING IN THE SEVEN UNDERWORLD REGIONS!
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the procedure for extracting the syllables of the root mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 5.
Therefore, he says: "Having known," and so forth.
*Śrīheruka* is the mantra by which one achieves accomplishment as Śrī Heruka;
having known that—that is, having realized it to be the source of accomplishment—one [should know] the other mantra-word (*mantrapada*) beyond that.
"Like straw":
this is a superimposition of action,
because it is fruitless in view of the result to be accomplished.

A *ghuṇa* is a specific kind of wood-boring insect. Wood eaten by it is called *ghuṇa*. Therefore, the meaning is this: the yogi considers another type of mantra to be devoid of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), like wood eaten by a *ghuṇa*, and fruitless, like straw; [only] that which is proclaimed as the root-mantra is [considered effective].
Having been analyzed by extracting the syllables, it is proclaimed as the "Prakīrtita. || 26 ||
Regarding the phrase "from the treasury," he says: "the root-mantra" (*mūlamantra*).
It is the root of all accomplishments (*siddhi*), and it is also a mantra; thus it is so called.
The sense is that the root-mantra is distinct from the King of Vidyās (*vidyārāja*).
And that [mantra] consists of eight syllables through the purity of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
The syllables are the consonants.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Cakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 5.
The sixth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for Extracting the Armor of the Six Heroes.
Hereafter follows the twenty-two-syllable Heart-mantra and the seven-syllable Sub-Heart-mantra. The seed-syllable is the eighth from the *ya*-group, likewise with twelve morae.
He says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to indicate that for those who prefer brevity, the instruction on the mantra has been condensed.
Since the teaching of the mantra was condensed for the sake of those who prefer brevity,
for that reason, there is the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) consisting of twenty-two syllables.
Because it is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The prefix *upa-* has the sense of "inferiority";
however, this inferiority pertains to the syllables, not to the result.
The meaning is that both of these will be explained further on.
Furthermore, he first states the abbreviated armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra), beginning with "the eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group" and so forth.
The eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group is the letter *ha*.
The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only) or the sense of a qualification (*viśeṣa*).
By "measures" (*mātraiḥ*), meaning by measures (*mātrābhiḥ*) excluding the neuter;
likewise, by those [syllables] which abide in specific meanings (*arthaviśeṣavartinībhiḥ*).
The third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic mark. || 1 ||
Having interspersed the syllables, the six-limbed Śrī Heruka is proclaimed;
through the unions with the six heroes, they are established in the single syllable. || 2 ||
"Having interposed the syllables" means having placed that seed-syllable between the syllables. "Śrī Heruka is called" occurs when the case ending has been elided.
And that consists of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), meaning it has six components.
Namely: *ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ*.
The connection is that Śrī Heruka is said to be [expressed] by making each syllable separated and interspersed with the next syllable.
For the purpose of grasping, from the syllable *ha* comes *hā*; from *hā*, separated by *hi*, comes *hī*;
from *hī*, from *hu* comes *hū*;
and from *hū*, from *he* comes *hai*.
From that *hekāra* as well, by means of *haikāra*, *hokāra* arises;
from that *hokāra* as well, by means of *haukāra*, *haṃkāra* arises.
Thus, according to the instruction regarding this "double intervention," these six are grasped.
These syllables are as follows: *ha*, *hi*, *hu*, *he*, *ho*, and *ham*—these six.
When do these become the non-dual vajra of Śrī Heruka? To this he says: "The six," and so forth.
Just as the mantras of the six heroes (*ṣaḍvīra*) are established in each individual syllable, at that time there is the state of the six limbs of Śrī Heruka.
The word "vīrāḥ" [is used] due to the elision of the nominative plural ending.
To the question "How are they such?", he says: "by means of the *samāyogas*.
*Samāyogas* are those yogas which are correct (*samyak*) from the beginning; by means of them.
The meaning is that before the letter *ha* and the others, there are the six beginning with *oṃ* and the heroes (*vīra*) and so forth. || 2 ||
The practitioner should know that the heart-mantras are those joined with *oṃ namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*. || 3 ||

He states the *oṃ* syllable and so forth: *oṃ namaḥ svāhā vauṣaṭ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the first [group], with the plural number elided. It should be understood that these are joined together as they occur; they are the "objects of knowledge," the heart-mantras of the six heroes.
By the word "tu" (but), he states by whom they are to be known: "by the practitioner. The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. || 3 ||
The first is indeed the heart, the second is remembered as the head;
one should assign the third to the crest-lock (śikhā), and the fourth shall be the armor (kavaca).
The fifth shall be the eye, and the sixth is called the weapon (astra).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the procedure for extracting the armor of the six heroes, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"But first, the heart itself"—
the word "but" (tu) includes one's own deity;
the same applies in the subsequent cases as well.
Oṃ ha, the heart.
Vajrasattva is the first. The nominative case in "heart" (hṛdayam) is used in the sense of the locative.
The second head is "Smṛti" (Memory). For Vairocana is remembered upon the head; "smṛtam" means that which is contemplated.
One should give the third as the *śikhā* (topknot),
with "Svāhā" and "Hūṃ" [as the seed syllables];
the fourth shall be the *kavaca* (armor).
The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a continuation.
"Vauṣaṭ" is for the head.
It should be understood from the oral instruction that "Kavaca" (the armor) is Śrī Heruka on the two shoulders.
"The fifth, however, shall be the eye.
*Hūṃ hūṃ ho*, O Vajrasūrya, [place these] upon the two eyes. "The weapon of the sixth is now declared."
*phaṭ haṃ Hayagrīvaḥ*.
The weapon-mantra (*astra*) is for all the limbs.
In the phrase "of the sixth," the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative.
In the case of "hṛdaya" and so forth, where the locative sense is intended, the nominative case is used for the accusative;
in all instances, the term "hṛdayāni" follows from the word "hṛdaya. (4)
These mantras, or those perfected from them, are the heroes (vīras) in these locations;
this is the Armor of the Six Heroes (Ṣaḍvīrakavaca),
because it cannot be pierced by the Māras.
Its extraction; the sixth chapter (paṭala) which expresses that [extraction].
In the reading "ṣaṣṭham," the letter *m* is used in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 6 ||
The seventh chapter: The Procedure for Extracting the Mantra.
Then:
[The mantra is formed] by joining the second syllable with the thirteenth of the vowels.
It is conjoined with the eleventh vowel and adorned with the sixth letter. || 1 ||
Previously, the extraction of the syllables of the eight-word mantra was performed.
Now, beginning the process of joining those syllables with the vowels, he says "of the vowels," and so forth.
In that context, the genitive case in the word *tatraiva* (in that very [place]) is used for the purpose of determining the extraction of the syllable *a*.
The thirteenth is the syllable *mokāra*.
The letter *ca* indicates a specific meaning.
The phrase "the sun's radiance, blazing with a thousand rays, when meditated upon on the head, forehead, and heart, brings about subjugation"—the particle *eva* emphasizes this very meaning.
"Joined with the second syllable" means that the second syllable is the letter *ma* following *na*; they know that it is joined with that [to form] the vowel *o*. From that, the form *mo* arises.
Thus, the sixth [vowel] and so forth indeed begin from the first letter *na*;
the eleventh vowel is *e*.
And that which is conjoined with it is "sa-tathā.
Therefore, it is adorned by the sixth vowel, the letter *e*;
from that, the form *te* would arise. (1)
They know the seventh syllable to be joined with the fourth vowel,
and the eighth syllable to be joined with the eleventh vowel.
The fourth of the vowels is *ī*.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the short vowel.
Thus, the seventh syllable indicated by this is *va*.
By that, it would be *vī-ru-paṃ*.
They know the eighth syllable to be the letter *ra* joined with the eleventh vowel; by that, it would be *re-ru-paṃ*.
This ritual applies everywhere. || 2 ||
Then, taking the ninth syllable conjoined with the second vowel, the twelfth syllable is likewise joined with the second of the vowels. (3)
"Then one should take the ninth"— that is, the letter *śa*. "From that" means from the first letter *na* which has been extracted.
The second vowel is *ā*;
by that, the form of *śā* is produced.
The twelfth syllable is *ha*.
They know it to be joined with the second vowel;
by that, its form shall be "hā. || 3 ||
Then, having taken the twenty-first [consonant] conjoined with the second vowel, it is considered the fourteenth syllable, joined with the twentieth syllable. (4)
Taking the fifteenth syllable joined with the third vowel, and likewise the fifteenth of the vowels, this beautiful sixteenth syllable [is formed]. (5)
"Then one should take the twenty-first":
having taken the twenty-first syllable, the letter *pa*,
conjoined with the second vowel, they know that the fourteenth syllable, the letter *la*, is joined with it.
From that, the form *lpā* would result.
Regarding "twenty syllables":
the twentieth syllable is the letter *na*.
Therefore, they know that the letter *ga*, joined with the fifteenth vowel below it,
is marked by the third vowel among the vowels, which is *i*.
By that, it would take the form of *agni*.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the long vowel.
The anusvāra is the fifteenth vowel.
They know that the sixteenth syllable, the letter *sa*, is honored by him;
through that, there would be the form of *sam*. (4–5)
The seventeenth syllable is joined with the third vowel,
and it is joined with the eighteenth syllable by means of the second of the vowels.
They know the seventeenth [letter], the letter *na*, conjoined with the third vowel as the "Supreme Benefit" (*paramaṃ hitam*).
This is because it effects the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of those who cause harm to the Guru, the Buddhas, and others.

Or, like one mounted upon a circle of wind, one visualizes the syllable *ta*—resembling a mass of smoke—at the heart, throat, navel, and both feet of the person to be targeted; by means of that, one expels it with the syllable *na*, whereby it becomes formless (*nirūpa*).
Furthermore, the eighteen-syllable mantra contains the syllable *bha*.
They know it to be conjoined with the second vowel. || 6 ||
The twenty-first syllable is conjoined with the vowel *ā* and the consonant *k*;
conjoined with the fifth letter of the alphabet (*m*), it becomes the twenty-third syllable. (7)
"Endowed with the natural sound of the letter Ā":
this refers to the twenty-first.
They know the twenty-first to be the letter *ṭa*.
The letter *u* is the fifth of the *mātṛkās*;
they know that the letter *ka*, when joined with it, consists of twenty-three syllables.
The thirteenth of the vowels, joined with that [consonant], forms the twenty-fourth syllable;
taking the first of the first [group], it is joined with the conjunct syllable to form the twenty-fifth syllable.
Taking the thirteenth vowel, which is the letter *o*, and knowing that it is joined with the twenty-fourth consonant, the letter *ṭ*;
they know the first letter of the first [group], which is *ka*.
The word *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

The letter *ka*, possessing a brilliance equal to the sun and joined with the *bindu*, when placed upon the heart, navel, and head of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), brings them under control. The particle *eva* serves to restrict the meaning to what has been enumerated.
To explain what kind of [letter] it is, he says: "joined with twenty-five syllables."
"Pañcāvaśati" refers to the twenty-fifth letter, which is *takāra*. It is joined with the preceding [letter] above; by that, the form *tka* is produced. || 8 ||
The first [syllable] of the third [group], however, joined with the second vowel, shall consist of twenty-six syllables;
and the twenty-eighth [syllable] is honored by the fifteenth.
Regarding the phrase "the first of the third," they know it to be the letter *ṭ*.
The letter *ṭ* has a radiance equal to Indra’s bow (a rainbow); when placed upon the forehead, heart, and throat of Sādhya, it brings him under control—this is the meaning of the word "tu.
It is conjoined with the second vowel.
The letter *ṭa* joined with the second vowel—that becomes the twenty-sixth syllable;
the meaning is that it takes the form of *ṭā*.
According to an alternative reading, "the first of the third, however, would be that of the second."
But for the second [syllable], it is indeed the second *mātrā*;
by means of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it is exactly like the form of *ṭā*.
And likewise, it is the twenty-eighth.
They know the letter *da*;
the letter *ca* is for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned.
The letter *da*, having a luster equal to a cloud, when visualized upon the head of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), paralyzes him.
The word "eva" is used here for emphasis.
The anusvāra is the fifteenth vowel;
by that, they know it as "arcita" (worshipped).
Therefore, it would have this form: || 9 ||
The first [letter] of the third [varga], joined with its lower part and conjoined with fire (the letter *ra*), and likewise joined with the second vowel, becomes the twenty-ninth syllable. || 10 ||
It is joined at its lower part with the first *ṭa*-consonant of the third group;
below that, it is joined with the fire-syllable *ra*;
and likewise, by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also joined with the second vowel, thus becoming the twenty-ninth syllable.
Therefore, there would be the form *ṣṭrā*.
The letter *c* is for the purpose of including [the rule regarding] *saṃyoga*. || 10 ||
The thirty-first syllable is joined with the second vowel;
the thirty-second syllable is joined with the thirteenth vowel. || 11 ||
The thirty-first syllable is the letter *repha* (the sound *ra*). When joined with the second vowel (*a*), it becomes the form *rā*.
The thirty-second syllable is the letter *la*.
Joined with the thirteenth vowel, it would be the form "lo. || 11 ||
Joined with Bhāskara (the letter *ra*), it becomes thirty-three syllables;
joined with the fourth of the Mātṛkās (the letter *ī*), it becomes thirty-four.
It should consist of thirty-three syllables joined with Bhāskara.
Bhāskara is the letter *repha* (r). The thirty-third syllable is the letter *ga*; when these are conjoined, they form the shape *gra*.
The *mātṛkā* is the fourth vowel, the letter *ī*.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the short vowel.
[This occurs] in the word "catustriṃśati" (thirty-four).
The thirty-fourth syllable is the letter *bha*.
By that, the form *bhī* would arise. || 12 ||
Accomplishing all desires and goals by means of the fifth *mātṛkā* alone, this practice joined with the thirty-seven is known as the *ḍākinī-sādhana*. (13)
The letter *u* is the fifth of the *mātṛkās*.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the long vowel.
"Thirty-seven" [refers to the number].
The thirty-seventh syllable is the letter *ma*. When joined [with a vowel], it takes the form *mu*. The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is *ḍākinī*.
The *sādhana* of the *ḍākinīs* consists of the entire mantra;
or else, the thirty-seven *makāras* alone, visualized correctly upon the head of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as radiant as the sun, subdues the *yakṣas* and other beings—
this is the *sādhana* remembered as that of the *ḍākinīs*.
It is approved by the ḍākinīs. || 13 ||
And the thirty-eighth [letter], joined with the second vowel, is likewise the means for accomplishing all the deities; of this there is no doubt. (14)
"And the thirty-eighth as well.
The thirty-eighth syllable is the letter *kha*. Through its conjunction with the second vowel (*ā*), it takes the form *khā*.
And here, in all instances,
the nominative case is used in connection with the verb "should be" (*bhavet*);
they know that the syllable *kha* is the means (*sādhana*).
The same applies elsewhere as well.

When one visualizes [the syllable] *kha*, which has a luster like that of an *indragopa* insect, upon the head and other parts of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it brings all the gods and others under control.
The particle *ca* (and) is used for conjunction, while the particle *eva* (only/just) serves to emphasize.
Therefore, he says: "The means," and so forth. || 14 ||
The forty-second [syllable] is indeed conjoined with the letter *daha* (the letter *dh*), and the forty-third syllable is in the lower part (*adhobhāga*).
"Forty-second" refers to the forty-second syllable, which is the letter *sa*.
The word "and" (*eva*) serves to confirm the meaning previously stated.
"Fire" (*dahana*) refers to the letter *ra*.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
That which has this lower part (*adhobhāga*) is called "lower-parted" (*adhobhāga*). The forty-second syllable is joined with that; by means of it, the form *stra* would result.
"And the practitioner should know that"—this is the ellipsis for the verb "should know.
"The forty-third" means the forty-third syllable, which is the letter *bha*. 15.
The fifty-fifth [syllable] is joined with the fifth vowel, and it is also joined with the second vowel. (16)
It is joined with the fifth of those vowels;
by that, the form *bhu* would arise.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the long vowel.
The forty-fifth;
the forty-fifth;
the letter *bha*.
The word "ca" (and) serves to confirm the meaning as a collective of what was previously stated;
when joined with the second vowel, it becomes the form "bhā". || 16 ||
The forty-sixth [syllable], joined with the fifth of the vowels and worshipped by all heroes;
and the forty-seventh, joined with the second vowel. (17)
"With the fifth of the vowels" is as before. "Combined with the forty-sixth" means that the forty-sixth syllable, the letter *sa*, joined with the vowel *u*, becomes the beautiful form *su*.
"And the forty-seventh" means the forty-seventh letter, which is the syllable *repha* (the letter *r*).
The word *caiva* (and indeed) serves to both collect the previously mentioned meaning and to emphasize it.
When joined with the second vowel (*a*), it takes the form *rā*. || 17 ||
Vajrasattva is indeed that supreme fifty-first [letter], and likewise, it is considered the most excellent when beautified by the fifth of the vowels. (18)
"Vajrasattva is indeed that supreme [syllable].
That very syllable *repha* is Vajrasattva.
The fifty-first is the letter *śa*.
The phrase "and likewise" indicates that this [sūtra] has the same meaning as what was stated previously.
Regarding the words "but by the fifth":
the word "but" (tu) signifies a distinction.

The syllable *U*, which has a radiance equal to Indra’s bow (the rainbow) and is meditated upon at the throat of Sādhya, brings that person under one's control. Furthermore, it would have a beautiful form; thus it is considered the supreme excellence. || 18 ||
And the fifty-second [syllable], joined with the second vowel, is likewise the means for accomplishing all the gods; of this there is no doubt. (19)
"And the fifty-second" means the fifty-second syllable, which is the letter *pa*. The particle *caiva* (and indeed) serves to include an unstated meaning and to provide emphasis.

Driven by the wind and mounted upon a cloud, smoke-colored, when meditated upon at the throat, heart, waist, and soles of the feet of the practitioner, it uproots that [target]; thus, the letter *pa* causes expulsion (*uccāṭana*).
When joined with the second vowel, *pā*, it becomes cruel (*rūpa*). || 19 ||
Likewise, the fifty-third [letter] is joined with the thirteenth vowel;
having extracted the letter *da* from the fourth group, it is joined with the fifty-fourth [vowel]. || 20 ||
The fifty-third is the fifty-third *śakāra*.
The phrase "likewise again" (*tathā punar*) indicates the previously mentioned meaning.
The continuation of the action is expressed as "they know that very [letter] joined with the thirteenth vowel."
Therefore, the form would be *śo*.

Regarding the statement "having extracted the letter *da* from the fourth group," although it should have been said "having extracted the third [letter] from the fourth group," the fact that *da* was mentioned is for the purpose of indicating its position as the fourth letter of the *ka*-group.
Otherwise, there would be doubt as to whether it belongs to the *avarga* or the *kavarga*.
Consequently, due to a scribal error regarding the letter *da*, one might wonder whether this pair of vowels is a pair of *u*s or a pair of *d*s.
[The number is] fifty-four.
The fifty-fourth is the letter *ya*. They know it to be joined with that;
by means of that, there would be the form *dya*. || 20 ||
The fifty-six syllable mantra, joined with the sixth vowel,
is certainly the destroyer of enemies when combined with the fourth letter of the antaḥstha group.
The fifty-sixth letter is the letter *śa*.
They know it to be joined with the sixth vowel, *ū*;
by that, the form *śū* arises.
"Surely it is the destroyer of enemies" because of the victory over the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The letter *va* is the fourth among those situated within [the consonants]. The third case ending is used in the sense of "together with. || 21 ||
Joined with the second vowel and likewise endowed with the fifteenth,
this means of accomplishment for all siddhis shall consist of fifty-nine syllables.

The fifty-ninth syllable, joined with the letter *va* combined with the second vowel (*u*), and likewise conjoined with the fifteenth [consonant], becomes the means for all accomplishments (*sādhana*). "They know" (*viduḥ*) is either a verb or the accusative case;
by that, the form would be *ṭvām*.
And this is the benefit of even a single syllable "ṭa," or of the entire mantra. || 22 ||
The excellent ones know it as joined with the sixty-first letter by means of the second vowel;
likewise, they know it as the sixty-second.
The sixty-first letter is *dhakāra*.
Joined with the second vowel, they know its form to be *dhā*.
The word "tu" indicates that the solitary *dhakāra* conveys the meaning previously stated.
In this very way, the Buddhas are known as the "excellent knowers.
Regarding "the sixty-second," they know the sixty-second syllable to be the letter *repha*.
The phrase "and likewise" (*tathā caiva*) serves to collect and confirm the manner of the meaning previously stated. (23)
Joined with the third vowel, this is considered the supreme [mantra] of the Ḍākinīs;
furthermore, sixty-three [syllables] are likewise joined with the eleventh vowel. (24)
When joined with the third vowel, it becomes the form *ri*.
Regarding "the sixty-third":
this refers to the letter *ma* (or *ṇa*) as the sixty-third.
The words *punaścaiva* signify repetition, conjunction, and emphasis. They know that the form *ṇe* arises from the combination of that [letter *na*] with the eleventh vowel (*e*). (24)
The beautiful, supreme syllable "Śobhana" (ŚRĪM), as well as the sixty-fifth [letter], pierced by Vajrasattva and joined with the second vowel. (25)
"Sixty-five" refers to the syllable *gha*.
"Vajrasattva" is the letter *ra*.
And the phrase "just so" (*tathā caiva*) serves to emphasize the inclusion of the manner of meaning previously described.
By that, one should perceive form through the nose. || 25 ||
This seed-syllable is supremely divine, bestowing both supernatural powers and liberation;
it consists of sixty-six syllables joined with the third vowel. (26)
The Tathāgata spoke this [which grants success] in all undertakings:
it is joined with sixty-seven syllables and conjoined with the second vowel. (27)
"Sixty-six" refers to the sixty-sixth syllable, which is the letter *ja*. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
The letter *ca* serves to aggregate the meanings previously stated.
When joined with the third vowel (*i*), it becomes the form *ji*. Regarding the phrase "the sixty-seventh letter," he stated that the sixty-seventh letter is *na*.
The form of the letter *n* joined with the second vowel would be *ṇ*;
and that is combined with its meaning. || 26–27 ||
In all the activities of the Yoginīs, it is exactly thus; there is no doubt.
Furthermore, one should join the syllable *baka* (ba) there sixty-eight times.
With this seed-syllable, one should arrange it in the lower part;
it consists of seventy-one syllables and is joined with the second vowel. (29)
"Sixty-eight":
he stated that the sixty-eighth syllable is the letter *ma*.
"And again" (*punaścaiva*) serves to both collect the previously mentioned meaning and to emphasize it.
"One should join the letter *ba* there" means one should place it below the letter *ma*; by that, the form *mba* arises.
This consists of seventy-one syllables.
He spoke the seventy-first syllable, the letter *repha*.
The word *ca* (and) serves to collect the previously mentioned meanings and to indicate emphasis.
When joined with the second vowel (*a*), it takes the form *rā*. || 28–29 ||
This is indeed auspicious for all castes, there is no doubt;
it is the seventy-fourth [letter], joined with the second vowel. (30)
"Seventy-four":
he spoke of the seventy-fourth syllable, the letter *ha*.
The word "and" (*ca*) is as before.
In conjunction with the second vowel, the form shall be *hā*. || 30 ||
This bestows primordial accomplishment, having emerged from the mouth of the Tathāgata;
it is the seventy-fifth [chapter] and also the sixth [section] on the Mātrikās.
"Seventy-five":
he spoke of the seventy-fifth syllable, the letter *dh*,
and likewise [the rest] as before.
And through its conjunction with the sixth *mātrikā*, that form becomes the letter *dhū*. || 31 ||
This is the most excellent yoga, the best among all yogas;
it consists of seventy-six [syllables] by means of the second [letter] of the Mātṛkā.
One should divide the seventy-sixth syllable, the letter *ma*, with the second vowel (*mātrikā*).
The word *ca* (and) is as before. || 32 ||
One should indeed split it with the Sun (Sūrya) and join the letter *va* there;
there is nothing else more auspicious than this mantra, which consists of seventy-seven syllables.
One should indeed split the letter *va* with the Sun (*sūrya*); there, one should join their form between the two [letters] which have become positioned below.
By that, the form *mvrā* shall arise.
There is nothing else more supremely beautiful.
"From the seed-syllable *mvrā*.
Regarding "the seventy-seventh syllable":
he spoke of the letter *na*, which is the seventy-seventh syllable, as being conjoined with the meaning previously stated. || 33 ||
One should join the letter *dhakāra* there, which is beautiful according to the *Ḍākinīmata*;
it is the seventy-eighth [letter] joined with the second vowel. (34)
Through the conjunction of the letter *dhakāra* with the lower part, the form *ndha* arises.
Regarding "the seventy-eighth," the seventy-eighth syllable is the letter *kakāra*, which is just as before; through its conjunction with the second vowel, the form *kā* arises. || 34 ||
This supreme, divine seed-syllable is considered the ultimate cause;
it consists of eighty-one syllables and is differentiated by the vowel at the end of the fourth [group]. (35)
The eighty-first syllable is my syllable *pa*.
In the division of the fourth vowel, *pu* would be the *puruṣa*;
and this is just as before. || 35 ||
For this brings about primordial accomplishment and sets all accomplishments in motion;
it consists of eighty-two syllables and is likewise joined with the second vowel. (36)
The excellent ones know this supreme, divine root mantra to be the abode of all accomplishments and the crusher of the hearts of the ḍākinīs. (37)
"Eighty-two letters of mine"— the eighty-second letter is the syllable *ṣa*, as before;
when joined with the second vowel, it uttered the form *ṣā*.
This root mantra consists of eight words;
therefore it is said: "The excellent ones know this as the root mantra. (36–37)
This mantra of the Lord Śrī Heruka, the King of Vidyās, is accomplished through recitation.
Joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and *phaṭ* at the end twice, this root mantra accomplishes all desired aims. (38)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the procedure for extracting mantras, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
The one who plays with Śrī Heruka is the deity Śrī Heruka.
His king of vidyās, the mantra, begins with *karakara* and so forth.
"Joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and ending with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*" means it is to be recited as a single, uninterrupted, protracted utterance (*pluta*).
This qualification applies to both the root mantra and the King of Vidyās (vidyārāja) as seen through the power of the mantra.
Therefore, he says: "this mantra.
The meaning is that it is not only the root mantra characterized by the words beginning with "Oṃ," but rather this King of Vidyās as well.

"Devoid of all means of accomplishment" means that they are free from all means of accomplishment such as writing [the mantras], including the heart-mantra, the near-heart-mantra, the armor-mantra, the root-mantra, and the king of vidyās. || 38 ||

The extraction of the root mantra in its entirety and the partial extraction of the King of Vidyās, as well as the chapter that explains their ritual procedure—this is the seventh [chapter], being thus [described].
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 7.
The eighth chapter: The Procedure for Extracting the Mantra of the Six Yoginīs of the Inverted Heart.
Then, [one should meditate on] oneself as the union of all heroes, the source of all accomplishments, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
The *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya* mantras have been previously indicated;
the *ṣaḍyoginī-kavaca* mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra of Vajravārāhī have been subsequently indicated.
To the question "What are all of them?", he says: "Then," and so forth.

From that very collection of vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), one should extract the *Sarvavīrasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*; this is to be understood by the passage beginning with "all" (*sarva*).

The mantra of Śrī Heruka is also spoken in that same way: just as these syllables such as *hā-svā-ra* and so forth are shown to be established within the mantra, so too are such [syllables] separately extracted from the vowels and consonants themselves;
thus is the extraction (*samuddhāra*).
Because he is being extracted from the cow by way of reverse order;
as to what [he extracts], he says: "his own self," meaning his own mind. || 1 ||
Hā svā raṃ va saṃ la jā nī ki ḍā ṭpha hūṃ hūṃ kaṃ ru ru he he jrava śrī oṃ || 2 ||
The heart of the King of Vidyās has neither been, nor will it ever be. || 3 ||
*Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvara svāhā*. Writing [this] in direct order (*anuloma*) is the extraction (*samuddhāra*).
This heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) consists of twenty-two syllables.
To the question "Whose heart [is this]? he says: "The Vidyā," and so forth.
The heart-mantra of the King of Vidyās, beginning with *oṃ kara kare* and so forth, and its eight-syllable heart-mantra are here stated in brief.
Regarding its power, he says "na bhūta" and so on; the sense is that in the past and future times, this mantra has not been taught by me to anyone, nor will it be taught. (2–3)
ṬPHA HŪṂ 2 HA HA HRĪḤ OṂ | ṬPHA HŪṂ HREṂ HRĪṂ HĀṂ OṂ || 4 ||
He states the extraction of the mantra for the armor (*kavaca*) of the six yoginīs, beginning with *ṭpha*:
"Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—this collection of syllables, namely *ṭpha hūṃ hreṃ hrīṃ hāṃ oṃ*, has been thus properly arranged. (4)
The syllable VAṂ, the syllable YOṂ, the syllable MOṂ, and likewise the syllable HRĪṂ;
the syllable HŪṂ and the syllable PHAṬ are proclaimed—the six Yoginīs are thus celebrated. || 5 ||
The syllable *vaṃ*, the syllable *yoṃ*, the syllable *moṃ*, the syllable *hrīṃ*, the syllable *hūṃ*, and likewise the syllable *phaṭ*.
The syllables beginning with *oṃ* are to be joined at the beginning of those beginning with *vaṃ*.
*Oṃ vaṃ Vajravārāhī* at the navel.
Hāṃ Yoṃ Yāminī is in the heart; Hrīṃ Moṃ Mohanī is in the face;
Hreṃ Hrīṃ Saṃcāriṇī is on the head.
HŪṂ HŪṂ TRĀSANĪ at the crest-lock;
PHAṬ PHAṬ CAṆḌIKĀ as the weapon for all limbs.
The word "and" (ca) applies everywhere and implies mutual dependence.
The particle *eva* serves to restrict the meaning to its own specific sense.
"The six yoginīs are proclaimed" refers to Vajravārāhī and the others. (5)
Hā svā ye nī ca ro vai jra va oṃ!
This great vidyā of the ḍākinīs has not existed, nor will it ever exist. || 6 ||
This armor-mantra of the six yoginīs has been extracted: *oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā*.
This subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) of Vajravārāhī was extracted from the secret place (*gopa*).
For while *oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā* remains, the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* were concealed.
And those two [are recited] prior to the utterance of *svāhā*.
Regarding "Ḍākinī":
the mantra of Vajravārāhī and the others is called *Ḍākinī*.
The word *tu* (but) is used to demonstrate his greatness.
Regarding the phrase "not yet become" (*na bhūta*), it is in the singular number because it qualifies a specific mantra, which is a genus. || 6 ||
On this earth, there are four jewels: the mantra-garland is the most excellent;
the Ḍākinī is the great spell (mahāvidyā), and Heruka is the king of spells (vidyārāja).
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the procedure for extracting the mantras of the six Yoginīs of the reversed heart, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"Upon the earth," and so forth.
"In as many world-systems as there are, those [masses] of earth therein"—the singular number is used because it refers to the genus.
"The four jewels."
There are four jewels, so called because they extend delight (*rati*). To ask what these are, he says: "The mantra-garland," and so forth.
The mantra-garland (*mantramālā*) is the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*), and that consists of eight words.
Therefore, the word "tu" is explained as having the sense of a distinction;
for this very reason, it is supreme.
"Ḍākinī, however,
is ignorance" refers to the mantra of Vajravārāhī and others;
the word "however" (tu) is used for emphasis.
The King of Knowledge (vidyārāja) is "Oṃ kara kare," and so forth. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. [This refers to] Śrī Heruka.
This is the knowledge of the meaning [of the mantra], as well as its form consisting of arms, faces, and so forth. || 7 ||
This is the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Extracting the Mantra of Vajravārāhī, the Six Yoginīs of the Inverted Heart. This is the summary of this chapter.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The Ninth Chapter on the Ritual Procedures for the Root Mantra.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the excellent ritual applications of the root mantra exactly and in their proper sequence:
whatever exists within the three worlds, all that one shall accomplish in an instant.
Since there is no application of the mantra without hearing its efficacy,
he speaks the ninth chapter in order to explain that, beginning with "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" means immediately after the extraction of the mantra.
The connection is: "I shall speak of the ritual action (karma)," and that [action] is the desired boon. To the question "Why?", he says: "Therefore."
Since there is no engagement with a means without seeing its result,
and because the root mantra was mentioned first,
the ritual action must be performed.
And the Blessed One himself has stated this correctly through the accumulation [of words]:
"in succession" means according to order.
He declares the agency of the mantra: "whatever exists or is found in the three worlds..."
Whatever there may be, all that he shall accomplish without exception in a moment, immediately following the recitation of the characteristics. || 1 ||
It performs all rites; by a single recollection, it slays all nāgas, all gods, all yakṣas, all gandharvas, and beings of every birth;
it terrifies the clouds, causes them to rain, and stops them;
it dries up the oceans.
It brings a river to the bank;
it restrains Indra;
by reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, one causes the earth to tremble.
Having climbed a tree, he goes wherever he desires;
he steals all mantras and steals all siddhis;
he attracts whatever is desired.
Again he dismisses them; he creates many thousands of forms;
he appears according to his will.
It is not seen by will;
it pulverizes palaces, tree-tops, and so forth;
it turns poison into nectar.
He turns nectar into poison;
he turns soma into milk;
he turns milk into soma.
He removes all odors and moves wherever he desires.
He who practices with women during the conjunction of the moon is a supreme man, a Garuḍa-faced one who creates vehicles.
In that regard, fortune that has come into one's hand is not thwarted by anyone.
Thus, when joined with the ritual procedure, one shall partake in the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
By mere remembrance, it causes death.
He produces fire;
he splits open the underworld (pātāla) and causes a thunderbolt (aśani) to fall, and then he restrains it again.
Through recollection, one produces lightning;
one causes the images of all the gods to dance.
For whomever this is accomplished, by merely uttering their name once and reciting the mantra, that person dies at that very moment.
He becomes the enjoyer of all worlds without exception; this Blessed One gathers them at will. No vow, no practice, and no fasting is prescribed for him.
By means of this ritual application, one should perform whatever action is desired.
He states the activity of the practitioner with the words beginning "all," etc.
The particle *vai* is used for emphasis.
He states the ritual action with the words beginning "all," etc.
All the nāgas, such as those whose gaze is poisonous and who cause harm;
for they have been mentioned previously.
All the gods, such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha.
[He protects] all yakṣas, such as the Nojāhara and others.
Regarding "all wombs":
these are cruel humans.
The first case is used for the object.
"Devas" refers to those who perform divine acts through [the commission of] killing and so forth.
The practitioner kills them, that is, deprives them of their life-breaths.
The capacity [to act] toward those who are cruel while remaining neutral has been stated.
Furthermore, the capacity for their regeneration is also to be inferred; otherwise, it would follow that the Compassionate One lacks power.
Now, he states the capacity with regard to insentient things, beginning with "the clouds," and so forth.
It terrifies and shakes;
the meaning is that it breaks it into pieces.
That which obtains rain is "varṣāpaḥ."
"He causes it to rain" means he causes the clouds to rain;
the rest is easily understood.
Regarding the word "nadīm" (the river):
[Vegavatī].
To the question "What [is accomplished] by this?", he says: "She wards off Indra.
The word "Indra" is used in the singular to denote the class.
"Indra-ti-iti-indrāḥ" means that he negates the lords of the sentient and insentient, as well as [the notions of] non-action and cause-and-effect;
"cālayati" means he shatters them.
By the words "a tree," and so forth, he shows that one makes an insentient object appear as if it were sentient.
"All mantras" means that one even seizes those that have already been brought down.
Thus, the theft of speech has been shown.
"All-accomplishment" (*sarvasiddhi*) refers to the accomplishment or completion of all things, such as the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth;
the sense is that it even carries away accomplishments such as material wealth and the like.
"It draws away the desired food" means that one takes what is desired and liked from elsewhere;
"then releases it again" refers to the mantras and so forth.
He speaks of the power of the mantra residing in the body, beginning with "rūpa" and so forth; by this, the state of having many arms, faces, and so on is demonstrated.
[The word] "icchayā" means:
By the will of the yogin, the yogin is seen and not seen; thus, the accomplishment of invisibility is the power of concealment.
Alternatively, having known that whatever form the observer of the yogin shall see is unattainable for him, he shows it; this is "vision by will.
By the words beginning with "palace," the disintegration of even that which is well-constructed is demonstrated.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), stones, mountains, walls, and so forth are indicated;
thus, the capacity to dismantle what is well-constructed is shown.
By the phrase "poison," etc., the capacity to effect a transformation in the essential nature of things is shown.
Soma is wine;
*payaḥ* is water.
By the words beginning with "all," the removal of the odors of wine and so forth is shown.
By this yoga, it is indicated that the capacity for subduing [the disciple] must be established with respect to him therein.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "all nāgas" refers to all afflictions (*kleśas*).
"All gods" (*sarvadeva*) refers to the objects such as forms and so forth, because they sport by means of these.
"By means of these, one is victorious in every way"—
thus [it refers to] all the yakṣas.
Regarding the letter *ja*, the letter *ya* is an etymological substitution (*nairukta*).

And those sense faculties belong to all; the sources are the causes of birth, namely all sources and all rites for accomplishment. Through recollection—that is, through the contemplation of the mantra—[these are attained].
Killing is purification.
It terrifies, dissolves, and causes rain to fall upon the clouds— the junctions of the *ḍākinī* channels—
and it causes the *bodhicitta* to descend.
It restrains those [defilements] and further stabilizes them; it dries up the oceans of evil and raises the seeds of the rivers upward.
The mind is Indra;
it restrains and stabilizes [the practitioner] through supreme sovereignty.
This is accomplished by reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times.
In the phrase "of the mantra," the genitive case is elided.
"Lakṣa" means Śrī Heruka; it is derived from the root *lakṣ* with the suffix *ac*.
Its recitation (*jāpa*) is a mental activity; the meaning is that it is meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The sense is that all of this is accomplished through the recitation of the mantra and the meditative cultivation of Śrī Heruka. At the time of drawing the mandala, the supplication to the Earth is the shaking of the earth.
The tree is the fivefold yoga; having ascended it, one obtains whatever one desires to obtain wherever one wishes.
It is called "invoked" because here, Śrī Heruka alone is the desired object.

The method for rendering the *praṇava* and other elements devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇa*) through the procedure stated in the *Sādhana*—namely, by the entry of the *nāda* and so forth into the *bindu* and so forth—is established by the passage beginning with "all" (*sarva*). Furthermore, by the passage beginning again with "all," the accomplishment of the entry of the *nāda* and so forth is shown; and from the emergence of the *nāda* and so forth, there is the presentation of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The passage beginning with "what is desired" (*rucita*) explains the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) and so forth.
The division of the mantra is indicated by "rūpa" and so forth, and by "oṃ kara kara" and so forth;
the aspiration (praṇidhi) is indicated by "icchayā" and so forth; and "na" indicates the absence of dogmatic attachment (anabhiniveśa).
The body (*kāya*) is called *prāsāda* because the mind finds delight (*prasīdati*) in it.
It is called *dru* because it flows (*dravati*). According to the rule that "the teaching of grammatical augmentations is not universal" (*āgamaśāsanamanityam*), the suffix *tuk* is not applied here.
The tree itself is sensation (*vedanā*);
the peak is the mind (*citta*);
and by the word "etcetera," the mental factors (*dharmas*) are meant.
It is pulverized and analyzed by the weapon of wisdom.
Thus, by stating that there are four recollections (anusmṛtis), emptiness (śūnyatā) is demonstrated.
Poison is the sense object; nectar is that which is like nectar.
He makes the nectar an object of non-favor and cultivates it;
he makes the nectar like the extinction of a lamp—that is, the liberation of his mind—like poison because it is not to be cultivated.
The sense is that, having purified form and the other aggregates, he consumes them.
Regarding "Soma": it is called *soma* because it exists together with *umā*; thus *soma* is the syllable *oṃ*. *U* and *ma* are the two [sounds], joined in reverse order (*vilomena*).
This is because of the instruction regarding the half-moon and the nāda;
the letter *pa* is water because it belongs to Varuṇa;
and it "makes" (*karoti*) in both cases.
Again, "payaḥ somam" is as before.
Then this mantra:

"om va va om. In the circle of Varuṇa, one should visualize four mantras, white as jasmine and the moon, in the four directions; and if there is a person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should visualize him in their midst, adorned with pure garments and the like, and [recite] that mantra in front.
One should sprinkle him with dripping drops of nectar and recite [the mantra].
To the question "What is that?", he says "all," and so forth.
"Gandha" refers to disease, poison, and the like.
The rest is clear.
"Mukha," "dvāra," and "upāya" are synonyms.
Because he proceeds by means of two "mouths"—that is, two methods—just as a *garuḍa* proceeds by means of two wings, he is called *mukhagaruḍa*.
Alternatively, "mukhena" [is used] with the elision of the instrumental case ending.

Garuḍa is so called because he moves his two arms like wings; he is the "creator of the vehicle's movement," meaning he effects the production or accomplishment of the vehicle's motion. Thus, he is the Yogi.

He practices that union of the two *soma*s— the *bodhicitta*s arising from wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*)— which is the union of men with women who possess the menstrual flow (*puṣpavatī*). Because of his discernment (*viveka*),
he is the most excellent and extraordinary.
Having taken that *bodhicitta* with one's mouth and flapping both wings like a *garuḍa*, one should place it in the mouth of wisdom (*prajñā*) and consume the remainder oneself.
This is to be accomplished as equal to the recitation of the eight-limb mantra of one hundred thousand repetitions.
Having entered and remained therein, the fortune and prosperity that arise cannot be thwarted by any son of the gods (*devaputra-māra*), meaning they cannot be obstructed by obstacles.
This is the instruction: "By the application of the loss of the two *kūṭas*, it is remembered as *murmukuṭa*. Thus, *mu* is the root, purified by the knowledge of the two faces;
*ga* is the subsequent [syllable], purified by the emptiness of causes and so forth;
*ru* is the final [syllable], purified by liberation from aspiration.
The syllable *ḍo* signifies that he is nowhere established and is pure;
because his faces are Garuḍas by their very nature, he is "Mukhagaruḍa," namely Śrī Heruka.
This should be construed as: he who practices the union with Soma is Mukhagaruḍa.
To the question "Of what nature is he?", he says: "The creator of the emanation of the vehicle" (*yānasṛṣṭikṛt*).
The "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the knowledge of wisdom and skillful means; the "emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is its arising, and he is the one who performs that.
To whom does he belong? He says: "of women," meaning of the *yoginīs*.
The letter *sa* is the half-moon because it is the seed-syllable of nectar;
from that comes the letter *u*.
Then, the syllable *khaṇḍam* denotes the *anusvāra*;
the letter *a* denotes the staff on the lower side;
and the letter *ha*, which joins with *soma*, is called *somasaṅgama*.
The syllable *hūṃ* is [formed] by the combination [of its parts]; the *nāda* [is included] because of the oral instruction. To "practice" it means to know it, that is to say, to cultivate it.

Regarding the word *nara*: the root *nṛ*, meaning "to lead," belongs to the *bhūvādi* class. One is called *nara* because one beholds the Goddess in her proper place; this is formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
He is "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) because of his leadership (*nāyakatva*).
The syllable *hūṃ* is the hub, and upon it stands the *hūṃ*-vajra; from that is born Śrī Heruka.

"The creator of emanation" is the collective meaning. In this context, the Fortune (*lakṣmī*) held in his hand—Vajravārāhī—is not struck down by anyone between the two armors, nor can she be reached by any limb.
In this way, by being endowed with the previously mentioned method, one shall become a partaker of the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Through the passage beginning with "by remembrance," the capacity [to affect] those situated in the human, animal, and hellish realms is indicated.
Having visualized the fire as the letter *ra* (repha) within the fiery mandala—the *ra* being triangular—one generates fire through the impelling of the wind mandala.
Or it may happen suddenly,
because the power of mantras is inconceivable; thus,
it pierces through the netherworld (pātāla).

The meaning is that he mocks the multitude of serpents dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), implying, "You are powerless, for he rends asunder even the netherworld itself," or rather, "He terrifies them. It also means that he causes the thunderbolt (aśani) to fall.
By the word "and" (ca), another specific weapon is indicated;
the alternative meaning is that she brings down a thunderbolt (*aśani*) from somewhere at will.
[The word] "lightning" (*vidyut*).
The nominative case is used for the object [of the action].
The arising of lightning without a cloud;
the splendor of lightning is its radiance.
"From recollection" means from contemplation;
or, it brings that [Vidyujjvālākarālī] forth.
An alternative meaning is that one brings forth Vidyudvasudhārā from the syllable *HŪṂ* through recollection.
The remainder is clear.
Regarding the phrase "for whom success occurs by the mere mention of the name": this means that for such a person, success in mantras and the like arises simply through the utterance of the name.
The meaning is that even one who is preeminently accomplished in mantra;
the collective sense is that "accomplishment in mantra" is achieved by the mere utterance of the name.
Such a person also dies by means of the mantra recited but once.
The power of the mantras and supernatural attainments (*siddhi*) of the most eminent non-Buddhist teachers;
one who is the enjoyer and protector of the worlds such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
or alternatively, the one who expands or creates the worlds.
Therefore, he says "by desire," and so forth.
He says "this," and so forth, to show that it is accomplished without [the need for] ritual observances (*niyama*) and the like.
This is the eight-word mantra here.
The connection is that he should perform whatever action he desires. "Vow" refers to the Great Vow (mahāvrata) and so forth.
"Conduct" refers to the state of being an Avadhūta and so forth.
Fasting is the state of remaining for a day and night without food;
for this very reason it is said that it is "accomplished through recitation.
This refers to the Kalpaśāstra.
In this regard, "conduct" (upacāra) refers to the prescribed rule;
it is the wandering at will. || 2 ||
If he recites it once while angry, he kills ten million;
if recited with a peaceful mind, he restores them to life.
If one strikes someone with charcoal from a cremation ground over which the mantra has been recited once, that person falls down instantly.
If one recites over ashes and strikes Yama with them, he is seized by a *piśāca* at that very moment.
If one writes the name of someone on a wooden board or a wall using charcoal from a cremation ground at night, that person is seized by a great spirit (*mahāgraha*).
If one strikes Yama with a single branch of the *atimuktikā* creeper over which one has recited [the mantra] once, he arrives at that very moment with the speed of the wind.
If one strikes someone with sugar over which [the mantra] has been recited once, that person becomes paralyzed;
he can then transfer himself to wherever he desires.
Having recited [the mantra] once over guggulu resin, one employs it as incense.
He causes all beings to enter [the state of absorption]. Having recited the mantra once over his hand and covered his face, he raises up one bitten by the God of Death (kāla).
By reciting it once over water sealed with the ḍākinī-mudrā, he paralyzes [the enemy].
By reciting [the mantra] once over a *karavīra* creeper, one causes the fetus to move to wherever one desires. || 3 ||
Now he describes the efficacy of the mantra that acts as a medicinal assistant, beginning with the words "If" (*yadi*), and so forth.
If one, being enraged, recites the mantra once while chewing iron dross and the head of such-and-such a person, he kills ten million beings.

By means of a peaceful mind free from anger, by wrapping [the victim's] living head and reciting [the mantra], there is a restoration; "living water" (*jīvāpaḥ*) refers to the attainment of life, and he who performs this is said to "revive" (*jīvāpayati*).

On the night of the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take a branch of the *ariṣṭa* tree located toward the southern direction that has been cut by the axe of a *caṇḍāla* or similar person; having burned it in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), one should extinguish the embers with the juice of its leaves and collect the ashes.
Alternatively, [the word] "in the cremation ground" [is used].
The ash found in a cremation ground;
this is when there is elision of the third case ending.
[It means] "with charcoal."
The collective meaning is that this rite is to be performed with the ashes collected on a Tuesday during a Tuesday.
After the recitation of one hundred thousand mantras, having entered the circle of the *atimuktaka* creeper,

one should wrap a thread spun by a maiden around a branch of that tree located in the western direction— which has been tripled and dyed with the juice of turmeric— and remain naked with disheveled hair until the release of the lunar eclipse.
Holding [it] with the left hand, one should recite [the mantra] continuously;
then it should be grasped.
It moves forward by the *agra* [mantra] and returns by the *mūla* [mantra].
"In the case of 'sakṛjjaptena' (by reciting once), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
'Stambhitaḥ' (paralyzed) [is achieved] through the visualization (*bhāvanā*) of yellow.
The rest is easily understood. || 3 ||
He who desires the accomplishment of knowledge without knowing the wisdom of Śrī Heruka is like one who threshes husks while devoid of this mantra. (4)
He says that it is indeed permeated by selflessness in the passage beginning with "not having known," etc.
The knowledge of Śrī Heruka is the knowledge [expressed in] such statements as "the syllable Śrī is non-dual knowledge.
The word "siddhi" (attainment) is used in the nominative case in the sense of the accusative.
The prefix *tu-* has the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*).
It means that he desires a distinguished, desired accomplishment (*siddhi*). As for the phrase, "he threshes the husks": it refers to him.
The threshing of that which is without essence is indeed [futile].
For by threshing what has essence, one discards the non-essential and remains with the essence.
The point is that because the essence was not grasped at the very outset, its accomplishment does not occur for him.
He states that there is no accomplishment without the mantra of selflessness: "Devoid of this mantra," and so forth. [This refers to] the root mantra.
Therefore, the unique nature of the mantra has been explained. (4)
A person does not attain accomplishment nor happiness if,
without knowing this mantra, they desire the state of a yogi.
*Siddhi* is that which is accomplished or manifested, namely, *samyaksaṃbodhi*.
*Saukhya* is supramundane bliss and so forth. *Nara* refers even to one who abides in the *naya* (method).
He says "without knowing," etc., because [the goal] is not accomplished without the yoga of the non-duality of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyādvayayoga*).
"Mantra" refers to the yoga of wisdom and means. (5)
His labor will be in vain, and he shall not obtain its fruit;
this mantra, which grants all accomplishments, is one whose practice may be undertaken according to one's own desire.
[The practitioner] need not observe vows, nor perform austerity, meditation, recitation of mantras, or ritual gestures (mudrā).

Having understood that which was praised by the Sugata, the practitioner indeed attains food and drink, sacrificial offerings (caru), various edibles, flavors, and all supernatural accomplishments (siddhi). || 7 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the ritual procedures for the root mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
His exertion, characterized by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, is thus in vain; such is his activity.
This mantra is one of unrestrained conduct (*kāmācāra*);
it is perfected through the enjoyment of the five objects of desire.
Therefore it has been said: "Not a vow," and so forth.
To the question "What is this mantra? he says: "By the Sugatas," and so forth;
that is, described and determined by the Sugatas.
Having known such [a state], the practitioner becomes one who accomplishes the deities born of mantra, mudrā, and mantra. "Khāna," etc. [follows].
"Food" refers to eating, drinking, and intoxicating drinks; by the word "etcetera," it includes things to be licked, sucked, and so forth.
"Caru" means that which has been offered as a sacrifice.
"Bhojya" means that which is to be eaten;
its consumption is "bhoga.
"Rasa" means sound.
By the word "first," form, smell, taste, and touch are to be understood.
Having recognized these as the worship of the Self, the practitioner becomes one who possesses all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
He is so called because from him all accomplishments arise.
By this, neither the pursuit of arbitrary conduct nor the enjoyment of sense objects has flourished;
rather, the knowledge of selflessness has been adorned. (6–7)
The ninth chapter, which explains the ritual procedures for the root mantra, is concluded.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 9.
The tenth chapter on the ritual procedures for the heart-mantra of the accomplishment of the three bodies.
Now I shall explain the three bodies through the non-dual yoga of Śrī Heruka;
by the mere knowledge of which, they are accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
If it is asked, "If Śrī Heruka consists of the three bodies, what are those three bodies?"—this is the meaning of the word *atha* (now/then) used when the question is posed by oneself.

Therefore, the sense is this: if you ask, "What are those three bodies?", the reply is that "the three bodies will be explained. To the question "Of what nature are they?", he says: "Through the non-dual yoga with Śrī Heruka."
Śrī Heruka is undoubtedly joined with that which is "thus" (tathā);

[the suffix] *tasil* is used here after a word ending in the first case. By the words "by which," etc., he shows that it is precisely this distinguished triad of bodies (*kāyatraya*) that is to be accomplished here.
"By mere cognition," "by mere realization," and "by direct perception"—this is the meaning.
The word *mātra* is used for emphasis.
They are "accomplished" means that the yogins attain what they desire, such as the *dharmakāya* and so forth.
"Not here":
regarding this established state, there is no doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist. || 1 ||
When one becomes an adept regarding the bodies of the Dharmakāya—for those who possess such thorough discernment—then I shall proclaim that knowledge. (2)
He speaks of the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*: "Dharma... and so forth.
That which is both *dharma* and *kāya* is the *dharmakāya*; those whose body (*śarīra*) is such are the *jinās* (Victors).
When one becomes their accomplisher—that is, when one brings them to perfection—then I shall proclaim the Gnosis (*jñāna*).
I discern and ascertain that gnosis is the *dharmakāya*, which is devoid of being one or many, the domain of the Tathāgatas, eternal by nature, and luminous by nature.
And that *dharmakāya* is the very essence of the Victor; such is the summary. Thus it is said:
"That which is neither one nor many, which serves as the foundation for the great perfection of the welfare of oneself and others..."
Neither non-existence nor existence, like space, it is of equal flavor, its nature difficult to discern;

unstained, changeless, auspicious, unequaled and yet equal to all, pervasive, free from conceptual proliferation—I bow to that incomparable Dharmakāya of the Victors, which is to be realized within oneself. (2)
When the practitioner becomes one with the bodies of the saṃbhogakāya, then I shall explain the enjoyment of those who are in meditative equipoise. (3)
He speaks of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) with the words "In enjoyment," and so forth.
When he performs the teaching of the Dharma endowed with a form that is not to be satiated by looking upon, at that time the enjoyment body is the domain of the bodhisattvas.
The enjoyment body is eternal by way of its continuous flow.
It is so called because the Buddha and Bodhisattvas, through correct practice, enjoy it—that is, they take it as their own.
And thus it has been said:
"Transcending the world, inconceivable, the creeper of the fruit of well-performed deeds."

He who, for the sake of bringing joy to the wise, proclaims his own manifold and great majesty in the midst of the assembly— the Buddhas’ sound of the true Dharma, which has spread throughout all worlds and whose uplifting resonance never ceases.
I here pay homage to that Saṃbhogakāya, which is established in the great kingdom of Dharma. Thus, [verse 3].
When the practitioner attains the bodies of the nirmāṇakāya, then I declare that one-pointedness of mind is the nirmāṇakāya. (4)
He speaks of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) with the words "the emanation," and so forth.
The emanation body is common to all sentient beings and is eternal by way of its continuity. And thus it is said:
"For the sake of maturing sentient beings, he appears in some places like fire, blazing brightly."

I pay homage to that Emanation Body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Munis, which is seen in some places at the time of perfect enlightenment and in others at the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, yet remains ever quiescent; which manifests in manifold forms through various means in its universal aspect to remove the fear of the three realms of existence, and which extends throughout the ten directions for the great benefit of beings. Thus, [verse 4].
One attains the wisdom, enjoyment, and emanation bodies; of this there is no doubt.
One accomplishes the glorious Heruka as one's own self; of this there is no doubt. (5)
I shall declare the heart of this mantra; listen, O secret practitioner! (6)
[The three bodies are indeed established because they are that which is to be accomplished.
To the question "What is stated by that?", he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.
"[The glorious Heruka as one's own self]" means:
The connection is that Śrī Heruka attains his very own self.

To explain how this occurs, he says "the wisdom, enjoyment, and emanation [bodies]," and so forth; here, "wisdom" refers to the *dharmakāya*, and the singular number is used for the sake of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Thus is the accomplishment of that which is to be attained.
Again, asking "of what nature is it?", he says: "the Self.
For the sustenance of the Self is also called happiness because it serves as the cause.
The meaning is that it has the nature of bliss.
Regarding the phrase "they succeed":
the conclusion is that those who possess the yoga of the three bodies succeed.
The mantra of Śrī Heruka who has become thus is also of that same nature; thus he says, "Of this," and so forth.
The heart-mantra consists of twenty-two syllables;
its purpose is also the heart.
Just as "ghee is longevity," he asks, "In what state shall I speak? and says: "The secret achiever.
He is so called because he accomplishes—that is, brings to perfection among yogins—the secret, which is the nature of mind and so forth, namely the three bodies (*kāyatraya*).
And you, being such as you are, listen. || 5-6 ||
By reciting the heart-mantra, one flies up to ten million yojanas;
one goes and comes;
and one assumes many thousands of forms.
Having ascended palaces, trees, and celestial abodes for ten million *yojanas*, he travels together with a *ḍākinī*.
Having gone into the sky, he returns again.
By his will he is seen; by his will he is not seen.
By his own will, he assumes the form of a child, an old man, or a youth; by his own will, he assumes the form of an elephant,
a buffalo, a gayal, a tiger, a lion, a bull, a hare, a cat, or a camel.
By his will, he assumes the form of a peacock, a cock, a swan, a ruddy goose, a crane, an owl, a hawk, a vulture, or a crow;
he takes on the very form of whomever he desires.
He steals speech,
he steals hearing, he steals sight.
It carries away the sense of smell, it carries away the sense of taste;
at will, it draws out the blood of anyone [it chooses] or causes it to be paralyzed. || 7 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the activity of the heart-mantra of the three bodies, in the glorious *Herukābhidhāna*. 10.
"Ut-patati" means he goes upward.
"Gacchaty āgacchati" means that he goes and returns;
the sense is that he travels ten million *yojanas* in a mere instant and returns.
