By this, the supernormal power of mind-swiftness (*manojava-ṛddhi*) is demonstrated. In the phrase "palace-tree" (*prāsādadruma*),
the dual ending is elided.
"In the worlds" means in the three worlds beginning with heaven (*svarga*).
"Ten million *yojanas*" is an instance of the elision of the accusative case ending.
The term "ḍākinī" indicates sexual delight (*rati*).
Likewise, having gone through the sky, she returns again.
The remainder is easily understood.
[Regarding the passage beginning with "form" (*rūpa*), he provides the explanation for the ninth section indicated: "by desire, a child," and so forth.
A person is called "youthful" (*yauvana*) because youth belongs to him, or simply because he is young;
this refers to the capacity associated with that stage of life.]
By the words "at will, an elephant," and so forth, he is shown to assume the form of a beast;
by the words "at will, a peacock," and so forth, he is shown to assume the form of a bird. Thus, his capacity to exist as an animal has been described.
By the words "of whom," etc., its nature as a universal is established.
The remainder is easily understood.
And [the phrase] "it causes to paralyze" means:
Attachment and so forth obstruct [the mind];
therefore, the word "or" (vā) is used to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. // 7 //
The tenth chapter, which explains the accomplishment of the three bodies and the ritual procedure for the activities of the heart-mantra.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The eleventh chapter, on the procedure for the characteristics of one born seven times [as a Brahmin].
Now I shall describe another [practice] by which the practitioner may attain accomplishment;
by merely consuming it, swift success proceeds.
Now he describes the efficacy of the heart-mantra, which functions as a companion over seven lifetimes, beginning with the words "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" (now) is used in the sense of conjunction.
I shall explain another application of the heart-mantra for seven lifetimes.
Alternatively, the meaning of the word "atha" (now/then) is that it follows immediately after the inquiry, "What are the applications of medicinal remedies for the heart?
He explains what kind of application it is by saying "the practitioner," and so forth;
the connection is: "I shall explain that application by which one attains accomplishment."

By merely smelling it—that is, by the mere act of smelling—there arises the accomplishment of the thorough knowledge of seven lifetimes. The meaning is that, in brief, there occurs the accomplishment of that knowledge. || 1 ||
That man from whose perspiration a sweet fragrance emanates, who speaks the truth, who blinks slowly,
and who is free from anger— [he is a holy person].
A fragrant breath issues from his mouth;
he becomes born as a human being for seven lifetimes.
Having eaten him, *rocanā* appears in his heart.
Having taken that, one makes a *tilaka* with the heart-mantra of Śrī Heruka recited one hundred and eight times;
it rises upward.
One should continue the recitation for one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*); one travels across ten million *yojanas*.
By merely consuming it, one becomes a knower of the three worlds;
having traveled fifty million *yojanas*, one returns within a day and night and attains a divine body.
Whoever knows the heart-mantra of Śrī Heruka obtains whatever desires he may wish for.
He gives those various [gifts]. || 2 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the section on the characteristics of one who has seven births, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 11.
"Of which person" means that the mass of merit exists in the form of a person;
"sugandhagandha" refers to the sweat whose odor is like that of fragrant substances such as *kasatūryā* and the like.
The remainder is well-established.
It should be understood that he who speaks the truth keeps his eyes open for a long time and is free from anger.
The word *niśvāsam* (exhalation) is used in the neuter gender because it is accompanied by fragrance (*saurabhyānvita*).
He whose breath possesses fragrance has been born as a human for seven lifetimes;
that is to say, having been born as a human through an uninterrupted lineage for seven births, he is the best among humans.
Or [the phrase] "born as a human. Regarding the purpose of the sign of the odor, it says "smelled" and so forth;
it should be understood that [the person] is to be known by smelling him.
He asks, "What is that? and replies with the words beginning "of that" (*tasya*).
For by means of its fragrance, that [cow] is inferred, because it is the effect of the *rocanā* [pigment];
in that case, there is no possibility of it being born from another source.
With the words beginning with "tām," he states the purpose of the *rocanā* (yellow pigment): "A recitation of one hundred thousand [times] is to be performed.
"He goes for ten million *yojanas*" means that he ascends a path measuring ten million *yojanas* in height.
"Fifty crores" refers to *yojanas*.
Since it is a divine body, that divine body is the heart.
Whatever desires the practitioner wishes to give, she grants them. || 2 ||
The eleventh chapter, which explains the characteristics and the ritual procedure for the seven births.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 11.
The twelfth chapter, the ritual procedure for the *upahṛdaya*.
Now I shall declare the *upahṛdaya* mantra, which accomplishes all siddhis;
whatever exists within the three worlds, it shall accomplish all that in an instant. (1)
"Then," and so forth. "Then" means immediately after the explanation of the procedure for the heart-rite (*hṛdayakarma*).
The remainder is easily understood. || 1 ||
ṬPHA HŪṂ HŪṂ HA HA HRĪḤ OṂ. This is the upahr̥daya (near-heart) of the heart [mantra].
By reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, one causes even the three worlds to tremble.
It attracts gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
it dries up and paralyzes rivers, oceans, ponds, and the like.
In whatever place one recites this mantra, all ḍākinīs become the servants of the practitioner.
Having recited this over water, if one washes one's own eyes with it, one knows seven births;
one sees even those whose life has ended as if they were dead, and one sees those with long lives as living.
Having consecrated one's eye [with this], whomever one looks upon becomes paralyzed. || 2 ||
ṬPHA HŪṂ HŪṂ HA HA HRĪḤ OṂ.
OṂ HRĪḤ HA HA HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. This is the mantra that has been rectified; this is the upahr̥daya (subsidiary heart-mantra) of the Heart [mantra].
The prefix *upa* has the sense of "inferiority.
This inferiority consists in having one fewer syllable than the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), and not in its lack of efficacy.
Alternatively, it has the sense of "proximity."
"Of this" refers to the recitation of the syllables of the *upahṛdaya*. That recitation consists of one hundred thousand repetitions.
By the words beginning with "O Goddess," the capacity for attraction is stated.
A pond is a lake;
it causes [water] to solidify—
this is the solidification of water.
"In that place" means where one recites the mantra seven hundred thousand times. "They become servants" means...
The sense is that they do not cause obstacles.
And this is the efficacy residing in mere recitation (*jāpa*).
"By this" [refers to that].
By means of the knowledge-mantra (*vidyā*) consisting of seven syllables. "Water" refers to the efficacy of water acting as an auxiliary to medicine.
"Seven births" refers to...
Having consecrated the eyes with [the mantra] "seven births past and future," the phrase "water" ceases [to apply]. || 2 ||

Taking the skin from the sole of the foot of a hero who has died a natural death, grind it with human blood; place *srotoñjana* in the middle of a ball and saturate it with *manaḥśilā*, *gorocanā*, saffron, and blood.
Drying it in the shade, wrap it in the three metals (*triloha*), perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) again, and prepare it under the asterism of Puṣya.
Having placed it in the mouth of Śrī Heruka and covered the mouth with the left hand, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times once more.
At that very moment, he becomes invisible and his radiance vanishes;
he is not seen even by the gods, let alone by insignificant mortals.
Thus it is seen when removed from the mouth.
In this tantra, this pill for the accomplishment of moving through the sky (khecarīsiddhi) was spoken by the Hero himself;
it is the heart and sub-heart of Śrī Heruka. || 3 ||
He states the efficacy of the *gulikā* (pill) practice with the words beginning "Vīra... and so forth.

"The skin from the sole of the foot of a *vīra-mṛtaka* (a hero who has died [in battle])"—one should grind this with the blood of that man; having ground it, [place it] in the middle of a *gokala* (cow-dung cake).
The sense is that it should be made into a pill (*piṇḍī*). "Srotāñjana" means *stroto'ñjana*.

"Manaḥśilā, rocanā, and kuṅkuma"—this refers to the elision of the second case ending (*dvitīyālope*). The collective meaning is as follows: having impregnated *srotāñjana*, *manaḥśilā*, and so forth with blood, having placed them inside that ball (*golaka*), having dried them in the shade, and having encased them in the three metals (*triloha*), one should cause it to be made—that is, one should prepare it.
"Furthermore, 'he' refers to the yogi who has recited the mantra seven hundred thousand times. 'Having consecrated' means— "

Having visualized the wheel-bearer of the Heruka maṇḍala there within a ball encased in three metals, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times at the change of time; this is the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
"By Puṣya" means by that [constellation], or by any other auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and so forth.
He states the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) with the words "of Śrī Heruka," and so forth.
The practitioner of the Śrī Heruka yoga, having placed that pill—which contains the mandala circle—within his own mouth, should recite the mantra as prescribed.
Thereupon, it will occur as described.
The weights of gold, silver, and copper are four, three, and four māṣas respectively;
these are the measures for the sequence of binding the pills, increased by seven, three, and five raktikās.
Thus is the rule for the three metals (*triloha*). The remainder is well-established.
To the question, "Of whom is that which is this *upahṛdaya* (near-heart mantra) the *hṛdaya* (heart mantra)? he says: "Of Śrī Heruka," and so forth.
Regarding "of Śrī Heruka," [the mantra begins with] *oṃ kara kare*, and so forth. || 3 ||
With this mantra, using the tip of the index finger, one makes the skull devoid of flesh and bone and churns it;
this draws forth its blood.
By churning with the left hand, it enters back again.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, one should deliver a blow with the fist to the skull;
for whomever one gives it by name, that person suffers a headache.
Recalling the mantra, one should fill the skull with milk.
It pacifies [disturbances].
Having recited the mantra over yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*), one should apply it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*);
whoever one looks upon becomes sealed [subjugated].
Having recited the mantra over the threatening finger (tarjanī), whoever one threatens with it falls down at that very instant.
[This is done] after the mantra has been recited.
If one strikes the ground with one's foot while uttering the name of someone, that person dies at that very moment.
If one consecrates water with mantras and sprinkles it upon the ground, [the same occurs].
Furthermore, he restores the dead to life;
by threatening with the tip of his index finger empowered by the recitation of the mantra, he can threaten even a thousand people,
and all who see him become paralyzed.
He liberates by means of speech.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times over the ashes of a Caṇḍāla and striking someone while recollecting the being [to be liberated],
he assumes that person's form.
Having consecrated the ashes of the sacrificial fire by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, he who strikes with them cannot be seen even by the gods;
one may likewise strike with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times.
It is seen again:
having formed the *kapāla-mudrā* in the hollowed-out position (*sampuṭa*), one should recite [the mantra] without breathing,
while enraged, using the name of the person [against whom it is directed].
At that very moment, he becomes insane;
even a thousand people become insane.
He liberates them by means of his mind.
Having consecrated a lock of hair ten times with the name of whomever one desires, one should bind it;
all ḍākinīs will come. Having gone to a deserted place, one should bind a lock of hair after reciting [the mantra] a hundred times.
Having opened one's eyes, one should recite [the mantra] until they become invisible;
once released, however, they are seen again.
Having empowered a sugar-cake (*śarkaroṭā*), one should throw it upward, downward, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
All gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas shall be bound.
A ḍākinī robs one of all yoga.
Upon seeing a woman or a man on a seat, a bed, or in a sleeping place, one should recite the mantra one hundred times.
He causes it to be fastened.
Liberation is attained through the mind. Having recited the *śarkaroṭā* mantra, one should throw it into rivers.
He causes it to flow in the opposite direction.
With that very pebble, he arrests the wave.
He recites the mantra mentally.
Looking upwards, one should recite it a thousand times;
this wards off heavy rain.
Having performed the recitation a thousand times while facing an enemy army, one may enter into battle.
No pain arises for one being struck by hundreds of weapons,
nor is one pierced even by thousands of weapons.
One becomes possessed of a vajra-body. || 4 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the ritual procedure for the subsidiary heart-mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 12.
"By this," and so forth.
"Head-skull" (*śiraḥkapāla*) is a word without a case ending;
and that is indeed the skull itself.
"His flesh has been pierced" means "fleshless" (nirmāṃsa) due to the piercing of the veins;
"upādhi" refers to the body,
and he is "nirmāṃsa-upadhi," meaning one whose bodily substrate is devoid of flesh.
Having thus made or caused to be made the body of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) into such a state, he rubs it or causes it to be rubbed.
To the question "How?", he says: "With the index finger," namely, with the right [hand].
And [one should strike] with its tip.
This is to be visualized through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Having taken up the skull-bowl, the yogin of Vajrarudra, having emerged from within his own right nostril as Khaṇḍarohā—born from the utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ* and holding a weapon in her hand—should perform the piercing of the five heads while pronouncing the name of the person [to be targeted].

The collective meaning is as follows: having caused [the victim] to be killed, one should visualize his skull being filled with blood; then, by means of that mantra recited seven times over the tip of the index finger, one draws out all the fleshless blood from within his body.
He states the method for bringing [the victim] back to life with the words beginning "Now," and so forth.

By means of the tip of the left index finger, through the state of a peaceful mind, because of the churning of the interior of that body, the one to be accomplished (sādhya) becomes possessed of a body completely filled [with blood].
Why is this so? It says: "it enters," because of the entry of that very blood.
"Having consecrated" refers to the head of the target.
A blow with the fist should be administered with the visualization of a skull.
This is because, through the visualization of a "skull," there is both the filling of the skull along with the upward stroke and the direct filling of the interior of the skull.
"Chanted with mantra" (*mantrajaptam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
The rest is easy to understand.
"All the ḍākinīs come."
*Ḍākinī* is [formed] by eliding the first plural ending;
*śarkaroṭā* is [formed] by eliding the second case ending.
"It seizes all the yogas of the ḍākinīs" means by means of the sugar-candy cast in every direction and intermediate direction. "Lying down" refers to sexual intercourse.
For that purpose, she has gone to a seat or a bed, or she has come to a seat or a bed; "or that woman" indicates a conjunction (*samuccaya*); or "in battle."
The word "vā" (or) carries over [the term] "śarkaroṭa. || 4 ||
"Upahṛdaya" refers to the *upahṛdaya* mantra; the chapter that explains its ritual procedure is the twelfth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Ritual Procedure for the *Upahṛdaya*.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 12.
The thirteenth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Application of the Armor Mantra (Kavaca-mantra).
Now, I shall describe the ritual application of this armor exactly and in due order:
whatever may exist in the three worlds, all that which is desired by the mind [is accomplished]. (1)
Now, immediately after the explanation of the *upahṛdaya* mantra and its ritual procedure, the ritual application of the *kavaca*, that is, the *kavaca* mantra, will be described:
"Oṃ ha, namaḥ hi, svāhā hūṃ."
The mantra is: "vauṣaṭ he, hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ, phaṭ haṃ."
"Successively" means in the order of demonstrating the efficacy of recitation, medicinal herbs, and so forth.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The three worlds," and so on.
"All that which is desired by the mind" means that which is longed for by the mind. || 1 ||
In that regard, while reciting the Kavaca, one may travel upon the road;
there shall be no fear from thieves, tigers, and the like.
While reciting the *kavaca*, one enters the inner courtyard of the royal palace and remains unseen; or, taking whatever one desires, one departs, invisible even to the gods.
With the hand that has recited the *kavaca*, whomever one touches—
He becomes paralyzed as if by a stake;
he cannot be moved even by the gods of the thirty-three.
By reciting the mantra and striking him with one's foot, there is liberation.
Having applied a forehead mark (tilaka) made of one’s own blood or one’s own semen, over which one has recited the mantra three times, with whomsoever one speaks,
whomever one looks upon, and whoever looks upon him— [all these are affected].
It draws out the blood of all.
If one who is possessed by anger recites [the mantra] a thousand times in someone's house, everyone there will suffer from fever.
One should sprinkle water over which the mantra has been recited five times; this is the rite for bringing back [the speech].
By gazing at the face of someone while reciting it, one seizes that person's speech.
Standing by a river or a pond, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times; then one should walk upon the water.
Just as on dry land, so too does one move upon the water.
Entering the water of a river or even standing in the ocean, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times while rotating with both hands;
the yoginīs will become submissive. || 2 ||
The meaning of the passage beginning with "the armor" (*kavaca*) is as follows: for one who travels on a road while reciting the *kavaca*, there is no fear from thieves and the like;
furthermore, he may enter the royal court—the king’s palace—and yet he remains unseen.
He states where [the practice] is not observed: "in the precincts of women" (*aṅganādhiṣṭhāne*). This means in the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*).
For here, indeed, a subtle scrutiny of other men is performed.
In this case as well, the efficacy of the mantra is such that one is not seen; the connection is that having taken whatever object from the treasury one pleases, one departs unobserved.
Even here, because of his extreme subtlety of vision, he cannot be perceived; such is the power of the mantra.
It is said that he is not seen even by the gods;
for even with their physical eyes, the vision of the gods is unimpeded.
Because they too do not perceive it, there is the efficacy of the mantra;
"like a stake" means as if it were driven in.
Because it has entered deeply, it becomes motionless.
Regarding the passage beginning with "one's own blood" (*svarakta*), etc.,
it is easy to understand.
In the phrase "yasya gṛhe" (in whose house), the word "tatra" (there) is to be supplied;
[the form] "yoginī" is due to the elision of the nominative plural ending. || 2 ||
And likewise the Yoginīs of various forms, as well as the Ḍākinīs, Lāmās, and those with the forms of Khaṇḍarohā; these and others are thus proclaimed. (3)
All become submissive and follow his will.
Having prepared a cloth-painting during the conjunction of Puṣya, one whose body is covered by it and who has entered into union with the Yoginī should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
thereafter, he becomes accomplished.
With his body enveloped by that, he becomes invisible in the sky for a thousand yojanas;
he goes wherever he desires and wanders across the earth as far as the oceans.
Or he goes with his stream directed upwards. || 4 ||
The word *yoginīścaiva* uses the accusative case in the sense of the nominative;
the particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the various divisions; and *eva* (indeed) functions as a restrictive particle.
He speaks of their manifold forms with the words "ḍākinī" and so forth.
"Ḍākinī" refers to the various classes of ḍākinīs;
"lāmaya" refers to the various classes of lāmās.
"Rūpiṇī" refers to those of the *rūpiṇī* class. According to etymology (*nairukta*), they are so called because they "go upward in a stream" (*ūrdhvastrotas*);
the letter *s* has been elided.
The meaning is that he arrives by not transgressing the flow of the river in the reverse direction.
When the jewel—the bodhicitta—is made stable within, the yogi directly arrives at and realizes the innate (*sahaja*) state from above; this is another interpretation. (3–4)
Whatever sense faculty should enter the path, each and every one, by its very nature,
should carry forth everything as consisting of the Buddha through the yoga of supreme absorption.
Explaining the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), he says "that which," and so forth.
One should go—that is, proceed—to the path or the range of the sense faculties (*indriya*), such as the eye and the rest.
Whatever [practice] there may be, such as recitation (*jāpa*) and so on, all of that one should carry—that is, experience—as being composed of the Buddha, consisting of Vairocana and the others.
Regarding how one experiences through the nature of experience by means of action, he says: "by means of the yoga of supreme absorption" (*paramāhitayogena*).
Absorption (*yoga*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that is placed (*āhita*), that is, superimposed, upon the Supreme (*parama*), which is Śrī Heruka.
This constitutes the nature of all Buddhas: Vairocana in form, Akṣobhya in sound, Ratnasaṃbhava in odor, Amitābha in taste, and Amoghasiddhi in touch.
The meaning is that the mantra is to be recited while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure. || 5 ||
Taking the juice of the *pārijāta* tree in one's hand and reciting the mantra a thousand times, if one applies it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*) upon someone, that person becomes a tree.
If one sprinkles [the person] with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, this brings about their restoration.
Taking dust from the sole of an elephant's foot and reciting [the mantra] one thousand times, he who strikes [someone] with it becomes an elephant. || 6 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the armor mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 13.
Regarding "pārijāta": *pārijāta* refers to the *bhadradala* and so forth; the remainder is easily understood. || 6 ||

The application of the armor-mantra by means of its division is the "armor-mantra-application" (*kavacamantrayoga*). That which prescribes this very [application] is the chapter (*paṭala*); thus, it is "that [chapter]," namely, the thirteenth chapter (*trayodaśaḥ paṭalaḥ*).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 13.
The fourteenth chapter: The Procedure for the Transformation into Śrī Herukī through the Ass-Form Yoga.
Now I shall explain that accomplishment by which practitioners attain success—the self-nature of the ass-form yoga—for the sake of bringing the impulse of the mind to rest. (1)
The word *atha* has the sense of "again.
The connection is: "I shall again state the means for the heart-mantra.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "By which," and so forth.
The meaning is that "sādhana" is that by which practitioners achieve success (*sidhyanti*).
To the question "For what purpose?", he says "mind," and so forth.
The "impulse of the mind" (*manovega*) is the kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*); its cessation occurs because of its having been accomplished.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because its nature is associated with the form of a donkey.
This means: because of its association with the form of a donkey. || 1 ||
The Yoginīs—Lāmā, Rupiṇī, Ḍākinī, as well as Khaṇḍarohā and Kāmarupiṇī; the Ḍākinīs Gardabhākārā, Rudhiravaktrā, and she who is encircled by a trident in her hand—have been accomplished.
By means of them, one may perceive even one whose life has reached its end as long-lived.
In this state, however, the yogi who is like a good donkey will see;
then he will see both the donkey and the elephant that he saw previously.
Whatever birth a person brought about in a previous life, that very form of theirs is seen here by the yogi.
That man shall be a bestower of success; he is a human being who has reached the seventh birth.
By him, the bali-offering and fire-sacrifice (homa) should be performed, and thus the practitioner attains accomplishment.
With the words beginning "the Yoginīs," he speaks of the deities of the mandala: "Yoginīs" refers to those who abide in the three wheels.
"Kāmarūpiṇyas" means they have faces like the blood of a donkey.
Therefore he says: "and with faces of donkeys, blood, and [other] forms," due to the elision of the first plural ending;
likewise, "the ḍākinīs."
The ḍākinīs, beginning with Kākāsyā, all possess the form of a donkey, excluding the four-faced goddesses starting with Kākāsyā.
Regarding the phrase "encircled by tridents":
having set aside the *khaṭvāṅga*, they hold tridents in its place; furthermore, the colors of the thirty-six divine yoginīs are according to the sequence of their respective sādhana practices.
One who possesses the yoga of Śrī Heruka with a donkey face from which blood flows is himself [the deity].
By this it is stated that the specific distinction is having a donkey face from which blood flows;
everything else is exactly as described in the *Sādhana*.
When [one asks], "At what time?", he says: "Having accomplished" (*sādhitā*).
The sense is that this practice must be performed when the heart-mantra has been recited seven hundred thousand times.

This is stated according to the oral instruction: having drawn the mandala of *rajas* as the foundation, one should contemplate the syllable *hūṃ*, surrounded by the fifty letters, in the center of its eight-petaled lotus.
On the petals of the cardinal directions are the heart and near-heart mantras of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady.
On the petals of the intermediate corners are four skull-cups filled with blood.
On the twenty-four spokes are the twenty-four mantras beginning with *oṃ khaṇḍakapālini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

"Oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," and so forth; thus, including those of Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, as well as Pracaṇḍa and the others, there are forty-eight mantras in total. Within the root sūtra are the eight [mantras] of Kākāsyā and the rest, and above that, at the four gates, are the four mantra-words of Sumbha.
Outside the wall, above the gate, and at the joints of the *niryūha* projections, there are two armor-panels;
on the *cakravāta* (or *cakravāṭa*),
there is the heart-mantra of the Bhagavatī.
One should visualize an enclosure formed by the outer seeds beginning with Pullīra and the syllables beginning with *puṃ*.

Having placed within the center of the mandala an effigy made of rice-flour in the shape of a donkey, smeared with oil and lac, and anointed with clarified butter, the practitioner— possessing the yoga of Heruka with a donkey's face from which blood flows—
should light lamps in the four corners and, becoming one-pointed in mind, recite the heart-mantra while gazing at the effigy.
Then, he says this very thing—“one should see [the signs] as described”—beginning with “whose life has departed,” and so forth.
The word *api* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). As for the phrase “in this case” (*asmiṃstu*):
The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of a restriction (*niyama*).
The meaning is: "only when this very procedure has been performed.
[Regarding the term] *sugadarbha*:
If the donkey had previously been a yogin, then he would perceive himself as a donkey.
The word *hasti* ends in the vowel *i*.
He says "of whom," etc., to show that he perceives the genus (*jāti*) of others as well.
"Of whom," such as a human being and so forth—this refers to a "sentient being" (*sattva*).
"Of the yogin" is a genitive used in the sense of the instrumental.
By this, he states that the vision of the seven births is easily attained, beginning with the words "he" and so forth.
The bali-homa and the consumption [of the offering] should be performed by one who intends to perform them. By performing that bali-homa, the practitioner becomes a yogin.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because the adept's goal is accomplished."
In this [practice], the practitioner attains perfection within seven lifetimes according to the stated sequence. The word "yoga" is used here without a case ending;
the meaning is that this is the "donkey-yoga" (*gardabhayoga*). || 2 ||
Likewise, he ascends a hundred thousand yojanas upward in an instant;
this is the supreme yoga of the excellent mantra, the practitioner of which accomplishes the yoga of the ḍākinīs. (3)
Whoever recites this sign of yoga for one month attains perfection;
this is the secret of the tantra, the supreme heart of the mantra.
He who knows this in its true essence is a yogi; of this there is no doubt.
This is your Heruka, the Hero, the *Saṃvara* of the *Ḍākinījāla*. 5.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for the transformation into Śrī Herukī through the yoga of the donkey-form, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
The term *mantravara* refers to the yoga that possesses the most excellent mantra;
this is because it functions in conjunction with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).
The same applies even when the reading is *mantradhara*.
It is "supreme" because it accomplishes what is desired.
*Ḍākinī* refers to Vajravārāhī;
through union with her (*yoga*), one achieves the vision of previous births.
The meaning is "one who has attained that [state].
The passage beginning with "by yoga" and so forth is easy to understand.
Regarding the term "secret":
The essence of this tantra—what is it? It says: "the heart.
This refers to the heart-mantra.
To whom does "the heart" belong? He says: "of the mantra," that is, of the King of Vidyās.
That yogi who knows it in its true nature as non-different from the King of Vidyās, Śrī Heruka, [is the one].
In the reading *jñānasya*, it refers to mere knowledge; he who knows the heart is the yogin.
"This is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*" refers to Śrī Heruka, since the gender of the word is not restrictive.
This very thing is appropriate; by means of this, the state [of mind] is concentrated.
If the reading is *eṣata*, the root *eṣ* has the sense of "going.
It should be explained as: he attains (*eṣate*), that is, he reaches, the knowledge of the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. || 3-5 ||

That by which one becomes Śrī Heruka is "becoming Śrī Heruka" (śrīherukīkaraṇa); through the yoga of the donkey-form, this is the ritual procedure for becoming Śrī Heruka, the means of accomplishment (sādhana), and the fourteenth chapter is that which explains it.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 14.
The fifteenth chapter: The Procedure for the Secret Signs (*chomma*).
Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret signs (*chommaka*) within all the vows;
he who knows them in their true essence attains accomplishment, without a doubt. (1)
The word "atha" (then) is used in the sense of conjunction;
"ataḥ" (hence) is used in the sense of cause.
Not only is he a yogi who knows the heart, but he is also one who knows the secret signs (*chommaka*).
To explain for what purpose the method of secret signs connected with yoga is intended, he says: "In all the vows" (*sarvasaṃvareṣu*).

This means: for the sake of those vows, which are the protections (*saṃvara*) consisting of the concealment from śrāvakas and others of all [matters] such as [the nature of] persons and so forth. || 1 ||
The syllable *ḍā* is known as the male, and from that, *ḍī* is the female;
*ṣu* signifies immobilization, and *su* signifies devouring.
By what means is the apprehension of the connection [between them] effected?
He states those very [means] with the words "Ḍā" and so forth.
"Is remembered" (smṛtaḥ).
It was designated by infinite Tathāgatas as "ḍī" for women and "tata" for men;
this is the application of the verbal root *ḍīṅ*, meaning "to move through the sky."

The word *tata* signifies that from which there is, in reality, a connection (*anvaya*). The syllable *ḍī*, when formed with the suffix *kvip*, means "it flies" (*ḍīyate*), that is, it pervades everything. The syllable *ṣu* signifies "stopping" (*stambhana*); this word is conventionally established (*saṃketita*) in the sense of stopping.
Like the word *ḍittha* and others, it refers to a particular tree.
Regarding the word *su*, it signifies "eating" as well.
By the two words *ca* and *eva*, its status as a conventional term (*saṃketitatva*) is both conjoined and clarified. || 2 ||
"Mā" is indeed known as "mother," while "ye" refers to the wife;
"bhī" is likewise the sister, and "vī" is proclaimed to be the female friend. || 3 ||
"Mā" means "mother," as it is traditionally remembered; that is to say, "like a mother. "Ye" means "wife," while "vai" is indeed [an emphatic particle].
The meaning is that the wife alone is distinguished.
"Bhī" is remembered as "sister";
this is according to the literal sense.
The word *vī* is said to mean a female friend; it means a beloved woman. || 3 ||
"Lu" is to be understood as the daughter, "strī" as blood;
"so" is the drinking of semen, and "pe" is likewise that which is to be drunk. || 4 ||
"Lu" means "daughter," which refers to one's own offspring;
"strī" (woman) is to be understood as blood, that is, *rakta*.
"So" means "the drinking of Soma";
it is the drinking of nectar. "Pe" means "that which is to be drunk," and "tathā" means "that which is to be drunk"—the meaning is a liquid substance.
The word "tathā" (thus) indicates that the convention is established only by way of a part [of the object]. || 4 ||
*Hī* means meat; *bha* means eating;
*bhū* means the gathering (*melāpaka*); and *pī* likewise means the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). || 5 ||
*Hī* means "flesh," that is, meat itself;
*bha* means "eating," that is,
consuming.
*Bhū* means *melāpaka*, which is a specific location for the assembly of yoginīs.
*Pī* means it would be a *śmaśāna*, that is, an abode of corpses. || 5 ||
"Hū" is known as Mṛtakā; "dhī" is remembered as Yoginī;
"ga" is likewise Lāmā; and "trī" is indeed Rupiṇī.
"Hū" is known as the corpse; the Yoginīs know the corpse to be infinite. "Dhī" is remembered as the Yoginī.
She possesses concentration because she has a dual nature.
*Ga* refers to the *lāmas*; likewise, the various *lāmīs* (or *mās*) are established as conventional designations.
"Three indeed, and those who possess form"—the meaning is that only the classes of beings possessing form are intended by this designation. || 6 ||
*Ku* is known as Ḍākinī, and *hā* is indeed Khaṇḍarohā;
*ja* is the pair of shanks, and *ka* is the pair of arms.
"Ku" refers to Ḍākinī;
"tathā" (so be it) refers to the classes of Ḍākinīs because they are designated in that very way;
"ḍā" refers to Khaṇḍarohā; and "vāyi" refers to [Vārī].
They are indeed of the Khaṇḍarohā class.
The word *ḍā* also has two meanings;
*ja* refers to the pair of shanks (*jaṅghā-yugala*).
The two shanks;
the convention [applies] by way of a single part. || 7 ||
"Bha" is the greeting; "su" is the act of welcoming.
These single-syllable signs are to be known as the "heroine-sisters" (vīrabhaginī). || 8 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of the Syllable Symbols, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 15.
"Bha" is a term of salutation; it signifies veneration. The word "bha" has two meanings.
"Su" means the act of welcoming; it is the performance of a welcome. All the syllables [are to be understood in this way].
These are words beginning with [terminations] devoid of case-endings.
Furthermore, these are *chommaka*s consisting of single syllables;
that is to say, those which possess one syllable each.
"She should be known as the sister of the heroes. Here, "heroes" (vīra) refers to yogins,
and "sisters" (bhaginī) refers to yoginīs.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis.
*Sā* refers to those secret signs (*chommaka*),
because they have been designated as a plurality.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
they are to be known by the heroes and the yoginīs,
because they are the constituent parts of its conventional usage.
Alternatively, the *chommakas* consist of twenty-four syllables, corresponding to the purification of the twenty-four yoginīs. || 8 ||

The "syllable-chommakas" are those chommakas consisting of single syllables. The method for explaining them is the "method of the syllable-chommakas. The fifteenth chapter, which expresses that [method], is the fifteenth.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 15 ||
The sixteenth chapter: The Procedure for Examining the Characteristics of the Seven Yoginīs.
Now, O practitioner, I shall proclaim the secret great accomplishment; those who abide by the supreme commitment (samaya) are worthy and provide pleasing assistance.

Now, immediately after the syllable-secrecy (*akṣarachommaka*), I shall proclaim the great accomplishment of the secret ones—the yoginīs—which is the great certainty-accomplishment, the secret great accomplishment (*guhyamahāsiddhi*).
The meaning is that I shall explain it by way of its modes and divisions.
The word "ha" serves as an ornament for the sentence.
Because the indeclinable [term] has multiple meanings:
"sādhakaḥ" means "for the sake of the achiever" (sādhakāya); here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the dative.
He asks, "Which are the yoginīs denoted by the word 'secret'? and replies with the words beginning "pare" and so forth.
"Supreme" (parama) refers to the commitment (samaya) consisting of colors, fragrances, and so on.
"Abiding" (sthitāḥ) means having remained for a long time.
To the question "Of what nature are they?", he says: those from whom pleasing assistance arises for practitioners are the "yoginīs who provide pleasing assistance. || 1 ||
This must be given to a devotee who has grasped the distinction between the castes, O non-dual yogi of heroes;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall attain perfection. || 2 ||
He explains for whose sake they are thus: "for the devotee" (bhaktāya). This means for those characterized by service.
Therefore, the sense is that an effort must be made to know them.
Explaining the *samaya*, he says "varṇa" and so forth.
The particle "tu" is for the purpose of restriction.
Establishing that restriction, he says "vīra" and so forth.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "I shall explain that [knowledge] by which, through the letters and so forth, the yoginīs may attain the direct realization of *siddhi* without the non-dual hero.
The sense is that those [letters], when known by the external yogin, bestow such a *siddhi*. || 2 ||
But that woman who is as pale-white as a lotus stalk, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, who always delights in white garments, and who possesses the fragrance of fresh sandalwood; (3)
He states the definition: "mṛṇāla... and so forth.
This is easily understood.
"Nava" refers to the well-known *candana*, meaning *gośīrṣa*.
She possesses the fragrance of fresh sandalwood; thus, she is "navacandanagandhinī."
She who delights in the assemblies of the Sugatas should be known as one born of a noble family and lineage;
she is a woman with the luster of molten gold, who is fond of red and yellow garments. (4)
Possessing birth, having a single fragrance, she follows the heroes; she is dark as a blue lotus and fond of one who wears blue garments. (5)
She who possesses the auspicious fragrance of the blue lotus and follows Śrī Heruka is indeed that woman who is beautiful and has the complexion of a lotus petal. (6)
Mṛṇālagandhā and likewise Vīramatī are always present;
and that woman who is reddish-fair, with a red face and beautiful form, [is Raktagaurā].
She possesses the fragrance of jasmine and blue lotus and is born of the Vajra family;
she is a woman who is yellowish-dark in complexion and fond of wearing white garments. (8)
She who has the fragrance of *śirīṣa* flowers on her head follows the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
she is a woman of reddish hue, wearing garments of that same color. (9)
Karpūragandhā always follows the Vairocana family.
These seven families of yoginīs have been described by me.
She is indeed delighted by assemblies of the Sugatas (Buddhists).

She whose family and lineage (*gotra*) are the Hayagrīvas is "one of the Śauṇḍinī family and lineage" (*śauṇḍinī-kulagotrā*). She who is born from such [a family] is "born of the family and lineage" (*kulagotrajā*), with the vowel shortened.
The hero is Ākāśagarbha; his follower is Cakravarmiṇī, who is so called because she is born from that same family.
She is the follower of Śrī Heruka;
she follows the family of Suvīrā.
"Vīramatī" means one who follows the Vīramatī family;
the Vajra family is the Vārāhī family.

The Tathāgata is Padyanarteśvara; because one is born from him, there is the "Tathāgata family," which possesses great power and follows him. "By me" means by myself. "For the sake of firm conviction."
This indicates the state of being immediately contiguous. || 4-10 ||
Those who are constantly devoted to the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) are indeed filled with their own mudrās and colors;
for the syllables of the family-mantra (kulavidyā) consist of six letters. || 11 ||
The women are beautiful; their conduct consists of excessive anger, egoism, and so forth.
The word "hi" (indeed) functions as a conjunction.
These are the people who are yoginīs.
Furthermore, as to what they are like, he says: "Their own mudrās" refers to their colors, such as white and so forth; "color" refers to being fair as pale as a lotus stalk and so forth.
They are "intermingled," meaning connected, with those two.
And also "the syllables of the family vidyās."
The family is the practitioner; its mantras are the very syllables, which are "vajras" because of the firmness of one's resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*); these are the yoginīs.
The meaning is that these goddesses become of unshakable form.
Thus, there are six colors.
The six syllables are to be known as the types of yoginīs;
for "hi" signifies a conjunction. 11.
For she binds her own mudrā and speaks speech born of her own lineage;
that woman who goes on the left, the Yoginīs always [go] to the left. 12.
One who speaks with great eloquence, gazes with a leftward glance, and laughs joyfully at women is called a *samayin*. 13.
He says of them: "he binds," and so forth.
He describes the binding of the mudrās: "with the left," and so forth;
that is, with the left [hand] of the yoginīs.
"Yoginīs on the left" means that for whomsoever the yoginīs are on the left.
He speaks of the speech born of one's own lineage with the words beginning with "speech," and so forth.

One who speaks so as to be great—that is, one whose nature is excellent speech. The particle *vai* is used in the sense of "indeed" or as a conjunction. Because his nature is to laugh with joy, he is "one who laughs with joy."
The letter *ca* is as before.
*Samaya* refers to a rule that is not to be transgressed; one who possesses such a rule is called a *samayin*.
The designation "man" is used here with reference to the community of yoginīs;
it may be due to a particular mode of expression or out of disregard, for this mode is but one. (12–13)
She who fulfills the desires of women is proclaimed as one of noble lineage;
she does not abandon the family traditions nor forsake what is taught in her own scriptures. || 14 ||
He who recites the vidyā of his own family is called a *samayin*;
for he who, having performed a salutation, always bows with his left side bent. (15)
One should engage in conversation with women through displays of genuine affection;
indeed, they will then scratch the ground with their left big toes.
One should scratch one's head with the left hand while looking askance;
for that practitioner, the recollection of his own vidyā is beneficial regarding that object. (17)
Placing a finger on the cheek, the chin, or the nose,
and reciting the mantra once while casting a sidelong glance, one should gaze upon the Vidyā;
thus the Yoginīs truly attain a state of sincere devotion toward those who observe the pledges (samayins).
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the procedure for examining the characteristics of the seven yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
The genitive case in "strīṇām" (of women) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
"Kulāni" (families/clans) refers to the practitioners (*sādhakas*). These very [families] are the "seeds" (*bījāni*), meaning the causes for proclamation.
They explain it by dividing it as follows:
the family ritual is the conduct of the observance;
the family knowledge is the family deity.
The second [point] is that which is stated in one's own scriptures and stated in the system of Mantra; this is what is being explained.
"Homage," and so forth.

"Indeed, by means of true devotion toward them"—this refers to the third [point]: that the practitioner (sādhaka), through such characteristics and by perceiving them as such, should indeed direct his devotion toward those yoginīs with prostrations and the like. "With the left thumb" [is the fourth].
"By the foot" means of the foot.
"She writes" means that which is written again and again should be understood as the type of Yoginī; this is the intended meaning. This is the fourth [section].
One should scratch the head; this should be done with the hand.
This is to be understood as being in the manner of the *yoginī* folk.
[She is ever-following.]
"It is beneficial for that practitioner within his domain.
Having seen her in such a state, it is appropriate for that practitioner to remember the Vidyā;
the sense is that he should regard her as his own Vidyā, like his own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).

He asks "Why? and says: "Because it is beneficial regarding the object. Since such an object leads to respect, the locative case is used in the sense of the first case (i.e., "in the object"); thus, the fifth [type of] collection of meaning is established.
"Gaṇḍa" refers to a section of the maṇḍala, or it functions as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
"Api" is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). "Tiryagdṛṣṭi" means a sidelong glance.
The sixth [point] is that a woman who has her fingers placed on her chin and so forth, and whose gaze is directed sideways, should be known as a type of *yoginī*.
Having seen them thus, what should be done? He says: "Reciting the mantra once, one should cause the *vidyā* to look [at them].
The mantra is the King of Vidyās (*vidyārāja*).
He says "What is the use of this? and so forth; the passage beginning with "the existence" (*sadbhāvam*) is easy to understand. || 15–18 ||
The term "seven yoginīs" is an illustration;
it refers to the characteristics of all six as well,
[making] thirteen yoginīs in total.
*Lakṣaṇa* means a mark or characteristic.

"The examination of the characteristics of the seven and six yoginīs" is the compound *saptayoginīlakṣaṇaparīkṣā*, formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopī-samāsa*). The sixteenth chapter, which explains that procedure, is the sixteenth.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 16 ||
The seventeenth chapter, on the ritual of signs and mudrās, in the section concerning the forms of all Yoginīs; following that:
"But the Yoginīs as well as the Ḍākinīs are indeed difficult to find."
Because of the true presence of the five nectars, she is Yāminī and Trāsanī. || 1 ||
The seven Ḍākinīs—Kāminī, Bhīmā, Rupā, Sañcārā, and Bhāsurā, along with [the remaining two]—have been gathered here; their own characteristics are now being stated. (2)
Immediately after the [section on] characteristics, he speaks the seventeenth chapter beginning with "Then they are difficult to find," and so forth.
In the phrase "of the yoginīs, the ḍākinīs," and so forth, the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative. Thus, "yoginīs" refers to the goddesses.
The word "turvi" has the sense of "especially.
Regarding the phrase "of the yoginīs":
*ḍākinīs*, *māniṣīs*, and *yoginīs* are those who follow the qualities of a yoginī; this is the meaning.
Therefore, there is the phrase "and likewise. Why? He says: "because they are difficult to obtain.
The meaning is that since the *ḍākinīs* possess the qualities of goddesses, they are obtained only with great difficulty.
If this is so, how are they perceived? He says: "Because of the presence of the five nectars.
The meaning is that these remain for the practitioner who makes use of them.
He states the characteristics of the ḍākinīs: "The seven ḍākinīs—Yāminī, Trāsinī, Kāminī, Bhīmā, Rupā, Sañcārā, and Bhāsurā—are gathered together."
The meaning is that these seven, beginning with Yāminī, have been withdrawn and thus briefly enumerated.
Regarding the phrase "its own characteristic is stated here":
the meaning is that their names are stated by way of explaining this characteristic through positive concomitance (anvaya). || 1-2 ||
Rūpikā, Cumbikā, Lāmā, Parāvṛttā, Sabālikā, Anirvṛttikā, and Aihikī—the goddesses are known as the seven Ḍākinīs. || 3 ||
One should observe her who, being unattached, yet raises her eyebrows;
she first withdraws her form and afterwards brings about destruction.
She should be known as Rūpikā, who is practiced by the non-dual heroes;
whether desired or undesired,
she embraces and kisses the child.
She should be known as Cumbikā, a ḍākinī who destroys evil;
she has a frowning face with a sidelong glance and threatens with a knitting of her eyebrows.
Otherwise, Niḥśvāsa Bhairava has designated Lāmā as follows:
the boar, the śarabha, the cat, the jackal, and so forth; the goat and the horse. (7)
Then she should terrify them all; for when she has turned away, she is said to be "reverted.
When she has gone off laughing in great joy, she does not return again. || 8 ||
When she laughs clearly while being affectionate, she is indeed known as Khaṇḍarohā;
yet when her mind is agitated, she strikes with her hand, a clod of earth, or her foot.
If she is touched by the edge of a cloth, a piece of wood, or by that [wind], she does not live;
one should know her to be irreversible, for she is proclaimed to be incurable.
He also states their alternative names along with their lineages: "Rupikā, Cumbikā, Lāmā, Parāvṛttā, Sabālikā, Anirvṛttikā, and Aihikī—the goddesses, the Ḍākinīs, are remembered as being sevenfold.
He states the definition of Rupā, whose other name is Rupikā, beginning with "aviraktām" (one who is not detached), etc., [ending] with "vīrādvayasevitum" (to serve the non-dual Hero).
The meaning is that she is one who serves the non-dual Hero (*vīrādvayasevinī*).
He states the definition of *Yāminī*, whose other name is *Cumbikā*— beginning with "or desired," etc.—
and [the mention of] *Ḍākinī*.
The meaning is "the destroyer of the multitude of dākinīs.
For this very reason, *yama* means self-restraint (*saṃyama*);
that itself is *yāma*, with the suffix *aṇ* used in its own sense (*svārthe*).
That which belongs to her is the night, because it brings about destruction. He states the characteristic of Bhīmā, who is also known by the name Lāmā: "with a sidelong glance," and so forth.
"They threaten" (*tarjayanti*);
the plural number is used for the singular.
Therefore, this is the meaning.
Otherwise, even though Bhairava is attached to desire, he exhales [his breath] with particular effort;
"tu" signifies a distinction. Therefore, she who delights with particularity is Rāmā.
*Lāmā* is so called because of the letter *la*.
She is indeed *bhīmā* (the Terrible One) due to her association with two characteristics.
He states the characteristic of *trāsanyā*, who is also known by the name *aparā* (the Other), beginning with the words "varāha" and so forth.
The *śarabha* is a specific kind of beast;
however, if the reading is *śarama*, it refers to a dog.
[The text says: "One should frighten all of them."
The meaning is that they are afraid upon seeing her;
therefore, she turned away.
The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because."
It is so called because others turn away from it. He states the definition of *sañcāra*, which is also known by the name *sabālikā*: "exultant," and so forth.
It is called *sañcāra* because it does not return again.
He states the definition of the *kāminī*, who is also designated by the other name *aihikī*, beginning with "anurukta" and so forth.
She is called *khaṇḍarohā* because she repeatedly ascends (*ārohati*) and remains (*tiṣṭhati*) upon a "fragment" (*khaṇḍe*), that is, an undivided region;
"hi" means "because."
The term *aihikī* refers to that which remains for a long time in this world.
He states the definition of *bhāsurā*, which is also known by the name *anivartikā*: "with an agitated mind," and so forth.
That which is called *bhāsurā* or *anivartikā* becomes agitated in mind.
And when touched by clods of earth or other such things by one who has become thus, a sentient being does not live.
Why? Because it is irreversible—that is, impossible to turn back.
To the question "Why?", he says: "For they are incurable. The word "hi" (for) indicates the reason. (3-10)
She laughs, speaks, or weeps, or she becomes angry without cause;
she is known as the goddess Aihikā, who speaks first.
She who delights in the assemblies of the Sugatas is born from the Vajra family;
one should recognize the families of the Ḍākinīs here as being great speakers. (12)
The skull, the axe, the fangs, the saw-banner, the sword, the terrifying [noose], and the conch are known as the eight; they are proclaimed as the family mudrās.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the section on the procedure for signs and mudrās, in the transformation of the forms of all yoginīs within the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 17.
"One should perceive the great families of the ḍākinīs here"—
this refers to the families of the yoginīs beginning with Vāyuvegā and ending with Mahāvīryā, as well as those beginning with Yāminī and ending with Aihikā.
*Ḍākinī* and *yoginī* have the same meaning.

In the alternative reading, "one should observe [them] to serve the passion (*vīra*) of the family-seals (*kulamudrā*) of the *ḍākinīs*," the families of the aforementioned *ḍākinīs* are indeed the seals (*mudrās*). Or, they are the yoginīs themselves, such as Vāyuvegā and the others.
One should observe them; that is, one should know them. "Vīrasevinī" means "served by heroes";
[this form arises] from the elision of the second case ending and the plural marker.
The skull, the axe, the tusk, the discus, the saw, the banner, the sword, and the terrifying [weapon]—these are the enumerations.
The word "and" (ca) is used for conjunction.
"Tusk" (daṃṣṭrā) refers to the tusks of a boar.
"Kacadhvajā" refers to having disheveled hair.
The eighth [category] consists of eight mudrās.
Among these mudrās, whichever one belongs to any particular ḍākinī—
In another reading, it is: "the skull, the axe, the fangs, and the terrifying sword";
here, "sword" (khaḍga) is without a case ending, and "terrifying" (saṃtrāsanī) refers to the knife (kartṛ).
Thus, there are exactly five mudrās. || 11-13 ||

And this—namely, the transformation of the forms of the *yoginīs*, the gazing with undimmed passion and so forth, the seals (*mudrās*) such as the skull-bowl, the ritual procedure, the purpose, the knowledge of the *yoginīs*, and their characteristics—is [the subject matter].
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The eighteenth chapter: The Chapter on the Ritual for the Colors, Characteristics, and Symbols of All *Yoginīs*.
Now I shall further proclaim another word of the ḍākinīs, by which one correctly understands the ḍākinīs who abide in the pledge (samaya). || 1 ||

Regarding the word *atha*: the connection is that immediately after the description of the transformation of form (*rūpaparivartana*) and so forth, I shall explain the next *pada*, which is the sign (*cihna*).
It is called a *pada* because by means of it, the *ḍākinī* is reached or understood.
To the question "Of what kind? he says: "By which," and so forth.
The word *ḍākinyaḥ* is in the nominative case used in the sense of the accusative. || 1 ||
For that woman who is reddish-fair and emits the fragrance of a lotus,
who has a gentle gaze and whose very nature is one of affectionate appearance— (2)
He states the verse beginning with "raktā" and so forth.
"Padyagandhagātrī" means one whose body emits the fragrance of a lotus.
"Saumyadṛṣṭiḥ" means one who possesses a gentle gaze.
Because it is free from frowning and the like;
whereas "with a gaze of passion" means because it is characterized by extreme attachment.
In the reading "saṃraktanayanānugeti," it means "accompanied by one with bloodshot eyes. || 2 ||
For that woman whose nails and eyes are likewise reddened, and who has the verse inscribed in her house, she is born of the lineage of Padyanarteśvara. (3)
Regarding the phrase "nakhā hi": the particle *hi* is used here in the sense of emphasis (*adhikārtha*).
The meaning is that the nails are exceedingly red.
Because this occurs in a section concerning passion (*saṃrāga*), the reading "padyaṃ likhitaṃ padyam" (a lotus-pattern has been drawn) is easily understood as the intended mark.
It should be understood that Amitābha is Padyanarteśvara, and those born from his family are likewise [to be known]. || 3 ||
One should always worship the trident situated between the eyebrows, as well as the dark-complexioned Śyāmā with a pale body;
and one should always honor the vajra drawn in the house, which is constantly meditated upon in the Vajra family.
She from whom a trident and indeed a spear are seen upon the forehead should be known as Vajraḍākinī, born from the family of Śrī Heruka. (5)
Red-eyed, reddish-white in complexion, and likewise with red feet and hands,
she who is constantly cultivated [in meditation] always delights in goats or even in cocks.
One should likewise constantly worship the vajra, her sign, in her house;
there is no doubt that these ḍākinīs are born from the family of Śrī Heruka. (7)
She whose wheel is seen upon her forehead and also in her hand, who is dark-complexioned like a rain cloud, and always wears a turban on her forehead; || 8 ||
She who is endowed with great good fortune, virtuous, and most excellent—
she indeed in whose house the drawn wheel is always worshipped.
Born from the family of Vajravārāhī, the ḍākinī is proud of her strength;
she who is dark like black collyrium and whose white teeth are prominent. (10)
She who is both fierce and always favorable, who is endowed with virtuous nature, who is constantly devoted to bathing, and whose speech is not talkative; || 11 ||
And the auspicious vajra, when inscribed, is constantly worshipped in the home;
fifteen thousand [beings] born of the family of Vajravārāhī [are thereby purified]. 12.
The trident situated between the eyebrows is a limb in the form of a trident; she is dark-complexioned and has a pale body— that is,
her body is both dark and pale.
A vajra is drawn on her own house;
one should worship the house.
"Tu" signifies certainty.
She should be known as one who has necessarily arisen from the family of Śrī Heruka;
*vai* is used as a particle for emphasis or to indicate an alternative; *api* expresses possibility.
In the sense of excellence:
"rakta" and so forth.
A *chāgala* is simply a *chagala*.
"Continuity" means uninterruptedness.
"Ḍākinī" refers to the ḍākinī.
"Lalāṭa" refers to the forehead.
It should be understood that [the location] is "in the middle of the forehead," as indicated by the word *tu*;
the particle *hi* denotes emphasis.
By the word "forehead" (*lalāṭa*), the hero's cloth (*vīrapaṭa*) is meant.
"Sādhvī" means a devoted wife. "Paratare" means most excellent.
"Daśanonnatā" means one with prominent teeth.
"Vāmā" means she who delights in the unreal state;
she is born from the family of Vajravārāhī.
He states how many there are: "fifteen thousand.
This means there are fifteen thousand yoginīs. (4-12)
A woman who is fair-complexioned like gold, as well as one with fixed eyes and hairy [limbs], or one on whose forehead or even in whose hand a thunderbolt is seen—[these are auspicious]. (13)
But she who has ascended the throne is ever proud, yet speaks the truth;
she is fragrant with the scent of jasmine, and the great thunderbolt engraved upon her is constantly worshipped. (14)
Khaṇḍarohā, born of the Kula, is the supreme Great Mistress of Yoga;
she who is eternally fond of meat, thirsty, and has the luster of black collyrium.
She whose forehead has the shape of a trident, who delights in cruel deeds, and who goes daily to the cremation ground, fearless and pitiless; (16)
She on whose forehead the trident and skull are inscribed, who is worshipped in the home—that ḍākinī is born of the lineage of the god Śrī Heruka. (17)
A woman who has the color of a cloud, whose teeth are unevenly set, who is constantly engaged in cruel deeds, and whose left canine tooth is prominent; || 18 ||
She in whose house an axe is kept and constantly worshipped is a ḍākinī born from the lineage of Vināyaka; of this there is no doubt. (19)
From the words beginning with *gaurī* up to *vare*, the characteristics of her who has arisen from the *Khaṇḍarohā-kula* are described.
She whose fragrance is like that of a jasmine flower—she who possesses such a scent—is thus called *mallikāmodā*.
From the words beginning with *māṃsapriyā* up to *ḍākinī sā kulodbhavā*, the characteristics of her who has arisen from the *Śrīheruka-kula* are described.
With the passage beginning with "jīmūta" and ending with "na saṃśayaḥ," the characteristics of one born in the Vināyaka family are described.
The phrase "daśanairviṣamasthitā" means having uneven teeth.
Vināyaka is the enemy of obstacles (Vighnāri). || 13–19 ||
This indicative description of the host of ḍākinīs, born from the family of Śrī Heruka, has been proclaimed for the benefit of practitioners. (20)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the procedure for the colors, characteristics, and signs of all yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
This has been proclaimed as the defining characteristic of the host of ḍākinīs, for the benefit of practitioners born from the family of Śrī Heruka.
This characteristic belongs to the host of ḍākinīs.
To the question "Of what kind [of practitioners]? he says: "born from the family of Śrī Heruka," which is a compound without case endings (*nirvibhaktika*).
Śrī Heruka alone is the *kula* (family) of that which arises from him.
There is a protracted pronunciation (*pluta*).
Words such as "and" (*ca*) and so forth are to be understood as having the sense of conjunction and the like.

The characteristics and families are not [to be determined] by mental conceptualization as they were correctly introduced in the sixteenth [chapter], but rather through the mixing of color, scent, and so forth, along with the family; thus, seven yoginīs are mentioned. By means of action alone, there are six.
In the seventeenth [chapter], there are seven [types] by means of the grasping of names and so forth, as well as the signs such as the skull-cup;
and here, there are eight by means of the signs such as color and scent associated with the *kula*. In total, there are twenty-eight.
The word "all" (sarva) denotes totality with respect to a specific location.
That which prescribes and explains the colors, characteristics, and emblems of all eight yoginīs is the "Chapter on the Rules for the Colors, Characteristics, and Emblems of All Yoginīs";
thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the eighteenth, in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 18.
The nineteenth chapter: The Procedure for Teaching the Mudrās and Counter-Mudrās of All Yoginīs.
Furthermore, I shall now fully explain the specific [mudrās] of the Lāmās, by which the practitioner may correctly understand the various parts of the limbs.
The word *atha* (now/then) serves as a conjunction for the [following] definition.
The word *aparam* (another) refers to the definition of the *lāmās*, meaning the *yoginīs* who belong to the class of *lāmās*.
The particle *tu* is used as an expletive (*vākyālaṅkāra*).

"Specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) means that while the general characteristics of those born into the *lāmā* family and so forth have been stated, what is now being said pertains specifically to those of the *lāmā* lineage; this is the distinction.
Because it consists of the constituent parts (*avayava*), it is a "characteristic of the parts" (*avayavalakṣaṇa*); the connection [of the sentence] is: "I shall correctly explain that.
In the reading "the practitioner" (*sādhaka*), although the dative case has been elided, because it serves that purpose (*tādarthya*), the nominative case also carries the sense of the dative. (1)
Her face is seen to be broad and circular;
there is always a beard upon her mouth, and her eyebrows are long and hairy.
Clad in white garments, pure, gentle, unshakeable, and speaking with courage—she who is ever devoted to the true Dharma is to be known as the Heroic Sister (Vīrabhaginī). || 3 ||
He states the defining characteristic: "the mouth," and so forth.
"Parimaṇḍala" means circular.
"Lomaśā" means having abundant hair.
"Clad in white garments" means wearing stainless clothes.
"Pure" means stainless.
"Unshakeable" means firmly resolved.
"Hero-sister" means a yoginī; in the alternative reading "hero-sisters," the plural is used despite the singular sense. (2–3)
Either the *padya-mudrā* or the *kūrma-mudrā* should be presented;
furthermore, the *ajina* and the *kamaṇḍalu* are prescribed as the counter-gestures (*pratimudrā*). || 4 ||
Having seen her, he said that the mudrā should be given, beginning with "padya" and so forth.
The *padya-mudrā* consists of the contraction of the fingers held in the *añjali* gesture.
Alternatively (*athavā*) refers to another option.
Furthermore, as an ornament for the discourse:
having extended the right hand and raised it, one should place the left hand, which is bent, upon it; this is the tortoise mudrā (*kūrmamudrā*).
As for "the deer skin and the water-pot": [these are held].
From the gesture of holding with the left hand the hem of the garment draped over the left shoulder comes the deer skin;
some say it is from the gesture of wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*);
and from the gesture of holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) comes the water-pot.
The word *ca* (and) is used here for the purposes of conjunction and emphasis.
One should show the deer-skin (*ajina*) to the one who holds the lotus-mudrā,
and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) to the one who holds the tortoise-mudrā.
From the yoginī’s showing of her mudrā, the yogin’s [response] is the *pratimudrā*. || 4 ||
The tenth lunar day is her festival, and a verse of hers is written in the home;
this is the characteristic mark of those who have attained prosperity.
Long-lipped and large-eyed, with reddish-brown eyes,
she was wealthy, fortunate, blessed, fair-complexioned, and resembled the campaka flower.
Neither short nor excessively long, she is fond of variegated garments;
and there are three lines on her forehead extending to the upper hairline.
He laughs and indeed takes delight, remaining fixed upon the path;
he always delights in stories of those who have died in battle.
Upon seeing such a young woman, one should cause the Śūlamudrā to be presented;
moreover, one should display a dance with the left foot contracted.

And the reversal is performed with the left hand; the counter-seal (pratimudrā) is prescribed for her. Furthermore, the fourteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight are prescribed as her sacred festivals (parvan).
Regarding the term *śriyāṇām*, it is due to the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*).
*Śrī* refers to Śrī Heruka when joined with Vajravārāhī; the yoginīs born from him are the *śriyas*.
[The passage continues with] "Lamboṣṭhī," and so forth.
Another says: "with the left foot drawn up.
This means one should display the *ardhaparyaṅka* (half-lotus) dance posture.
"Turning" (*parivartana*) refers to the act of turning away.
These two constitute the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*).
The lunar phases (*parvaṇī*) are times of merit (*puṇyakāla*).
On the lunar phases such as the fourteenth day, one should perform worship toward the Tathāgatas, the masters (*ācārya*), and others. (5–10)
One should constantly worship her, or have her trident painted in the house;
this is the characteristic mark of the Lāmās who are the mistresses of the world (lokeśvarīs). || 11 ||
She whose two pits are always visible at the junction of her cheeks, who is perpetually reddish-fair in complexion, and whose eyes are greenish-brown; || 12 ||
Likewise, his hair is curled, his head is bound with a silk cloth, and a single line is clearly visible established upon his forehead. || 13 ||
Likewise, she has a long neck and is tall, always fond of red garments;
she laughs and sings, yet she becomes angry for no apparent reason.
A woman whose mind is particularly fickle and who takes delight in quarrels—having seen such a young woman, one should display the Śaktimudrā. || 15 ||
The bell-mudrā should be offered with effort as the second;
however, the counter-mudrā is prescribed by means of the left hand's reversal.
She has short and thick shanks;
she always loves yellow garments and wears her cloth draped over her shoulder. (17)
Upon seeing such a woman, one should display the face-mudrā;
the conch-mudrā should also be offered with effort as the second. (18)
A reversal is performed with the left hand, and the counter-seal (pratimudrā) is prescribed;
on the fourteenth lunar day, which is a sacred festival, a vajra is to be drawn in his house.
This is the characteristic of those who possess the essence of Śrī Heruka:
she is hairy in all her limbs, and her eyes are blackish-brown. 20.
Karālī, Vikṛtā, Ghorā, Sthūlāsyā, Sthūlavaktrā, Lamboṣṭhī, Kṛṣṇavarṇā, Koṭarākṣī, and Bhagnanāsikā. || 21 ||
One who is constantly skilled in the arts of music, cloud-colored, and captivating—having seen such a woman, one should cause the seal of a Naga to be bestowed upon her. || 22 ||
The Śakti-mudrā should be offered with effort, and indeed the second [mudrā] as well;
furthermore, the counter-mudrā (pratimudrā) is prescribed by means of the left hand. || 23 ||
The Ekādaśī festival and her fang are depicted in the house;
this is the characteristic mark of the Vajravārāhī Lāmās. || 24 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the procedure for the instruction on the seals (*mudrā*) and counter-seals (*pratimudrā*) of all yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
Of the world-sovereign goddesses belonging to the family of Amitābha,
there are always two hollows at the junction of the cheeks on both sides of the face;
in some places, the reading is "kapolagaṇḍa."
In this context, *kapola* refers to the cheek.
The *śaktimudrā* is formed by holding the index finger raised upward due to the pressing of all the other fingers together by the thumb.
The *ghaṇṭāmudrā* is performed by mimicking the ringing of a bell.
One of the two mudrās should be given.
By the words "short" (*hrasva*) and so forth, he describes another: she whose nature it is to let the hem of her garment hang from one shoulder is called *skandhavastrāvalambinī*.

Having formed the vajra-añjali, having raised the two middle fingers, having encircled the two ring fingers with the two index fingers, and having straightened the two thumbs, one should hold that near the face; this is the *mukhamudrā*.
The Śaṅkha-mudrā is formed by contracting the three fingers beginning with the little finger of the upturned left hand, joining the index finger and thumb, and extending them.

The second counter-mudrā, the Nāga-mudrā, is formed by raising the left hand, placing the right elbow upon it, and holding the right hand with the thumb and index finger extended and the other three fingers contracted.
Therefore, he says: "The counter-seal" (*pratimudrā*) and "the second seal" (*dvitīyā pratimudrā*) are synonyms.
The characteristics of the five yoginīs belonging to the *lāmā* family have been stated.
By means of the collective [description], the characteristics of the thirty-two yoginīs are established through the observation of their characteristic seals (*lakṣaṇamudrā*).
The specific distinction is that "the counter-seal (pratimudrā) should be given.
The unspoken meaning of the words beginning with "tu" (but/however) is to be inferred by oneself. || 11-24 ||
By means of the mudrās and counter-mudrās, he states the summary meaning of the chapter, beginning with "sarva" and so forth.
The word "sarva" (all) is as before.

It refers to the mudrās of all five yoginīs and the counter-mudrās of the yogins toward them; the exposition—that is, the description—of these is what is being set forth, and since this is the chapter by which that is done, it is called such.
The nineteenth [chapter]:
when the letter *ta* is elided. || 19 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 19 ||
The twentieth chapter: The Ritual of the Hand-Gestures and Secret Signs of All Yoginīs.
Now, I shall explain another [matter], the secret sign (*chommaka*) of the left hand, by which one correctly recognizes a brother as well as a sister.
In the fifteenth [chapter], the code of syllables (*akṣarachommaka*) was taught;
here, however, he explains the code of hand gestures (*hastachommaka*), beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
"Now" (*atha*) means immediately after the explanation of the mudrās and counter-mudrās.
"Anyatamam" (one or another): the connection is that he will explain another form of syllable-signaling (*akṣarachommaka*) and hand-signaling (*hastachommaka*).
"But the left hand... and so forth.
Because it is to be accomplished with the left hand, it is the "left-hand code-signal" (*vāmahastachommaka*).
It should be understood that because [the right] is to be accomplished by striking, he will explain the "right-hand code-signal.
The alternative reading, "Henceforth I shall proclaim the characteristics of the *ḍākinīs*," is easily understood. || 1 ||
She who shows her left hand has said, "I salute you";
she who shows her ring finger has said, "I return your salutation. || 2 ||
She who strikes her belly signifies, "We are hungry";
she who shows her forehead signifies, "I have come from the sky. || 3 ||
She who inserts her finger into her mouth has said, "I am eating. She who licks her tongue has said, "I have eaten. || 4 ||
She who touches the knee has said, "I am weary";
she who touches the tip of a finger has said, "I have rested. || 5 ||
She who gnashes her teeth has said, "I shall devour you";
she who displays a frown has said, "I am bound. || 6 ||
She who shows the "teacher" (guru) mudrā has said, "I am liberated. She who shows a fist, to her one should show the *paṭṭiśa* [spear] mudrā. || 17 ||
To her who shows her hair, one should look back with a distorted expression;
to her who shows her nail, one should show a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
To her who shakes a limb, one should show two teeth;
to her who makes a hand strike against a hand with the hand, it is said that the offering (bali) should be consumed. || 9 ||
He states the secret convention (*chommaka*): "The left hand," and so forth.
The particle *tu* is used for emphasis.
"I salute" means "I pay homage"—this is what was said by her.
"Anāmikā" refers specifically to that of the left hand; "tu" (but/then) has the sense of specification.
Regarding the phrase "she who should strike": the word *tu* implies that she should strike both the belly and the tongue.
It should also be understood that she should display [these].
The phrase "it was said by her" is to be applied everywhere.
Regarding the expression "come from space," the words "it has been stated" are understood to follow.
"One should insert a finger" means it should be understood as "in the mouth"— this is the meaning of the word *tu*. "But she who touches the knee," etc.

In the case of a specific location: by coming from somewhere and touching her knee, it is implied by her statement, "I am tired," that she has arrived from a particular place; for the expression "I am tired" and so forth is based on a reference to a specific location.
And likewise, in the case of the feminine and masculine genders,
there is generally an equal expression regarding the vulva and so forth,
as in the phrase "the tip of the finger."

Regarding the phrase "one touches the tip of a finger with a finger," the meaning of the word *tu* (but/however) is stated as a distinction; therefore, in this context, that is precisely the intended meaning. "Garuda" refers to the tip of the nose.
One should display the left hand at the forehead in the shape of a hero’s turban-band, saying "paṭṭiśam" (the spear). Then,
[displaying it] at the hair, saying "keśān" (the hair).
In that context, it is due to the activity of the left hand. Regarding the phrase "and deformed":
the deformity consists in gazing with a frown.
From the word "and" (ca), the syllable HŪṂ is to be understood.
The display of the khaṭvāṅga is by means of the gesture of holding a khaṭvāṅga;
it is the convention for shaking one's limbs.
Here, there is an absence of activity with the left hand.
Having relied upon the two little fingers, one should place two vajra-fists in the two mouth-bindings;
these are the two fangs.
That which has two fangs is *dvidaṃṣṭrā*, the mudrā. "Bali" means that which is to be eaten; "bali" refers to worship (*pūjā*).
The meaning is that Bali is to be consumed;
the activity of the left hand alone is employed in all instances. || 2-9 ||
She who displays her right hand means "do exactly so";
she who touches her ear means "you must be brought under control. || 10 ||
She who scratches her nails with her nails—it is said that she is being led away as one dead. She who scratches the ground—it is said that "today I am entering the mandala. || 11 ||
She who touches her chin means: "My son must be protected. She who scratches the ground with her left big toe means: "My elders must be protected. (12)
