If she opens her eyes, it means "Do exactly so. If she licks her lips, it means "Sleep comfortably. || 13 ||
One should display all those who are messengers whatsoever. || 14 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the procedure for the conventions of the hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*) of all the yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 20.
He explains the *chommaka* (secret sign) of the right hand: "the right," and so forth, which is easy to understand. Regarding "the left," and so forth:
[it refers to] the thumb of the left hand.
"Two eyes" is the convention;
their function is in whatever manner [is appropriate].

Regarding the phrase "those which," etc., certain characteristics in the form of mudrās of the female messengers (dūtīs) have been described; the meaning is that when these are performed by the yoginīs, the male practitioners (yogins) should offer the counter-mudrās (pratimudrā).
"One should display all of them" means the counter-mudrās (pratimudrā).
This statement, being seized by the underlying intention (bhāva), must be understood specifically in this sense. || 10-14 ||
The word *sarva* (all) is a term denoting universality.

This is the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Hand-Signs and Secret Codes of All Yoginīs," because it is the chapter (*paṭala*) by which these hand-mudrās and secret codes (*saṅketa*) of all the yoginīs are prescribed.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 20.
The twenty-first chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Characteristics of the Mudrās of Vision.
Now, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the great secret of vision:
when a woman touches one’s crest-lock, one should display one’s head to her.
To her who shows her forehead, one should show the cheek;
to her who shows her tooth, one should show the tongue.
To her who shows her lips, one should show the chin;
to her who touches the neck, one should show the belly. || 3 ||
To her who shows her two hands, one should show the arm;
to her who shows the three joints of the neck, one should show the earth. || 4 ||
To her who shows her breasts, one should show the chin;
to her who shows her belly, one should show the navel. || 5 ||
To her who shows the secret [place], one should show the male organ;
to her who shows the thigh, one should show the anus.
To her who shows the knee, one should show the shank;
to her who shows the feet, one should show the soles. || 7 ||
Regarding the word "atha" (now): the connection is that immediately after the hand-gestures (*mudrā*), I shall proclaim the characteristics.
And as for what those [characteristics] of the yoginīs are like, he says: "the great secret of vision.
Because the yoginīs are great secrets for the sake of being seen, it is thus.
The *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) is the nature of touching the topknot (*śikhā*) and so forth.
Now, regarding the reading "atha ato hy aṅgamudrāṇām" found in some versions: here, "atha" is as explained previously.
The meaning of the word "iti" is "because they are known by their characteristics, therefore [they are called yoginīs].
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.
Those who possess the touching and so forth of the limbs are the *aṅgamudrā-yoginīs*.

"That which touches the crest" means that the mere touching of the crest— that is, the topknot— is the defining characteristic. Regarding "the head," the demonstration consists simply in the touching with the hand.
The same applies elsewhere as well:
one should display what has been shown.
Having opened the lips with the hand—
[referring to] "the tongue"— the tongue also [is to be treated] in the same manner.
"Trikaṭikā" refers to the joint connected to both buttocks. "Pṛthivī" refers to the earth.
The meaning is that one should display the earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśamudrā*).
"Secret" (*guhya*) refers to the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).
"Apāna" refers to the downward path.
"Tala" means the sole of the foot; this is easily understood. || 1-7 ||
To her who shows a finger, one should show a nail;
to her who shows the earth, one should show the sky. (8)
To her who shows the sky, one should show the sun;
to her who shows a river, one should show the ocean. || 9 ||
These are the limb-mudrās of the ḍākinīs; of this there is no doubt.
By displaying these constantly, the Guhyakas attain perfect vision. (10)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the mudrās of the limbs of vision, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
One should show the earth with the earth-touching mudrā alone;
its presentation in space is by means of a downward rotation,
and [the presentation] of the sun is by looking upward.
The river mudrā consists of the gesture of drawing a line in the space in the form of a river;
the ocean mudrā consists of both hands trembling in the space. 8–10.

The "Chapter on the Procedure for the Characteristics of the Gestures of the Limbs of Vision" refers to that by which the characteristics of the gestures of the limbs of vision are established; it is both that [procedure] and a chapter, thus: the twenty-first chapter on the procedure for the characteristics of the gestures of the limbs of vision.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 21.
The twenty-second chapter, on the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the special mudrās;
hereafter I shall explain the limb-mudrās according to the rule,
by which one specifically recognizes whether [the practitioner] is a brother or a sister.
If one shows a single finger, it means "Welcome. If one shows two fingers, it means "A very warm welcome. || 2 ||
These are proclaimed as the limb-mudrās of all the yoginīs.
One should know the eye-mudrā by means of two fingers forming a needle.
The practitioner of mantra should display that [mudrā] with the index finger slightly curled;
at that very moment, O Guhyaka, she comes under one's control for as long as life lasts.
"Beyond this" means after the description of the mudrās such as the touching of the crest-lock (śikhā) and so forth.
The connection is: "I shall now proclaim the limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrāḥ)."
Since they have already been mentioned, he asks, "What is the use of these? and replies with the word "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*).

This means that these are specifically the limb-seals (*aṅgamudrā*). Furthermore, this remains true even in the alternative reading: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the limb-seals according to the rule."
The word *atha* is used as a conjunction;
*ataḥ* is used in the sense of a specific reason;
and "a very warm welcome to the two fingers."
By showing the index and middle fingers [in this manner],
these are proclaimed as the limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrā) of all yoginīs.
The meaning is that the limb-mudrā is common to all yoginīs.

"Mudrās are proclaimed as the *potaṅgī* limb-mudrās"—in this alternative reading, the mudrās named *potaṅginī* are described: "One should know the eye-mudrā; with two fingers [forming] a needle, slightly bent is the index finger (*tarjanī*) of which; the yogi who displays that, the *guhyakas* come under his control at that very moment.

With the two—the thumb (*jyeṣṭhā*) and the index finger—located on both hands, having formed a needle (*sūcī*), while the remaining fingers are contracted, that mudrā in which the index finger is slightly bent is thus [described].
One should recognize that as the Netramudrā. "Of whom" means of whichever [yogin] the yogi should display this mudrā;
"he" means that those Guhyaka-yoginīs come under his control—this is the meaning. || 1–4 ||
The mudrā named Potangi is for as long as one lives, without a doubt; one should display the middle finger and likewise display the index finger of that [hand]. || 5 ||
To her who displays the ring finger, one should display the tongue;
to her who displays the *paṭṭiśa* weapon, one should display the trident.
To her who shows the head, one should show the earth;
to her who shows the earth, one should show the sky. || 7 ||
To her who displays a frown, one should show the hairline;
to her who shows her teeth, one should show the lip. || 8 ||
If she shows her neck, one should show her face;
if she shows her forehead, one should show her eyes. (9)
These are all the Yoginīs, whose limb-seals (aṅgamudrā) have been taught in sequence.
By displaying these correctly, the Guhyakas come to behold [the deity]. || 10 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the special mudrās, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"The mudrā named Potaṅginī [is to be held] for as long as one lives; of this there is no doubt.
This is the eye-mudrā known by the name Potaṅginī.
The plural designation in "these" and so forth is due to the connection with the various limbs of each individual Yoginī.
The *paṭṭiśa* is as before.
"One should show the head" means merely the showing of the head.
"The earth" has already been explained.
The faces are the face-mudrās.
These are all the yoginīs; they are taught as limb-mudrās because there is no distinction among all these yoginīs—they are indeed all limb-mudrās.
The meaning is "of all [these] indeed.
"By these" refers to the counter-seals (*pratimudrā*);
the third case ending is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And there is also a change of gender. 5-10.
That which prescribes the specific characteristics of the limb-seals (aṅgamudrā) is the "Chapter on the Specific Prescriptions for the Characteristics of the Limb-Seals";
thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 22.
The twenty-third chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Characteristics of the Special Signs and Mudrās of the Ḍākinīs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the ḍākinīs, by which the heroic brother may recognize the sister of heroes from afar.
Regarding the word "atha" (now): it signifies immediately after the description of the characteristics of the limb-mudrās (*aṅgamudrā*).

In the phrase "I shall fully explain," the term "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) is to be understood as continuing from the previous context, while the word "action" (*karman*) qualifies it as being distinct from what preceded.
Because the word *ataḥ* has a specific meaning, he asks:
"What is that specific characteristic? and replies: "It is known," and so forth. "Not far away" means without delay.
The phrase "of the heroes" (*vīrāṇām*) means "by the heroes" (*vīraiḥ*).
She is called the "sister of the heroes" (*vīrabhaginī*) because she can be understood only by heroes,
or because she bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon heroes.
Or because they share the same time-period.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the ḍākinīs; this reading is easy to understand. || 1 ||
He whose devoted consort is to be enjoyed by the heroes may perform the Yoga-saṃvara sacrifice, making the earth itself his support. || 2 ||
He explains how they become practiced and grant success with the words beginning "anuraktā" (devoted):
for that yogi whose consort (*samayinī*)—meaning a female practitioner (*yoginī*) who shares the same commitments (*samaya*)—is well-pleased, the earth shall be enjoyed by the hero (*vīra*).
A "hero" is a great warrior; she is "to be enjoyed by the hero" (*vīrabhogyā*) precisely because she belongs to him.
She is called Vasundharā because she "bears" (dhārayati) the "wealths" (vasūni), that is, the jewels;
the sense is that he enjoys the earth, filled with jewels, by treading upon it.
Furthermore, he says "the support," and so forth.
That by which happiness is supported is the *ādhāra* (support).
*Medas* is unctuousness (*sneha*). If she should be unctuous, then one should fix that *ḍākinī* as the support.
The connection is: "Having established the locus, one should worship the yoga-restraint (*yoga-saṃvara*).
Yoga consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*); the connection is that by this [yoga], one restrains (*saṃvṛṇoti*) the nature of duality.
The restraint (*saṃvara*) of yoga is *saṃyoga-saṃvara*; one should worship that, for it takes [the practitioner] up.

When, immediately after supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), the collection of sense-faculties withdraws from sense-objects and the mind rests upon mere bliss alone, then there is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
And thus, the withdrawal of the senses from sense-objects is "cessation" (*virama*).

The collective meaning is this: one takes hold of that very innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which constitutes the ultimate limit of that [bliss], whose nature is non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*), which is filled with unsurpassed happiness, and which is born from it.
Furthermore, although that [innate bliss] is perceived by means of stabilizing the bodhicitta within the jewel [of the sexual organ], it requires great instruction for its own realization.
For that purpose, one must propitiate the lotus feet of the venerable true guru alone.
Therefore, because it restrains that which consists of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), it is "restraint" (*saṃvara*); this is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
Through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), such knowledge arises from those very two.
It should be understood that wisdom and means, by which this priceless knowledge is born, are themselves like jewels. || 2 ||
For these ḍākinīs, there is a gaze that is contrary [to the norm], a deformity of the face, and the eternal bliss of the constant knitting of the eyebrows. (3)
He states the characteristics of the ḍākinī with the words "in reverse order" (*vilomena*).
Looking behind instead of looking ahead is "looking in reverse order.
He clarifies the deformity of her face as follows:
"An eternal bliss consisting of the knitting of eyebrows" means an eternally knitted brow. || 3 ||
Likewise, that which issues from a ḍākinī should be known as various and swift;
it should be recognized as having three curved and distorted lines arranged in a circular form.
"Thus, the manifold [reality] should be swiftly known as having emerged from the ḍākinī.
"Manifold" means it should be known swiftly and rapidly; "emerged from the ḍākinī" means a movement that is devoid of intentionality.
"Thus" (tathā) means being such as it is—that which is beyond the sphere of speech.
He states their various forms with the words "āvarta" and so forth.
Because they go in one way and then return again and again by another way, they are called *āvartas* (whirlpools);
hence they are distorted (*vikṛta*).
The three lines are of the nature of coming and going; such are the whirlpools.
Furthermore, he describes them as being circular because they have the form of coils. || 4 ||
One should indeed observe all the signs of a ḍākinī as she departs;
suddenly she turns back, her speech cut short by a broken word.
"Indeed, they are certainly departing.
He says that this is "the skillful observation of all characteristics": "one should observe every sign.
"They turn back suddenly."
The definition of "going" (gamana) is that even when the effect exists without a cause, it specifically ceases due to the attainment of an instruction.
"Previously shattered by the speech of words" means the shattering— that is, the breaking apart— of the utterance of former words.
The definition of a "verbal fault" (vacanalakṣaṇa) is that there is no connection between the preceding and following statements.
The reading "the meaningless statement is refuted" is easy to understand. || 5 ||
In that very same way, her voice was clearly manifest like the form of a thunderbolt, for her voice was always distinctly like the song of the cuckoo.
And in her house there shall be a sign: a mirror in the shape of a vajra;
while another form [of the sign] is a sword together with a mirror.
The banner, the spear, the casket, and the mirror are known as the eternal signs;
for these are the marks of the manifested form, even in its subtle state.
One endowed with these characteristics should be known as a supreme ḍākinī. || 9 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Special Signs and Mudrās of the Ḍākinīs," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"The shape of her [forehead] is clearly that of a vajra"—this is the characteristic of the forehead. "Her voice is clearly like the song of the cuckoo"—this is the characteristic of speech.
"And in her house," and so forth, describes the characteristic of the house.
And it is known that the banner and the spear are eternal;
"banner" refers to the *liṅga*, and she whose power (*śakti*) is that [banner] is thus described.
Regarding the characteristic of the mirror, it is a casket by means of a mirror.
The meaning is that "being in a state of union" (*saṃpuṭatva*) refers to constant observation by means of a mirror.
This is the definition of the mirror;
these are the signs to be known.
Thus he concludes.
Therefore, he says: "By these," and so forth.
To the question, "How does the yogi know those elements to be such? he replies: "For he has assumed a form."
Since he has mastered the nature of the signs of the Ḍākinīs,
he says "by these," and so forth;
[he is] "endowed" by way of necessity.
She is called "Supreme Ḍākinī" due to her possession of these specific characteristics; these are the marks of whichever single woman possesses them. (6–9)
The specific signs, such as the arrival of the ḍākinīs and so forth, are indeed characterized by the features of the mirror and other objects in the house of the mudrā.
Because they are characterized by these [signs], and because this chapter prescribes them, it is called the twenty-third chapter:
"The Chapter on the Procedure for the Signs and Characteristics of the Mudrās of the Ḍākinīs."
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 23.
The twenty-fourth chapter: The Procedure for the Language of All Conventions of the Fourfold Set.
Now, I shall further explain the secret signs (*chommaka*) in another language, by which a practitioner is recognized as a brother or sister; of this there is no doubt.
The word "atha" (now/then) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The syntactical connection is: "And I shall explain the *chommaka* in another language.
This is because the *akṣarachommaka* (the code of syllables) has already been taught in the fifteenth [chapter].
The word "tu" is a rhetorical ornament.
By which secret sign (*chommaka*) the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is known;
"brother" is an epithet for the practitioner, and "sister" refers to the yoginī.
The alternative reading, "they become speakers of other languages and users of gestures," is easily understood. || 1 ||
A *potaṅgī* is a salutation; a *pratipotaṅgī* is a return salutation.
*Gam* means "I am going";
*lum* means "I am coming."
The body is said to be the city;
it is said to be the gateway of the houses;
and it is the heart and the very cause of the heroes.
The killing is the Kaurava;
the bell is the pericarp;
the head is the bee.
The instrument is Vārāhakeśa;
the two ears are the auditory organs;
the place of nectar is the churning-stick.
The person is the assembly;
the *tilakas* are the *ḍākinīs*;
hell is the maṇḍala.
Such-and-such a cemetery;
Kāmpilyā is the gate;
Śvasana is the Brahmin.
The Kṣatriya is the enclosure;
the Vaiśya is cessation;
the Śūdra is the cruel.
Within is the Caṇḍāla;
the house is the finger-ring;
the Ḍākinī is the sister.
"Medaka" means water.
"Gṛhiṇī" refers to the mudrās.
"She touches her teeth with her tongue" means she is hungry.
"Thirst is the bearer of fragrance.
From what place does it come?
"The flower is the ray."
"Lamba" refers to laughter;
"dara" means a tooth;
"nirodha" means the obstruction of rain.
Satisfaction is consciousness;
Dhuryu is the exterior;
Meghā is fond of incense.
The mountain with its ridges;
the rivers, which are streams;
the parts of a finger.
The face is the mouth;
the *rājikā* is the tongue;
the *adanā* are the teeth.
The line is the banner; the meter is the garland;
the moving one is the wind.
The current carries away the boat;
the wild animal is a deer;
they move in a circle.
A level crossroads;
people [as] *phalguṣa*;
a great corpse [as] the great syllable (*mahākṣara*).
A large animal is a goat;
*nā* means a man;
*go* means a cow.
*Valīvardaḥ*:
"Ma" refers to the buffalo;
"bhā" refers to eating.
"Hā" refers to synonyms.
"Appakā" means a royal attendant or a king's man.
"Vanaṃ" means standing.
Touching the mouth signifies "it has been eaten"; touching the teeth signifies "it has been satisfied.
In some cases, *ho* is used as a synonym.
"Hrī" means shame. "Śūnya" means "there is not. "Sparśana" means "touching. Thus, "śūnyasparśane" means "when there is no [sexual] contact," [the meaning is] "do not engage in sexual intercourse.
"Ūru" means thigh. "Sparśana" means touching. Therefore, "ūrusparśane" means "when there is touching of the thighs," [the instruction is] "engage in sexual intercourse."
Likewise with the upward [gesture].
Thus, "there is nothing below" refers to the mudrās, the counter-mudrās, the secret signs (*chommaka*), and those called the heroes (*vīra*); this is the characteristic of the fourfold group. || 2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the chapter on the rules for the language of all conventions regarding the four aims. || 24 ||

"Potangy-abhivādana" means that the term *potaṅgī* is a designation for salutation (*abhivādana*). "Pratipotaṅgī" means a return salutation (*pratyabhivādana*). Thus, it refers to a return salutation.
Furthermore, there is a specific salutation:
by uttering the word "gamu," one indicates "I am going."
*Lumu* means arrival at the utterance of sound;
some say *lumbur*.
It is called a "city" because it has been stated that the body is a city; thus, it is a designation for the physical frame.
Regarding the statement "the *vaṭuka* of houses":
*vaṭuka* is a designation for a house.
In some readings, the word is *gṛhāṇām*.
"O friend, take the vessel"—
this is what is meant by "from the front," which applies everywhere;
[it means] "the heart of the heroes."
"Heart" (*hṛdaya*) is a designation for heroes.
In some readings, "the cause is the heart" (*kāraṇaṃ hṛdayam*), where "heart" refers to the cause.
The two particles *ca* and *eva* express conjunction and restriction, respectively.
"Kauravā means killing.
"Kauravā" is the name for killing;
the word *kauravā* is feminine in gender.
"Ghaṇṭā and karṇikā.
Karṇikā is a synonym for ghaṇṭā.
"Śiro'li" [is another term].
The term *ali* is designated as "head" (*śiras*). The term *varāhakeśa* is designated as "instrument" (*karaṇa*). Thus, the hair of a boar (*varāharoman*) is designated as an instrument.
"Śravaṇau" means "the two ears," according to the literal meaning.
"Amṛtasthāna" means "the churning-vessel";
the churning-vessel is so called because it is the place for extracting the nectar of immortality.
The word *samāgameti* is feminine in gender; it is a designation for a man. Regarding *tilakā ḍākinyā*, they are called *tilakā ḍākinīs*.
"Naraka" means "mandala";
"naraka" is a designation for the mandala.
"Amuka" refers to a cremation ground.
The term *śmaśāna* means "cemetery. *Kampilyā* is a word in the feminine gender, and it is also a designation for a gate.
"Breath is a Brahmin"— this is the designation "Brahmin.
"The enclosure-stick is a Kṣatriya"—
this is the designation "Kṣatriya."
"Abstinent is the Vaiśya" refers to the designation "Vaiśya.
"Cruel is the Śūdra" is according to the literal meaning.
"Antaścaṇḍala" is a name for a *caṇḍāla*;
"gṛhamaṅgulikā" is a designation for a house.
"Ḍākinī" and "sister" (bhaginī) are easy to understand. "Medaka-udaka" is a name for water.
"Housewife" refers to the *mudrās*.
"Housewife" is the designation for the *mudrās*.
Because she touches the teeth with the tongue, it is therefore called "food for the hungry."
The meaning is that he begs for food out of hunger. "Tṛṣṇā is the bearer of fragrance" is a designation for thirst.
"Whence is the coming?"—
the phrase "from such-and-such a place," ending in the fifth case, is established by its own nature;
this is the designation for the giving of a counter-gesture (*pratichommakadāna*).
*Kiraṇa* means *puṣpa*;
thus it is called *kiraṇa*. *Hāsya*, however, means *lamba*.
*Hasanam*, *hāsyam*, and *hāsaḥ* have the same meaning, namely "laughter.
The particle *tu* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*). *Daraḥ* means "a tooth."
The designation "tooth" is the name for rain;
the designation "obstruction" is the name for the cessation of rain.
"Satisfaction is cognition" means it is a designation for satisfaction. "The yoke-pole is outside" means... [it is a designation for being external].
The one situated outside is called Sthānā;
"Meghā is fond of incense" is easily understood.
"Sānu" is a name for a mountain;
"sarit" refers to rivers;
and "aṅgulyavayava" refers to the number of fingers.
"Vadana" means "mukha" (mouth) according to its true meaning;
"rājikā" is the name for the tongue (*jihvā*);
and "adanā" and "dara" are both synonymous with "danta" (tooth).
"Line" (paṅkti) means "banner" (dhvaja); thus it is called "banner. "Garland" (mālā) means "wreath" (mālā); thus it is called "wreath."
"The wind blows" is a designation for the wind;
"the current flows" is a designation for the current; "cattle and wild animals" [is a designation for those].
*Mṛgākhyā* (named after deer): from the word *paśu* (beast), there is elision of the nominative plural ending;
*yānti maṇḍalam iti* means it is called a *maṇḍala*, and it is also called a hell (*naraka*).
"Level crossroads" is a designation for a crossroads;
"trifling person" is a designation for a person.
The *liṅga* is not the primary factor;
it is the "great corpse" (*mahāśava*) and the "great syllable" (*mahākṣara*). This is a designation for the human corpse.
"Mahāpaśu" means a goat (*chāgala*). "Chāgala" is simply "goat," and that [goat] is the man.
Because the word "they say" (*āhuḥ*) is supplied as an ellipsis, the accusative case is used throughout.
Regarding "nā" and "naram": the word *nā* is feminine and denotes a person (*puruṣa*);
some say it is the word *nṛ*.
"Go" means a bull,
but it does not mean the referent of the word "gāvī" (cow).
"Ma" means a buffalo.
It is a partial form of the word *mahiṣa*.
*Bhā* means "eating";
this word is also feminine in gender.
Because of the statement, "He has eaten [it] as food," the words *hā* and *yā* are synonyms;
in some places, it is *yā*.
The word *rā* is also synonymous with "eating" and is feminine in gender, according to the statement: "They are to be taken away by [her] power. Thus, *appakā* means "in the presence of the king."
The meaning is "spy on the king's man," as seen in the expression "those stationed in small bodies.
[He] stands in the forest.
It is without case endings;
it is called the "abiding" (sthiti) of speech,
as in the expression "the touch of the mouth has been enjoyed."
The meaning is that the touch of the mouth indicates that one has eaten.
In the case of the touch of the teeth, it is easily understood that one is satiated.
"Ho" is a synonym.
"Kvacid" (in some cases) is a synonym for "satiated. Regarding "hrī" and "lajjā":
that which is called *hrī* occurs upon the touch of emptiness (*śūnya*).
"Engage in sexual intercourse"—this is easy to understand. Regarding the touching of the thighs:
"Thus [he says] with his hand raised."
The meaning is: "Do as you did previously.
Regarding the passage beginning with "below," etc., the sense is that from this point forward there are no mudrās, counter-mudrās (pratimudrās), nor secret signs (chommakas) by name. || 2 ||

*Ḍākinī*, *Lāmā*, *Khaṇḍarohā*, and *Rupiṇī*—these are the four classes (*caturvarga*). Their entire symbolic language (*sarvasaṅketabhāṣā*) consists of secret signs (*chommaka*), such as "ḍā" being known as "man," and so forth; that collection of letters and so on which has those [signs] as its primary elements is called "the entire symbolic language and secret signs of the four classes."

The term *vidhi* refers to those nine chapters (*paṭala*) in which the injunctions (*vidhi*) are prescribed; these are the injunctions concerning the four aims of life, all secret conventions, languages, gestures (*chomma*), and so forth.
This chapter is included within them.
In relation to the first chapter, it is the twenty-fourth.
In relation to the fifteen, even the tenth is included.
Therefore, having set aside the chapter on the procedure for transforming [the practitioner] into Herukī through union with the form of a donkey, the essential meaning of the ten chapters is shown.
This is another meaning of the phrase "in direct and reverse order."

The placement (*nyāsa*) of the yoginīs of the three wheels according to their respective locations, following the sequence beginning with the first day of the waxing moon (*śukla-pratipad*), by means of a counter-clockwise and clockwise rotation.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śrī-cakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The twenty-fifth chapter: The Procedure for the Concealment of All Root Mantras.

Now, for those beings of inferior inclination whose minds are shrouded by delusion and ignorance, [these mantras] are joined with the end of the eightfold concealment for the sake of all desired aims. (1)
The word "atha" (now/then) is used because of the doubt raised by the question: "What is the root mantra extracted previously like, and for what purpose was it concealed?
To this, he says "sarva... and so forth.
Therein, the connection is that "these mantras were concealed."
To the question "For whose sake were they concealed? he says: one who has desire—that is, longing—for objects in every way;
the meaning is: for the sake of one who seeks objects.
For by that [desire], it is easily accomplished (*susādhya*).
It is impossible to overcome; on the contrary, the implication is that one is under the influence of Māra.
To the question "How many are there?", he says: "Eight.
Because they consist of eight words, there are eight mantras.
The nominative plural ending is elided after the word *gopita*. It is joined with its own form by means of the suffix *-anta*.
One whose disposition (*āśaya*) is toward sentient beings of inferior inclination (*hīnādhimukti*) is thus [described].

The meaning is "also for the sake of the Śrāvaka. For he, desiring only his own self-taming and tranquility, possesses inferior resolve (*hīnādhimukti*). "Ignorance" refers to the mind and intellect of the false teachers; "for that purpose" means for the sake of protecting [the teachings] from those who are unworthy. By this, the intention is that they were concealed in order to guard them against the unrighteous. || 1 ||

There, this mantra was clearly spoken by the heroes and yoginīs: *Oṃ namaḥ bhagavate vīreśāya | mahākalpāgnisaṃnibhāya | jaṭāmakuṭotkaṭāya |* (Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lord, the Master of Heroes; who resembles the fire at the end of a great aeon; who is fierce with his crown of matted hair.)
To him whose mouth is fierce and terrifying with fangs as formidable as claws; to him resplendent with a thousand arms;
to him who wields the battle-axe, the noose, the raised trident, and the khaṭvāṅga staff.
To the one clad in tiger-skin garments;
to the one whose body is like a great smoky darkness:
*kara kara*, *kuru kuru*, *bandha bandha*, *trāsaya trāsaya*, *kṣobhaya kṣobhaya*, *hrauṃ hrauṃ* *hraḥ hraḥ* *pheṃ pheṃ* *phaṭ phaṭ*, *daha daha*, *paca paca*, *bhakṣa bhakṣa*!

O you who dangle garlands of fat, blood, and entrails! Seize, seize the serpent or snake dwelling in the seven netherworlds! Threaten, threaten! Drag, drag! Hrīṃ hrīṃ jñauṃ jñauṃ (jṇauṃ jṇauṃ) kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hīṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ kili kili sili sili hili hili dhili dhili hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! || 2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Concealment of All Root Mantras," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 25.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it refers to his own internal doubt.
As for the question, "How is it known that these eight words are concealed? he says: "They are clear," and so forth.
Although they are clear to the heroes (*vīras*) and yoginīs, they have not been spoken—that is, they have not been explicitly stated.
For a procedure devoid of a teacher indeed causes the loss of accomplishment in the Mantra system.
He states the mantras beginning with "Oṃ namaḥ" and so forth.
Because of their blending with the King of Mantras, there is concealment here of both the root mantra and [the king of mantras].
The application of the two syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*:
he says that this applies to both as well—*hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. || 2 ||
Therefore, he says "mūlamantra" and so forth.
*Mūlamantrasarvātmā* means that which has the nature of the whole of the root mantra; its *gopyam* (to be hidden) refers to concealment (*gopanam*).
The suffix *ṇyat* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

For in this extraction (*uddhāra*), the concealment of each individual syllable is prescribed; that by which or wherein it is done is the "chapter" (*paṭala*). Thus, it is the "Chapter on the Procedure for the Concealment of All [Syllables] of the Root Mantra.
This is due to the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*).
It is the twenty-fifth.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 25 ||
